COMPRISES THE Warrington 4- Nid-Clushire Examiner. pub- fished Saturday morning. The district covered by the Paper comprises many populous maxufatturing towns and villages, and a large agricultural tract. THE Earlestown and Newton Examiner,and Ashton, Golborne, and Haydock Reporter, published Friday afternoon. The district is in the heart of the Lancashire coal field.
THE St.Helens Examtner and Prescot Weekly News, published Friday afternoon. The district comprises the centre of the Mass, Chemical, and Watch Trades of the King- dom, Sm.

THE I?uncorn Examiner, published Saturday morn_ ing. It is the only Weekly Paper in the district. and offers the best and cheapest facilities to advertisers. THE Widnos Examiner, published Saturday morn- ing. Widnes contains the largest number of Chemical Works of any town in the kingdom, and is rapidly becoming an important centre of industry. Auction, Education, Wanted, To be Let, On Sale, Legal Pu lie Meeting. Sermon, Lecture, Bazaar, and other Public Notices, Advertisements (exceptParliamentary)are inserted in all the above papers at one charge. Bach of the above papers consists of 8 pages, 56 long and wide columns, each column admitting more matter than the columns of any other local paper--a fact deserving the atten tion of both advertisers and subscribers. Each Examiner, in addition to giving the local intelligence of the district, in which it circulates, contains the general news of the week.
Price of each Paper—ONE PENNI.

ALL snobs are todies, and toady to some other snobs. TE man who can't find anything to do is generally afraid he will. A MAN has a right to his opinions as long as he keeps them to himself. PENNSYLVANIA allows a man to marry his mother- in-law, but he doesn't. Disarm of the house—" if any one calls tell them lam not in." Servant of the period—" And what will I tell them if they don't call ?" A corrnuntiron writes :—"A send you a posthri- mus poem. If published, send me two copies." All right—addressed to which place? ONE of the cheerful things about the prevalence of hydrophobia is the statement that Ouida's nets' are dogs and that her villa at Florence is filled with

them. SISTERLY I Elder sister—" Oh, you fancy your- self very wise, I daresay, but I could give you a wrinkle or two I" Younger sister—" No doubt— and never miss them." EMPLOYER—" Don't you see what's on the door r Pat—V A bit ov paper, sur." Employer—" li says, 'Please shut the door.'" Pat—" Faith, I didn't hear it, sur." "Ma. JONES, you said you were connected with the fine arts; do you mean that you are a sculptor?' "No, sir, I don't scalp myself, but I furnish the atone to the man what does." TO say that a procession was three hours in pas- sing a given point dosen't necessarily show that it was a very long procession, since the given point might have been a public-house. Mits. ELBEnoN—"It seems to me Mrs. Exeter wears loud colours." Mr. Elberou—" Be charitable, nay dear. Perhaps you don't know that poor Mrs. Exeter is almost totally deaf." These modern inventions are well enough in their way, but it is quite useless to talk of them seriously to the autograph coltector who has sent a cleverly couched query to some public man, and receives a prompt answer written with a "type-writer." "Now," said the irate mother to her family of one boy and four girls, who bad been misbehaving themselves, "I am going to whip you all," and she seized on Jimmie to receive the first instalment of the chastisement. "Mother," Said Jimmie, "ladiel first, always." A LAWYER addressing a jury on a case proved by strong circumstantial evidence, repeated often that "ninety-nine guilty men should escape rather than that one innocent man butler." The Judge, in charging the jury, told them the "ninety-nine guilty had long since escaped." AT a recent meeting in Paris a speaker pathetic- ally inquired, "Why don't the great men of France bestir themselves? Why do they remain cold and nnmovtd at the calamities of our country 7 " "Be-
cause they are cast in bronze," shouted a sarcastic voice in the gallery.
As Irish soldier was stationed in a petty French town which had a very pretentious gate. A grocer, dilating on its grandeur, asked him what the Irih . would say if they possessed it. '"Faith, they'd
say," was his reply," we'll kape the big gate shut or the dirty little town will be after mania' out of It."
A LADY who had been teaching her four-year- . . _ . . . .

old the elements of arithmetic was astounded by his running in and propounding the following problem:—" Mamma, if you had three butterflies and each butterfly had a fly in his ear, how many butterflies would you have 7" The mother is still

on the problem. "•Wirxx I reckon up what it costs me for my Scotch shooting-box, and what I lose by neglecting my business," said a nouveau riche to a friend, "I find that every grouse I shoot costs me five pounds." "Then you can thank your stars that you only hit one in every ten that you shoot at," was the reply.

Mus. S., who had just lost her husband, was receiving a visit from a friend who tried to con- sole her. "Come, my dear, be reasonable. You must try to bear up under the grief." " Doni be alarmed," groans the afflicted one, wiping her eyes. "I am resigned at heart; only you know what my nerves are. It takes very little to upset them." there are no nice English pugs here." Father—" I see ; guess we have have got into the wrong place. But what magnificent watch dogs they have here! What breed is that handsome animal, Mr. De Brute?' Experienced Dealer—" He is a cross between a bull- dog and a tiger. That dog, sir, if given the word, would swallow a dude at one gulp." Father (quickly) I'll take him." '

GUEST.—" I want a room." Clerk—" Ton can't get tone, sir. All full." Guest—" Can't I get a bed, then?" Clerk—" Haven't got one in the house, sir." Guest—" Got one out of the house?" Clerk —"Oh, yes." Guest—" Well, I'll take that. Where is It?" Clerk —" Out in the back yard, sir. It's the strawberry bed. Don't roll over on the berries. Good-night, sir."

" JONES," said. one friend to another in my hear- ing not so long ago, "Jones, Mr. Robinson is dead, and I want you to sit up with the body to-night." "My dear Smith, I can't," the other said. "Oh, but you must. I counted on you certainly, as a personal friend, Smith. Come, consent." "I am

S-our friend, Smith; but can't. This is for Robinson. If it was your father, Smith, or if it was you, I would sit up with the body with the greatest plea- sure in the world—the greatest pleasure; but not for Robinson. No, sir!" COUNTRY editor (to new assistant)—" Mr. Smith, you write, 'An explosion in a Belgian coal mine last week caused the death of one hundred and thirty- seven men.' That is not an editorial paragraph, it is simply a statement of news." New assistant— " Yes, sir." Country editor-4 Such slipshod jour- nalism won't do. You should have added, "The sympathy of the whole world will be extended to the families of these unfortunate men,' or some- thing of that sort. Matters to be of an editorial nature must voice an opinion." A YOUNG lady belonging to one of our first families returned from a walk. Her mother, who is very strict with her, asked—" Where have you been ?" "I have just been taking a little fresh air." " Alone ?" "Alone!" Are you sure of it ?" "Of coarse I am; why do you ask?" "06, nothing at all, except when you went out you took with you a parasol) and you came home with a gentleman's cane in your hand." The young lady has taxon the matter to avizandum, and will bring in a verdict at an early date. A MEMBER of a Boston family was preparing to leave for Europe, and his wife, while packing his trunk, said, "Here is my picture; shall I put it in with the other things ? " " Yes, certainly; for I should feel lost without it. You know I take it

with me wherever I go." "Yes," replied the wife; but I don't believe you ever look at it! !' "Indeed I do, every night of my life ! " rejoined the loving spouse. The little velvet case was put into the trunk as usual. When the husband returned and the trunk was being unpacked by the happy couple, the wife found the case, and taking it out, said, "Well, tell me now—did you look at my picture while you were away 7 " " Look at it? Why it was the greatest comfort to me!" The wife opened the empty case and showed him that she had taken the picture out and packed only the case ; the likeness had remained at home in her own drawer. SAW Dogberry—" What ought Ito do? I told that Polish Jew to take one-and-sixpence for these drinks, and he got confused, and given me one-and- sixpence change out of a florin. Ought Ito tell him of his mistake, or devoutly spend the eighteen- pence elsewhere "1 Then spakc Outsider, who has qualified for the Mastership of the Roll—" If you look upon Vintners as a corporation, you can keep it; if as an individual you can't." Then said Dogberry —" if I say anything about it now, the poor man will get the boot for making a mistake. In the Interests of his wife and children, we'll have the other drinks somewhere else." So they adjourned. "My son," said a stern father to a seven year old hopeful, "I must discipline you. Your teacher said you were the worst boy in the school." "Well, papa," was the reply, "only yesterday she said I was just like my father."

Mr. William Black has taken Mr. Andrew Carnegie for the model of the hero of a story he is now writ- ing. Mr. Black was one of the party on Mr. Carne- gie's coach on the journey to the Highlands, when Miss Mary Anderson was one of his fellow-passen- gers.

Miss Annie Wilson Patterson,of Dublin, composer and conductor, is the only feminine doctor of music in the United Kingdom, with the exception of ,the Princess of Wales. Dr Patterson has written many capable poems and essays. She is director of the Dublin Choral Union, which • also possesses a well- known orchestra.

Harrogate is enjoying a brilliant season. Amongst the latest arrivals at the Northern Spa are the Countess of Carlisle (Castle Howard), who intends taking a course of waters ere proceeding to the Co- ntinent ; Lady Beaumont, the Hon. E. Bouverie and party, General and Mrs. Forthsyth, and the Lady ()skims (London), Lady and Miss Anson (Arundel), and Captain Kerr, V.C.

.7„ A funny thing has happened at my neighbour's house. In the kitchen was a cage with a favourite blackbird, which was well provided with seed and water. A grey rat cleverly opened the door and entered, no doubt, to feast on the seed. The black- bird had just time to fly away when the dOO% closed, and the rat, this time unable to open is, found himself in a big and unexpected trap, and met his death by drowning.

There is some hope among Mr. Robert Louis Ste- venson's friends that he may visit this country next summer in connection with the publication of his new novel "David Balfour." Dttring the later autumn and winter this story is to appear in serial form,but it will not be published as a book until the summer. Bournemouth was Stevenson's favourite tetreat, and if he comes here next summer he will, no doubt, make it his headquarters. Bournemouth, with its soft climate and its scent ot the pines, suits him better than any, other corner of our island.

The Duke of Devonshire's marriage to " Kim's " mother completes a romance which had its begin- ning when they were young people. Lord Harting- ton was to marry the beautiful young German girl, whose accomplishments were inferior only to her ambition. She mapped out a -oareer for him. The drawback was that it involved work, and Lord Hartington made a point of never doing what he could get others to do for him. This irritated the Count von Alten's daughter, and to punish him she married the late Duke of Manchester.

Nothing was to be seen in Lord Hartington's con- duct after this curious marriage to show that he felt the turn affairs had taken. He put on the mantle of indifference, but it was assumed. Soon he began to find his way to the Duchess of Manchester's receptions. Society noticed that on such occasions the Marquis and his old love were always together. There was not, however, a hint that their friendship was otherwise than platonic. The severest matrons declared that the duchess made a perfect wife to her husband, and the duke himself had unbounded confidence in her. The duchess became a great lady, at whose court all the young men who thought they had futures had to attend. Her advice was eagerly sought, and by none more eagerly than Lord Hart- ington,"who never took iv step in politics without first submitting it to her. It was owing to her healthy influence that the, bridegroom of Tuesday threw off his constitutionallethargy and played the part in affairs which is already history.

The vicissitudes of life in the colonies. Amongst the), rattlits of the Sydney unemplved was discov- ered the other day an ex-Cabinet Minister, who had taken,* prominent part aome twenty years ago in welcoming the Queen's second son to Australia. Drink was the cause of his downfall. For a long time past he has been a regular frequenter of the Sydney" doss-houses." In Melbourne not long ago an ex-Attorney-General of the colony and a mem- ber of one of the London inns was actually an un- successful applicant for the position of caretaker of a police-court.

Princess Aribert of Anhalt-Desseau, the daughter of Prince and Princess Christian,was(the Staatiirger Zeitung stares) presented by the English residents in the little duchy with a beautiful album containing sketches and other mementoes of her husband's family, on the occasion of the first anniversary of their wedding day. The deputation were warmly welcomed at the residence of the young princely couple, and afterwards invited to luncheon. The princess's name, it is said, has already become a household word among the working classes of her new country, and, like her mother, she takes great interest in philanthropic institutions.

Mr. John Jaffray is 'chief proprietor of the " Bir- thingliam Daily Post," a paper which ratted—not on Home Buie, for it approved of that—but on Chem- berlainism. Tears ago Mr. Jaffray built at his own expense a magnificent convalescent home just out- side Birming'.am, and got a prince and princess to open it. Most people expected that Mr. Jaffrey would then ba made a baronet, as it was supposed he desired to be. But Tories never miss an oppor- tunity of teaching the doctrine that benevolence is nothing and party service everything, and so Mr. Jaffray is to be made a baronet before the seals of office are delivered uq, and Sir John Will have the Qweet reflection that in his case " hart.," spells apos- tacy.

It cannot be too often innressel on the English public that the leading Welsh Nonconsformiat, are not the narrow Puritans that Tory imagination paints. Mr. Ellis was one of the most popular men of his year at Oxford, and has travelled greatly. He has a taste for poetry, and can grow sentimental over a Jacobite ballad, and few men can admire a landscape more. Mr. Lloyd George again is probably one of the few M.P.' s who have read right through Gibbon's" Decline and Fall" and Hallam s Constitutional Hist,ory. He also is so free from bigotry that he an follow with genuine interest all important movement in the Churches ot Eng- land and Rome, and reads weekly and enjoys the C'hurch Times.

Public speakers are not the only persons who misquote Scripture. Novelists and essayists, who have less excuse, have also been great offenders in this way. A writer in "Wit and Wisdom" points out that Carlyle makes a mistake as to Paul's cele- brated chapter in praise of charity; Dickens talks of a Second Epistle to the Eptiesians; Oujda puts into David's mouth the cry, "lpord, I believe; help Thou my unbelief." Professor Jowett, in th. "Essays and Reviews." confounds the pearl .of great price with the lost piece of silver, and. talks about sweeping the house to find it; while the Rev. C. C. Colton, author of "Lacon," speaks of the Poti- phars who tempt the poor young Josephs, and turns James's Epistle right about, making faith the soul of religion and works the body.

Talking about the Duke of York, it has probably been observed that Princess Victoria, the daughter of Princess Christian, has paid a somewhat lengthened visit, to Osborne, and dined on Nfonday night with the Queen, the Prince and Princess of Wales and Prince Christian, and Mr. Ritchie. This fact cannot help strengthening the rumours that point to the Princess as the future bride of the present neir to the crown. Everyone who has met Princess Christian in London or even" more on the Continent regard her as one of the most amiable and sensible of royalties. Princess Victoria is as clever as any of her family, and is believed to be very ambitious. She is not, perhaps, as inclined to familiarity with subjects as the Princess, and some think her more proud. To friends none can be more agreeable.

Prince Henry of Prussia, who celebrated his 30th birthday on Sunday, is to the German Emperor in some respects what the Duke of York was to the late Duke of Clarence. He is by far the cleverer and the more brilliant of the two brothers. tie has never been called upon, however, to act, as a Stimu- lus to the Emperor, but rather as a check on the im- petuosity of the latter. Ile is the cooler of the two, and the elder is fully conscious of the fact. Prince Henry is a hardworking prince. He has worked hard at the naval profession to which he belongs, and be has plunged deep into the myste- ries of government and statecraft, and has found time to become proficient in a private profession, so that if the trade of prince fails he can get a living for himself and his family by the other. Ills brother has treated him very liberally in the matter of money, and his future is provided for amply out of the Hohenzollern family fund. By his marriage with a Princess of Hesse, and a cous.in of his, he got hardly anything but a charming and devoted wife.

the Old nd New World as one ot most cultiva- ted awl het educated women in the world. She j was horn a Coleaville, N.J., being a daughter of Dr. James Freensan, and her childhood was spent on the banks of the Susquehanna, at Windsor. She re- ceived her early training at the academy there. ' When, at the time of her graduation, Michigan opened its doors to women, Miss Freeman became a pioneer in this experiment. She graduated in 1876, and taught for three years in the West, when the post of teacher of history atlWellesley.was offered her. In the following year she was asked tempor- arily to till the position of president, but her great popularity caused her to be unanimously elected at , the close of the term. In this post she worked for six years, resigning only to marry Professor Palmer, of Harvard. She now lives and continues to work in the cause of higher education in Cambridge, Mass. She will pnly visit Chicago periodically.

A "sepulchral voice answerld, "I ahm here Ike the late Mr. Pechter in the Duke's Motto; and then, from the curtain that was stretched across the lower end of the , shop, there emerged a tall lean head, the bald top of which somewhat re- sembled the phrenological specimen outside, minus the sticking-plaister, while its lanky fringe of black hair and lanky black whiskers looked as if all the starch was out of them. .This was the Ptofessor, and he wished to know what he could do for his caller.
"I shall be glad to be informed," said Mr. Griggs, "what your fee is for examining a person's head." _ _ .

"As reasonable as is possible sir," replied the tall lean man, "considering the care required. One florin for a verbal description of your most promi- nent qualities, or a more detailed description, four times the length, and in writing, for only twice the money." "Then I'll take twa shillingsworth," said Griggs. "If you please, sir," said Wagglesworth, "and I don't doubt I shall be able to give you satisfac- tion." Having passed behind tile curtain and removed his hat, our hero took a chair, and very soon felt two tall lean sets of fingers and thumbs prodding his cranium about ireall directions. Shortlyafter- wards the Professor opened his lanthorn jaws, and In a loud tone, as if he was addressing a large audience, thus began tb 'speak Your bump of language--" "Excuse me," interrupted Mr. Griggs, already growing very uncomfortable under -the ordeal, "I don't want to know anything about my bump of language. I'm rather pressed-for time. There are only four points on which I wish for information— I've noticed them marked on thebust—and I shall be obliged by your confining yourself to them. They are Conjugality, Combativeness, Self-esteem and Firmness." _ . . _

"Certainly, sir, as you desire," answered J. Octavius W., and once more lifted up his voice. "Your bump of conjugality is exceedingly well I developed, and shows that you are admirably fitted to be a family man. If I make so bold, sir, I should say, you are devotedly fond of your wife." , "I haven't one," put in Griggs. ; "Then you would be if you had," explained the Professor to his patient's great content. "Your bump of combativeness, also, is quite prominent, and tells me you would never submit to what you thought was wrong without making a hard fight _ font."

"Very good," said Griggs; "go on, pray." "Your bump of self-esteem is not so strongly marked, showing that you have a fair amount. of ' that quality, but not sufficient to permit it to degenerate into vanity." Quite right ; and now as to the firmness ?" "Your bump of firmness, sir, is as fully developed as your conjugality, indicating great stability of character and good power of self-control." "Thank you, Mr. Wegglesworth ; that will do nicely," said Griggis,-rhang ratidlrancli putting on his hat,. " Here s your fee; never mind the change. Good day to you." And depositing half a sovereign on the counter, Whurried out ofthe shop, leaving the Professor in a state of seioulchral chuckles at the success of his diplomatic diagnosis. The effect of this phrenological examination was momentous. The apprehensive bachelor appre- hended no longer; from alight hesitancy he passed to calm resolve. Ere nightfall he had made an offer of his heart and his hand; and within a few weeks Miss Judith Bootle adjured her single bloisneKlx,oaa,o.ol bcomunA Mr, Audrw Gri,=s. Tl4en the ability of the retired hardware trader to rule a very strong-minded wife was practically put to the test, and then (alas for the vanity of even professional opinions!) he was found wanting. Before three months had gone by, Andrew perceived that his lawful spouse wanystematically getting the better of him. So long as she had her own may, she PM Altogether ,sweet axed .affable,;, but if he ventured to oppose her wishes in anything, she soon made him see. she was not a woman to be trifled with; and, to' maintain peace in the house, he was driven to give in. When it came to a con- jugal duel, his courage was as evanescent as that of Bob Acres. She issued her orders, and he had to submit like a lamb. In their philanthropical, municipal, social-economical, or general reforming pursuits, Judith was the captain who gave the word of command, and Andrew was the humble sergeant who had submissively to see that it was .carried out, however he might disapprove of her tactics. He was abased; his gradual but sure self:. effacement preyed upon him, and he cursed the days wheii he was induced to put faith in a charla- tan and to entrust his happy liberty to the mercies of a determined wife. At last he could restrain his rage no longer, and, thirsting for revenge, he once again sought the street and the shop which he regarded as the source of all his woe. The Professor was at home, as before. "Oh ! you are here, are you?" shouted Mr. Griggs. " Still here, sir," answered the other; I' but I am leaving the town to-morrow." "And a good job too !" said Griggs, very ex- citedly. "If you'd stopped I'd have had you locked up, sir. I'll tell you what it Is, Waggles- worth, you're an impostor, sir, and I can prove it. Three months ago you felt my bumps, and all that you told me were lies—lies, sir. You told me I should be very fond of a wife if I had one. I've got one now, sir, and I likeNher less and less every day.,) "But that may be her fault," suggested Waggles- worth, soothingly. "No matter, sir. You told me I should never submit to what I thought wrong without making a hard fight for it. Now my wife is constantly Insisting on things I don't like, but I find I can't make any fight at all for it, sir." "I never meant that you should or would fight with your wife, sir, of course." "No matter. You told me I had a fair amount of seltestecm, That's another lie—it must have been, becalmed haven't a vestige Of it now, air." "I'm afraid things can't be going on well at home," observed poor J. Octavius W., on his defence. '
,--bleemedneacs,

"No, sir, confound you, they are not I" exclaimed • Griggs, whose face was flaming with passion. "And there's one more lie--you told me I had plenty of firmness, stability of character; if you asked my wife; air, she'd tell a different tale. And you said I had a good power of self-control ; do you dare say that now, sir?" And Mr. Griggs glared furiously. "I'm extremely sorry, I'm sure," softly answered the enemy ; "I really hoped I should have been able to give you satisfaction." " And so you shall, you infernal old humbug." This last remark led to a lively interchange of personalities, followed by an assztult and battery. Then the downtrodden Andrew rampe4l out of the shop, a smile of victory spreading promily over his countenance ; and on his homeward journey he consoled himself with the reflection that if he should unfortunately he compellea to take a back seat for the rest of his life, at any rate he was not the only sufferer. As for the tall lean Professor, for many. subsequent days he was feeling on his own cranium several new and prominent bumps, which were not to be found marked upon the model bust in the window, while he mournfully came to the conclusion that phrenology was not such a very complete or satisfactory science after all. JOHN NORMAN, in Hood's Annual.

div.p: A MUGFUEL 0' MISCHIEF.
BY GEORGE BULL. We laughed till we warched, . Though we knew t' a shame To play etch a trick On a simple owd dame,.
l'rolicsomc

" Just like Peggy," remarked John Hall; "aw knew her when hoo use' to live at Samlesbury, after her children, bed o getten wed. 1100 wer ter'ble peevish wi some OV us lads then ; an' we audn'd forged to pay her back for 't ; for we wer olez tor- rnentin' her. We played molly a scoot o' tricks on Peggy ; some on 'em ov a varra harmless sooart, an' others rayther to' bad. Aw recollect particular wedl one little dodge 'at we tried on one neet. Alisel' an' two moor lads lied bin peepin' an' tootin' abeawt welly an heawr, tryin to find sombry 'at we could mek a foo' on, when one e th' lads welly tumbled ' o'er a gred big mug just eawtside ov owd Peggy's door. There wer a " ceawnsel o' war" held then, to consider wod would be th' best thing to do wi th' mug. We pept through th' window an' could si nowt i' th' heawse. Then aw went off th' end an' looked up. Ther wer a window off th' end belongin' to th' bedroom 'at Peggy occupied, an' aw could see a bit ov a glimmer o' leet through th' blind o' this upstairs window. Yo see, th' beawse wer an owd thatched un, varra low; an' as th' greawnd rooase a decal at this end o' beawse id med th' window low too. At ony rate, id wer low enough for me to be able to reych id wi' a bit ov a stretch. Well, we seem' nowt deawnstairs, an' th' glimmer upstairs, we wer satisfied that th' owd dame bed gooan to bed; •so we soon Battled wod to do. We o spyled off th' corner, an' o' th' lads hid theirsels among th' trees except me an' Ned Humber. Ned wer th, tallest an' monliest lookin' lad among us, an' he carried th' mug ; while aw wer picked to do th' talkii,' because aw wer a bit ov a ventriloquist, an' could change ml voyce soo as nobry could tell mo th' dark.

Fost ov o aw gave a regular smart tap at th' I window wi' a bit ov a birch stick 'at aw bed, an' whitled at th' same time. We waited a bit, but nowt storred ; sooa then aw knocked harder an sheawted. Then there wer a bit on a din up aboon, and in abeawt a minnat th' middle part o' th' reavvm window wer shot up. Yo see it wer one o' these owd fashioned windows, i' three narrow parts, an' th' middle part wer only one 'at wer med to oppen. Ileawever, up id went, an, eawt popped Peggy's head. • Hello, theer ! Whoever are yo at's knockin' fooak up at this time o' th' fleet ?" hoo sheawted. " Nobry as'll hort yo," aw said, P ml best bass voyce, " but yo've bin verra near honing us, an' badly." " ileawever's thati ? "boo axed, "atc've done nowt at nobry aw'm sure." " Nowe," aw said, " but yo've left some'at eawt here 'at mut ha' brocken a leg—this gred mug. Ali friend here tumbled slap o'er id as he wer walkin' quately past yore door:. " Dear, dear o' me ! " boo said, "aw'd forgotten owt abeawt th' mug. Aw'm gradely sooary for yo, mayster. But iv yo'll wait till aw ged somerat on aw'll come deawn an' tek id in."
"0, never trouble 3 ersel, missis. Ali friend here's varra tall; iv 17°11 just shoot th' window a bit heigher he'll give id yo neaw, an' save yo o th' trouble o' commU' deawn."

'Yo're gradely obleegin'," boa said, " a deeal dif- ferent to some o' th' fooak abeawt here, for they treatin' nio scandalous, thad they do I Give iii mo up iv yo pleease." Ned slung th' mug up in a jiffy, an' Peggy geet howd o't. " Thank yo." boo said.—" 0, 3er welcome missis. Good fleet."

Vie wer welly reawnd th' corner as we spooak, but afoor Peggy could say "Good fleet" back ageean boo fun' hersel' in a fix, an' sheawted, "Here, maysters, here; come back a minnat, will yo! Th' mug's to' big to go through th' window." Of coourse, we wer suppooased to her gooan; but no fear! We wer just off th' corner, hearkenin'; an' th' other lads wer among th' trees watchin'. They said hoo wriggled an' twisted t,had mug i' o directions, an' we could hear her sheawtin' time after time for sninebry to come an' help net wi't. But nobry went; an' after wrigg:in' an' sheawtin' till boo wer booath ' mad ' and tired, boo 'vet id drop; an' bawled eawt as id smashed on th' floor. " Theer gooas another one an ninepence!"—From the " l'reston Guardian."

div.head: HORRORS OF WAR.
div.p: THE HORRORS OF WAR.
In the "London Quarterly Review" appears an interesting notice of Baron de Marbot's Memoirs, which gives incidentally some vivid pictures of what is actually meant. by "glorious victories."

AT THE BEIGE OF GENOA., The memorable seige of Genoa, the Austrians blockading the place• by land and the English by sea, lasted two months, during which the garrison and the inhabitants suffered fearfully from famine and typhus. 31arbot describes the privation and distress in the beleaguered city. The troops, privi- leged beyond the starving multitude, received a wretched ration of a quarter of a pound of hone- flesh, and a quarter of a pound of so-called bread, " a horrible compound of damaged flour, sawdust, starch, hair-powder, oatmeal, linseed, rancid nuts, and other nasty substances, to which a little solidity was given by the admixture of a small portion of cocoa." Little marvel that, out of 16,000 French- men, 10,000 died. One incident of the siege was the capture by the French of 3,000 Austrian grenadiers, who were sent on board the hulks in the harbour, and put upon half-rations—that is, half of the wretched allowance measured out to the French soldiers. The siege lastel fifteen days after this cap- ture, and Idarbot describes the unhappy Austrians as 'yelling with rage and hunger; at last, after having eaten their shoes, knapsacks, pouches, and ' even, according to rumour, the bodies of some of their comrades, they nearly all died of starvation.'l

THE HOLOCAUST HOLLABRUNN. " We were obliged to wait twenty-four hours at Hollabrunn, until the way was cleared through its streets destroyed by the lire, and still full of burn- ing planks, beams, and fragments of furniture. This unlucky town had been so completely burnt that we could not find a single house to take shelter in. During our compulsory stay in the place we were appalled by a horrible spectacle. The wounded, especially the Russians, had during the fight taken refuge in the houses, where they were soon over- taken by the fire. At the approach of this new danger all who were able to move had tied ; but many, wounded in the legs or otherwise severely injured, had been burnt alive under the ruins. Some had endeavoured to escape by crawling on the ground, but the fire had pursued them into the streets, and one might see thousands of the poor fellows half reduced to ashes ; some of them were even yet breathing. The corpses of the men and horses killed in the fight had also been roasted, so that from the unhappy town of Holle,brunn emanated a horrible and sickening odour of roasted flesh, perceptible at some leagues distance.' Four years later Marbot was again at this too-convenient battle spot, and, though the mischief eaused by the fire of 1805 was barely repaired,saw it again burnt, and again piled with dead and dying men in a halt- roasted state.

div.head: AFTER AUSTERLITZ.
div.p: AFTER AUSTERLITZ.

On December 2nd, 1805, the famous battle was fought near the village of Austerlitz, and Napoleon, now at the height of his successes, drove the van- quished Austrians and .Russians before him with terrible slaughter. "The greath part of the enemy, chiefly Russians,sought to pass over the ice. It was very thick, and olive or six thousand men, keeping some kind of order, had reached the middle of the Satchan Lake, When Napoleon, calling up the artil- lery ot his guartl, gave the order to ,fire on the ice. It broke at countless points, and a mighty cracking was heard. The water, oozing through the &sines, soon covered the floes,and we Barr thousands of Rus- sians, with their hones, gum", and wagons, slowly settle down into the depths.' It was a horribly ma- jestic spectacle, which I shall never forget. In an instant the surface of the lake was covered with everything that could swim. Men and horses strug- gled in the water amongst the floes. Some •-a very small number--euccoeded in saving themselves by the help of poles and ropes, which our soldiers reached to them from the shore,but the greater part were drowned."

div.head: lONIE,
div.p: lONIE,
PRIDE OF THE MILL
A THRILLING LOVE STORY. BY LAURA JEAN LIBBEY.
CHAPTER V.

div.head: STORMY SCENE-ARTHUR IS DISINHERITED.
div.p: A STORMY SCENE-ARTHUR IS DISINHERITED.

"Who is this girl whom you love—or think you do 7" said John Rochester, rising and facing his handsome young son. The words were spoken almost in a whisper, but they echoed like pealing thunder through the room, and seemed to repeat themselves over and over again during the moment of utter silence that ensued.

"Who or what is she 7" repeated the old million- aire. "Is she rich or poor? What is her name?" "Her name is lonie Lawrence, father," said Arthur, proudly. "She has no wealth, save a dower in her beauty, purity and goodness. She is the girl whom I perilled my own life to-day to rescue from death, She is employed in our mill." 'Mr. Rochester sinks back in his cushioned chair, and there is a look on his face that Arthur has never seen there before; his face is ghastly white, and his eyes have a glassy stare. ThMtvalm eyes of the son looked steadily down into the eyes ot the father, and he read a gathering storm in them. "How long has this thing been going ou 7 " cried Mr. Rochester, harshly, fixing his gaze keenly, steadily on his son's face. "How long have you been making love to this working girl, lonie Lawrence?"

Arthur's face flushed a deep red. "I have loved her from the first moment I saw her, father," he answered. "It was a case of 'love at first sight,' as the poets say, and I said to my- self, then and there: 'There is the only girl I will ever ask to be mine. I will win her, if I can, for my wile.'" "Your wife!" be gasped. "This girl whom I abhor from the bottom of my heart! I would rather see you lying dead at ray feet than married to lonic Lawrence. I will never give my consent to your marrying her while I live. Do you hear, sir? Never, while I live I" he thundered.
, "Do not be so hard upon me, father," pleaded the young man. "Remember, you were young once yourself, and loved my mother as I love lonic. I—"

" Your mother was an heiress and a senator's daughter; she was reared in the atmosphere of culture and refinement. She was a queen of society. I did not stoop to a misalliance with a wouking girl." "Love levels all ranks, father," said Arthur, raising his head proudly. "If she had been a nurse in the alms-house, you would have loved her, and would have been as anxious to marry her as though elle had been a society belle. For my sake—be- cause I love her—think more kindly of lonie. I—" "Stop I—stop right where you are I" foamed Mr. Rochester. "I will not hear it. This is but a mad infatuation you have for this girl. You must choose between us, Arthur," he went on, fiercely—" be- tween your father and his wealth or this working girl. Remember you are deciding your own fate. If you choose this girl, you shall never have one dollar of my money—do you hear, sir 7—not one dollar! I will make a bonfire of it first. You must give up that girl or me l" "Father l" cried the unhappy young man, "I can- not give lonie up—not even for your sake. Your wealth is as nothing when weighed against lonia's love. I cannot, and will not, give her up." "Do you dare defy me 2" cried John Rochester, fiercely. "I have not attempted to defy you, father," replied Arthur, slowly. "Do not put it in that way. I will respect your wishes in every other case but this, and try to follow them. In this case it is quite useless to attempt to persuade me. Every man should ruje his own love affair; no one has a right to interfere." "I have the right of a father over a son. I shall save you from yourself. You are not the first young man who has fallen in love with a pretty face, only to rue it bitterly six months after. You are infatu- ated with the girl now; a few weeks hence and you will wonder how you ever happened to make such a fool of yourself." _

"I am willing to stand all consequences. Love, such as I feel for lonie, is no boy's love. It is no romantic fancy, father; it is the deep, true love tbat comes to man hut once in a lifetime." "Have done with such nonsense 7" cried the old millionaire, hotly. "I stop pleading with you; now I demand that you have done with this love affair. Do you hear 2" Ask anything else and I will gladly do it," said Arthur, standing before him pale as death, but there was a fixed resolve in his blue, flashing eyes. "Do you know the consequences, then 7" "I cannot help the consequences," returned Arthur.
"You shall be disinherited before nightfall, cut off with one dollar. You are headstrong and you shall suffer for it."

"1 can work for our living, father," said the young man, bravely; "I am no better than other men who have had to face the world with nothing but a pair of hands and a resolute heart. Toil will be sweet when it is for lonie's sake." • "You shall have all the 'sweet toil' you want I" cried the irate old gentleman, " nothing will bring you to your senses more quickly. Go 1" Arthur took his hat and turned away. At the door he paused and turned back. "Why don't you go 7" thundered the old million- aire. "I am not a man to say one thing and mean another. Go 1 and never let me see your face again!" "There is one thing I must do before you leave me," said the old mill-owner, harshly. He went to the book-shelf, and took from it a large boot bound in calf; and Arthur saw it was the family register. Opening it, he laid it down on the table. -1
_ " Look 1" he said, pointing with his finger. "There Is the entry of my marriage with your mother. Here is your birth dated twenty-four years ago. Now see 1"
H b took a pen and dipped it in ink, and through the name of Arthur Rochester he drew a thick, black line with steady fingers. He wrote opposite to it:
"Dead to me r Then he closed the book and replaced it on the shelf.

"There is no more to be said or done," he con- tinued. "Go I" "Give me just one kind word, father," said Arthur. "Remember you are sending.. your only son out of your life forever. I cannot part from you so." "You have chosen; abide by your choice," re. tuned his father, bitterly; and Arthur turned away. In the corner outside he met his aunt.

"I have heard all, Arthur," she said. "Your father's voice was so loud and so angry. Oh, Arthur, for Heaven's sake I give up the girl, or your father will surely keep his word. "I cannot give up lonie," he replied. "I am going to her now to ask her to be my wife." "You have always been so petted, so worshipped. Arthur," she 'sobbed; "you have known every luxury, and never experienced one hardship—one want; bow can you struggle with laird poverty 7" "Other men do," he responded; "why should not I? I have been dependent upon my father's bounty too long. Every man, no matter if he is a rich man's son, should be put out to battle with the world's poverty for themselves—they will make better men." _ _

"That is all very well in theory, Arthur," sobbed his aunt, "but, oh, the experience is so bitter. I urge you—l plead with you to comply with your father's wishes." "You counsel me to be a traitor to my own heart, Aunt Hilda," he cried. "I always thought you too true a woman for that. Women are always tender of heart in viewing love affairs." "I gave up a lover at my father's command," she said, slowly. "And you have led a lonely, desolate enough existence of it; that broken love-dream has wrecked your life." She bowed her head with a bitter moan.

"It is true, Arthur," she whispered, huskily. "It has spoiled my life; but for my father, I might now have been a loved and happy wife. Ah, yes, love is best. I cannot counsel you to break your own heart and this poor girl's. The wealth of the world is nothing without love." The strangest part of the affair is, I have never breathed one word of my love to her," he said. "I am sure she loves me, though." "Few women could help it, my dear," replied his aunt; "you are so good and noble. When shall I see you again, Arthur ? " she asked, remembering that his father had forbidden him the house. He remembered it too. "I will write you, sending you my address," he replied, "and some time you will come and see me, and—and—" "I will come and see you—and lonie," she supple- mented—" will love her for your saVe. You know I
I am dependent upon my brother's bounty, Arthur," she said, sadly. "If I had a dollar of my own you should have it, in this the most trying hour of your life."

"I would not accept it," he answered, proudly; "never fear for me, aunt. I shall not sink." "Love is a great buoyer up of youthful hopes," she said, sadly. "I pray all may go well with you, my boy." He kissed her in his warm, impulsive fashion, and turned away when he reached the door, he re- turned and kissed her again. "It is not luoky to turn back like that, Arthur," she said, smiling through her tears. "Good-bye, aunt," he said; " you, at least, will miss me." And, little dreaming of the grievous disappoint- ment awaiting him—a disappointment which nearly unmanned him--Arthur Rochester hurried away to lonie's humble home.
---• CHAPTER VI.

ARTHUR ROCHESTER'S BITTER DISAPPOINTMENT. For the first time in Arthur Rochester's life, his heart beat strangely as he pulled the bell at the door of lonie's home—a lover's heart is always more or less in S state of doubt, hope and fear. Mrs. Gregory answered the summons, and her face lighted up when she saw who their visitor was, but she was greatly flustered at such a grand gentle- man as Mr. Rochester coming to their plain, humble home.
All in a flutter she took his card into the inner room to lonie. _ __

"He looks so kind and so noble," commented Mrs. Gregory, as she helped lonie on with a new frill of lace and a bit of ribbon about the slender neck. "You ought to have heard how nice he talked to me to put me at my ease. He isn't much like that other one—the dude, who looks around as if there was nothing good enough for him, and makes my blood boil when he dusts off my chairs with his silk hand- kerchief before he ventures to sit down."

"You are greatly prejudiced against him, poor fellow," said lonie, with a blush • but in a pained tone of voice adding, gently: "I hope you will like Mr. Lyons for my sake, if not for his own. A truer gentleman never lived." "All that glitters is not gold," insisted Mrs. Greg- ory. "Having the appearance of a fine gentleman don't make one. I'd give more for Mr. Rochester's little finger, as the old saying goes, than for Mr. Frank Lyons's whole body. I can't help my opinion, Miss lonie."

With a glance full of reproachful gravity, bole quitted the room walking slowly into the meagerly furnished apartment which Mrs. Gregory designated as her parlour. Arthur Rochester rose quickly, his fair face flush- ing, and came forward with extended hands to meet her.

Tears came into lonie's eyes. For a moment sobs choked her utterance. "I was trying to find words eloquent enough to thank you for what you have done for me, Mr. Rochester," she said, " and they fail me. I owe my life to you, and while that life lasts I shall be grateful to you." He raised the little white hands to his lips and kissed them, his whole soul in a tumult of gladness.

His heart seemed full. He found it difficult to give his thoughts the power of expression in words. When be was by himself words had risen in a tor- rent to his lips. He had thought of a thousand things that be wished to say to her. But now that he was in her presence he was mute. Yet this silence that had fallen upon him was more eloquent than language. He recovered himself and looked earnestly down Into the lovely young face. "Tell me one thing, lonie,—Miss Lawrence!" he said, huskily. "Do I owe all your favour to the fact that I saved your life 7" The little hands trembled in his, and the sweet face flushed under his searching gaze. She did not answer.
"You most tell me," he went on. "I must know. Do you like me simply from that one fact 7" "No," she answered ; "not altogether for that." . .
"Take care, lonie," fie said, "that you make no mistake. Your words are life or death to me."

She drew back with startled pallor. "Do you not know—can you not understand— lonie ?" he said, in a low, husky voice. "Have you not seen from the very first that I love you? Some men might tell their love in the beautiful language of the poets; but the truest hearts do not always find eloquent language in a moment like this. I cannot—my heart is too full. I can only tell you in plain but heartfelt words. bole—l love you, with all the strength of my heart, and I want you for my wife. Some men have had many loves," he went on. "I have had none save yourself. No other face has been imaged on my heart. I have never said to any woman before—l love you. Now, lonie, what have you to say to me ?" he asked, hus- kily, bending over her so near that his fair, cluster- ing hair touched the dark, curly rings that lay in soft love-locks on her white forehead—so near that the perfume of the two pale pink blossoms she wore reached him, She was silent from sheer excess of amazement; she almost believed her senses were playing her some strange trick. Mr. Rocliester—loved—her 1 And she—ah 1 she revered- him—she honoured him —her gratitude to him was boundless ; but this was not love. She drew her little hand away from him and raised those lovely, dark, childish eyes, running over with tears, to his pale face. "Oh, believe me, I would have saved you this, Mr. Rochester," she sobbed, "if I had but known— if I had but dreamed—for, oh I it breaks my heart to give you pain—you, who have been so good to me—to whom I owe my very life." He looked at her in horrible fear, a fear which drove the colour from his face. His heart heat; he would have faced death in any other form more willingly than from the Ups of this girl whom he loved so well—for it was death if she did not love him—death to his hopes, his happiness, and his future peace. "Let me know the truth at once, lonie," he said. " Suspense is killing me. Is my great, worshipful love in vain? Do you not care for me?"

"Not in the way you—you would have me, Mr. Rochester," she faltered. "Oh, believe me, I would love you if I could." "I know it is sudden," he answered, his fair, handsome face flushing and paling, "and the idea has startled you; but will you give me the hope that I may win you in time if I try 7" Her head drooped, and she shrank back from his outstretched hand. Again a great wave of fear swept over him. He came nearer to her, laying his white hand on the dark, brown, curly head. "Tell me one thing, bole," he said. "I have no rival in attempting to win you, have I? You do not love any one else?" She raised her head, her eyes heavy with tears, her lips quivering piteously. "I must answer you truthfully," she said. "I do love another, and as deeply—as—as—you—love me."

He stood quite still before her. No word, no moan, no sigh, escaped his lips to show how deeply the iron had entered his soul. This was an emer- gency he had not foreseen, and had not prepared himself for it. ---

He bowed his head, saying, huskily: " If it is decreed that I should not have her love, bitterly hard though it is, I will bow to Heaven's will. lonie, I will say good-bye to you," he went On, "for lam going away. lam only human, and I cannot mike such a martyr of myself as to remain and see you happy with another. I will not forget you. I have loved—l do love you too dearly for that. lam going to give myself up to hard work that I may not have time to think anegrieve in secret over my great loss. Let me say this to you in parting, lonic, he resumed. "I shall never love another. You are my first love. Ycu will be my only and my last one. If the hour ever come when you need a good, true friend, remember me--know that I would give my life itself to serve you. If you called to me, though I were at the other end of the world. I Would come at your bidding. Farewell, lonie, my lost love. May you be happy with the man who has won your love. Say one word of comfort to me— that I shall remember all my lonely life." "I —I do not know what to say," she sobbed. "Say 'Good-bye, Arthur. God bless you,'" he said. "Let me hear the name from your lips just once." _

-"Good-bye, Arthur. May Ood bless and keep you always," she repeated. The next moment he was gone. "If I had not met and learned to love Frank Lyons, I might in time have learned to care for Mr. Rochester," she sobbed. "He is so good, so noble. Ah, why did Heaven let bim care for me—to be refused r she murmured. "it was a thousand pities." How her heart ached for him with a strange, dull pain, which she did not quite under- stand then. " But do I love Mr. Lyons so t:ery much 9" she asked herself, in girlish doubt. "Some- times I think so, and again I—l am not quite sure of my own heart." Only that afternoon, when be had called, Frank Lyons had asked her to marry him. "I do not ask you for your answer now," he had said, carelessly. "'the nest time you see me will do (mite as wall. lonia

_ !row strangely formal and forced (now that she came to look at it) that proposal of marriage seemed to this! She went straight to Mrs. Gregory and laid her head down on her bosom. "The door was open when you passed the parlor," she said, in a low voice. "Did you hear— what—what—Mr. Rochester was saying 7" The good woman drew back in high dudgeon. "Do you think I'd be so mean as to spy on you, Miss lonie 7" she said. "Do you imagine I'd do such a despicable thing as to listen 7' "Mr. Rochester asked me to be his wife," said lonie, in a low, husky, quivering voice. A cry of delight broke from Mrs. Gregory's lips. "Oh, child, I can hardly believe it I" she gasped. "I always thought, though, that there was some- thing great in store for you—that you was meant to be a great lady, and live in your mansion, ' and have servants and horses and carriages, and "I refused lelr. Rochester," lonie says, in a low voice. The plate Mrs. Gregory holds falls to the floor with a crash. "You—refused—Mr. Rochester I" she gasps. " I
cannot believe it 1" "It is true," said lonie, gently. " I refused hira because I am going to marry Mr. Lyons, who ia Coming here to-morrow for his answer.' (To be continued.)

"Say, Joe, whar are you off to now? Gob' to tumble into the river agin, I reckon, and spile all your clothes ! You can't be happy without You go a-makin' trouble some way or another ; and then, 0' course, I hey to come and fix it. It's a niarcy your sister there ain't like you, or I'd be Orin. clean crazy." So said—or rather, screamed—a tall, lean, sun- burnt woman who was standing at the door of a farm-house on one of the lower slopes of a range of rocky hills in the north'of New England, in the full blaze of the bright morning sunshine. But the sturdy little seven-year-old curly-head to whom she spoke looked up in his mother's face with a tright, fear- less smile, knowing well that, however she might scold, she was really quite as fond of him as he was of her. " We're coin' to watch father and the men refill', ing, mother, Nellie and me are. We can go, cant we? Nellie wants to see 'em at it, and Bin going r° help if I can. See, ,'ve got a real sickle o' n:IY own !" And the tiny farmer flourished his bright little weapon over his head till it flashed in the sun like a sword. " Well now, if ever r cried the housewife, half pleased and half vexed. •• Do you want to cut your hand or your foot off, you Young mischief ?' Jist you go and put that thing right away whar you kot it." "Oh do let me take it along, mother!' pleaded the boy earnestly. " A man ain't of no account in the field without he's got his tools with him, Pn know." And his mother—who was secretly very proud of this active and daring son of hers, and rather en- joyed this new proof of his genuis—ended by con- senting to let him take the coveted sickle along with him. Overjoyed at this unlooked-for granting of their wish, the two children scampered off as fast as their slender brown limbs could carry the distant harvest-field, where the busy sickleB could be seen flashing in the sunlight, and the rip° corn falling in handfuls. But, quickly though they went, they never reached it. them toward Hardly had they got fifty yards from the door when a floating shadow, like the shade cast by a: passing wreath of clouds, fell across their path, and looking up, they saw, far above their heads, a broad black patch, standing out like a blot agaitlt the clear rich blue of the sunlit sky. 117 " Look, Nellie ! that's an eagle up yonder—seo • cried the boy excitedly, as he halted for a tuomentf to watch this pirate of the air on his cruise o_ destructio,n. _THE NEW MINISTRY.

The " Court Circular " of Saturday contained the fol- lowing :—" The Marquess of Salisbury, KG., arrived at Osborne and had an audience of her Majesty, when he tendered his resignation, which the Queen accepted with much regret. The Marquess of Salisbury has left Osborne."

Mr. Gladstone left London on Monday on his visit to the Queen at Osborne. Not only at Waterloo Station, but at many places on the jouriaey, and particularly at Portsmouth, he was loudly cheered. He embarked on the Royal yacht, Alberta, crossed to Cowes, and drove tO Osborne, where he had audience of her Majesty. He left Osborne about ten o'clock on Tuesday morning, and drove to Cowes, where he embarked with Sir Algernon West on board the Royal yacht Elfin. The right hon. gentleman was warmly greeted lsy the public, and the cheers were continued as the Elfin steamed out of the harbour for Southampton. On arriving at Southampton Mr. Gladstone was enthusiastically received. He ap- ?eared in excellent health, and stated that he felt not the eleast fatigued by his journey. He left by the 11.20 train for London.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

The special committee of the Manchester City Council charged with the consideration of the affairs of the Man. chester Ship Canal presented a report to the City Coun- cil on Wednesday. The report gives detailed statements concerning the financial position of the company, and the estimated cost of the works and equipment to open the canal for traffic to Manchester. The estimate of the engineers is that from the Ist June last until the 31st Dec., 1893—the date at which it is expected the canal will be completed—the total oetlay on the works being £2,183,433. They add that this estimate does not pro- vide for any contingencies such as damage by floods, other than a sum of £85,000 which is included in the amount of the total outlay. It appears from this that, in addition to the loan of £3,000,000 arranged by the cor- poration, the sum of £1,489,282 will be required for the completion of the canal. Sir John Harwood, in a report, of which an abstract has already appeared, recounts the proceedings which led to the City Council cousenting to a loan of three millions, and the subsequent action of the Council. The report then proceeds as follows :—" At the time the Snip Canal Company first approached the Corporation they were doing the work themselves, under the direction of a committee composed of directors elected by the share- holders. Upon investigation by the Corporation directors this course did not commend itself to them, it being open to very numerous and serious objections. To alter a policy of this kind, which had been inaugurated and carried on by the old Board, required very considerable tact and forbearance. Ultimately, however, that policy has been reversed as far as practicable, and this has been done without any very serious misunderstanding, but it has nevertheless entailed the devotion of much time and patient consideration upon the part of the executive committee, who had many difficulties to contend with. In the first place, the ground had been broken all along the line of works ; at some points the cutting was only just commenced, and at others half finished, so that the measuring up of the work remained to be done, and the preparation of specifications with a view to letting by tender, was a task of great magni- tude, and in fact prevented the executive committee obtaining tenders to the extent they would have liked. The response to the advertisements for tenders was very limited, and it is probable that if tenders had been in- vited upon the death of Mr. Walker there would have been a much better response on the part of capable and responsible contractors. Owing to these circumstances the executive committee have had to continue a large portion of the work under their own supervision, no tender being obtainable which they would have been justified in accepting. The Corporation representatives attended the annual meeting of the Ship Canal Company held in August, 1891, when it was stated by the chairman and others that the length of canal between Eastham and the Weaver Pool had been opened for traffic. We are afraid that this announcement gave the impression to a large number of the shareholders and the public that this length was finished ; but that was not the case, as pointed out to the Board at the time. Subsequently to the water being let into the cutting dredging has been going on, and since the annual meeting work which was estimated in September at only £15,979 has cost £3l, 907 15s. 2d. to the 31st May, 1892, or 3s. per cubic yard instead of is. 6d. as per schedule, and it is now estimated that there still remains to be done in this length dredging to the extent of £15,000. The un- reliability of these estimates is a source of continual anxiety to your representatives on the Board. One of the first things that impressed us, as representing the Corporation, was the enormous quantity of work that has beers done, which cannot possibly be called into requisition or earn anything for a very considerable period, and will be a dead weight upon the earning por- tion for a long time. Another point that struck us was the unnecessarily expensive character of some of the materials used, the coping of the docks being granite : whereas if mill-stone grit had been used it would have answered the purpose equally well, and about £60,000 would have been saved. This is only one instance, but such cases could be largely extended. The hydraulic power installation is of a most elaborate character. The amount of Armstrong's tender was £78,598. For a work of this magnitude we think that competitive tenders should have been sought. This contract was settled before the Corporation were repre- sented on the Board. A great many things might have remained over until the canal was earning money, and additions could have been made from time to time out of the profits. When the trade required extended accom- modation money would have been readily obtainable for the purpose. Of course, we are aware that when a thing is done it should be well done, but then this maxim must be taken in reason, and regard must be had to the means of the person carrying it out. A considerable amount of the present trouble must be attributed to this mistake. Having now dealt, necessarily very briefly, with the subject of our proceedings up to the I present time, we will proceed to the very important 4, question of the future operations necessary before the canal can be opened for traffic to Manchester, and the financial questions involved therein. The amount of work still remaining to be executed is very I considerable, including as it does the greater portion of the four contracts lately let, the Runcorn section,a very large amount of dredging, and other works. The en- gineers have been for some time preparing their esti- mates with a view to ascertaining what amount of money in addition to the £3,000,000 would be required to open the canal to Manchester. They have had this under their careful consideration, and the revised esti- mate was only furnished on Monday last ; and it would therefore, in the opinion of your representatives, not be desirable to set out the various items in the present report. After deducting works which may be deferred, the amount required in addition to the available resources of the company is (so far as can be at present ascertain- ed), in round figures, a million soda quarter. Further sums will, no doubt,have to be added to the above esti- mates to meet reasonable contingencies and other items. such as awards under arbitration. Sm. After the state- ments that have been made from time to time and proved so unreliable in regard to the cost to finish the canal, it will be for the consultative committee to determine whether they would think it desirable to have any fur- ther professional opinion upon the detailed estimates when submitted. The question naturally arises as to the action to be taken by the Corporation in regard to future advances and the obtaining of further statutory powers. This subject, we think, is one which should receive attention upon the part of the consultative com- mittee (which has recently been enlarged), and it will be our endeavour to bring before them all the information in our power which may be of use to them in the consi- deration of this important question." The report is signed by Sir J. .1. Harwood, Aldermen John Mark and S. Chesters Thompson, and Councillor J. W. Sou thern,directors of the Corporation upon the Man- chester Ship Canal. The committee, upon the presenta- tion of the report, resolved :—" That this Committee approve the report of the corporation directors upon the executive committee of the Manchester Ship Canal now submitted, and in presenting the same to the City Coun- cil, desire to express the firm opinion that, the Council should take the measures necessary to enable them to complete the undertaking." The Council authorised the payment of the balance the loan of three millions sterling to the Ship Canal Company. The discussion on the report was deferred till the next meeting of the Council, after the half-yearly meeting of the shareholders of the Company has been held.

div.head: HORRIBLE AFFAIR AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: HORRIBLE AFFAIR AT ST. HELENS.
A CHILD WOItRIEDBY A PIG.

On Tuesday afternoon, Mrs. Fairclough, wife of a labourer living in Back College-st., St. Helens, left her house for the purpose of getting meat for the pigs, leaving her child Alice, aged five months in the cradle. While away, one of the pigs by some means got into the house, pulled the child out of the cradle, and commenced to worry it. The child, who when found was terribly mutilated, the face being nearly eaten away, Is not expected to re- cover.
RIIYMES FOR THE PEOPLE.

NO. 3. CHUKCII AND STATE. 0 blest were the de vs when the priest and the squire, Could order all things to their own heart's desire. And the people their garments would kiss ; Then, duly exalted, the Church and the Crown, On the rabble below would deign to look down, And descry in their ignorance bliss ! Mere hewers of wood were our ancestors then, The poorest of serfs, most benighted of men,

'And their living a series of doles : For minions of State, with unscrupulous hands, Laid hold on themselves, and their houses and lands, While the parsons neglected their souls. But the Church that was formed by kingly self-will, No longer, alas ! can its functions For the spirit of Truth is abroad : And the squire and the priest, co-workers of old, In every direction are losing their hold, And the Crown is no longer a God. The will of the king is no longer supreme His pretensions to rule are nought but a dream, For true knowledge is spreading around : Despoiled and opprest in the centuries past, The people will be their own rulers at last, And for kingcraft no place will be found. The Nazarene's faith is no council-made creed, No bundle of theses for schoolmen to "'read," • And in orthodox fashion explain : 'Tis the Spirit of God implanted in souls, A Power that enlightens, directs and controls, And preserves them from idols profane. The Nazarene's Church is no thing of the State, No sacred preserve for the rich and the great, Its disciples are lowly and few : They are not of the world, though in it they move, And their thoughts and their hopes all centre above, In the One who is faithful and true. It has no domain for feminine Popes, No thrones for the bishops in mitres and copes, For the Saviour Himself is its Head : Its members are taught by His Spirit alone, And not by the hirelings ordained by the throne, Who usurp the priest's office for bread. Then pull off the mitres and clerical gowns, Such garments are suitable only for clowns, And they puff up the clergy with pride: Next sweep the imposture of tithe-rents away, And let the Apostles no longer have pay, For the Lord for His own will provide. LOCAL GOVERNMENT INQUIRY AT WIDNES.
PRIVATE AND PUBLIC IMPROVEIIENTS.

Mr. T. H. Tulloch, C. 0., an inspector of the Local Government Board, on Tuesday morning, held at Widnes Town Hall, an inquiry into an application for sanction for the Local Board to borrow .C 12,000 for a term of 10 years for the purpose of carrying out certain works of public and private improve- ments in the district. Vie only member of the Local Board present was Mr. J. Taylor, and the officials in attendance were Messrs. 11. S. Oppen- heim (law clerL), T. Craig (assistant law clerk), J. S. Sinclair (surveyor), S. Hoyle (accountant), Dr. O'Keeffe (medical officer), and W. Lowe (nuisance inspector), Mr. C. H. Lewin, solicitor, appeat•ed for about ten owners of property in East-st.,Edward-st. and Warrington-road, in opposition to the scheme of private improvements; viz.—Messra. J. Taylor, Jno. Hunt, J. Edwardson, John Wilson, John Valentine, Thomas Ireland, Edward Ireland,Edward Hardman, Robert Riley, and Mrs. Rachael Brown. Mr. J. Randle and Mr. T. Higginson were present. It was decided to deal with the application for the loan of £6,000 for the making and sewering of a number of streets in various parts of the town.— Mr. Oppenheim said it was decided to borrow money on the security of the general district rates, and the main object of the loan was to give the owners of property abutting on the streets to be made and sewered time in which to repay the .Board the cost of the work. This method was a great convenience to owners of property, and had worked satisfactorily in the past, and the sanction of the Local Government Board had been granted to precisely similar proposals in the past. The whole of the streets mentioned in the applica- tion had not been levelled.sewered.or metalled,and there were houses in the whole of the streets. The customary orders had been issued to the owners to do the work,and the work had not been done.—The Surveyor proved serving the orders and notices and produced the plans. —The Accountant said the assessable value of the dis- trict was £122,907 and the outstanding debt was £65,067.—Mr. Lewin cross-examined the surveyor at considerable length to show that East-street and Edward street were adequately sewered and that the streets were level and in good condition, but the surveyor held a different opinion.—The Clerk said that inquiry was no for discussing the desirability of the work at all but of the application of a loan.—The Inspector said he would rathei hear what Mr. Lewin had to say, and the cross-examination was continued. Afterwards Mr. Lewin commenced to call the owners whom he represented to protest against the expenditure of money on East-st. and Edward-st.—Mr. Oppenheina said if the Local Government Board refused to sanction this loan the officers of the Local Board would be obliged to carry out the order of the Board and make and sewer those streets, and then the Local Board would not be able to give the owners any time to repay the money.—Mr. Lewin: But if we den't protest now we shall have no other cpportunity.—The Inspector said Mr. Lewin was right in opposing the loan, but the Local Board as the Urban Authority had power to make and sewer these streets if they were not satisfied. If they did that with- out a loan, then the frontagers would have to pay the money in a shorter space of time than they would have to do if the loan was sanctioned.—Mr. Lewin said he was not dealing with the loan at all; he wished to show the Inspector that there was no necessity for this meney to be spent in the neighbourhood.—Mr. Lewin called Messrs. James Taylor, Thomas Ireland, Jno. Hunt, Mrs. Brown, and Mrs. Edwardson, who all said the drain at present made and the streets were in good order and sufficient.—Mr. Thomas Higginson, former surveyor to the Local Board, and occupier of No. 5 Castle-st., one of the streets to be made, gave similar evidence. He said there was no nuisance, and the drain was capable of carrying all the water away.—Mr. Oppenheim drew the attention of the witness to a report by the medical officer in July, 1891,which stated that there were several cases of diptheria at 6 and 8 Castle-st., and he found 21ins. of mud underneath the floor, and the foundations altogether damp. There was a most offensive odour,and the houses were unfit for habitation.—Mr. Fligginson said he was not living in Castle-st. at that tune, and was not aware of that report.—Mr. Lowe, nuisance inspector, corroborated the medical officer's report, but said he had received no complaint of the Edward-st. drain.—There was no other opposition to the schieme of private improvements.—Mr. Oppenheim said the scheme for public improvements might be divided into two dis- tinct parts. The first had reference to the construction of several new sewers from Birchfield-road to the junc- tion of Moor-lane and Lowerhouse-lane, and the second had reference to a road-widening improvement. The sewers were intended to more efficiently drain the western part of the district. The want of such a system of sewerage had been felt for a considerable time, and more than one scheme had been before the Highway Committee and before the Board. It was considered that no scheme would be satisfactory unless it had a proper outfall in connection with the present outfall. In constructing a sewer of any length, which was net along a public road, the question of wayleaves through land was of very serious moment. Some time ago a very offensive nuisance existed upon some property which was on land belonging to the trustees of the late John Shaw Leigh, who are owners of a very large and valuable pro- perty in the district. Negotiations took place between the trustees and the Board, and the results were extremely satisfactory. An agreement was entered to, which pro- vided for the Leigh trustees granting an easement with- out any payment whatever. In addition, as the trus- tees would be relieved of the nuisance on their property, they further agreed to give the sum of £236 towards the cost of the sewer, that being the cost estimated by the surveyor of remedying the nuisance. The court of chancery had confirmed that agreement. The entire estimato for the construction of the sewer was £3,565 us. Bd. which would have to be provided out of the rates, less the sum contributed by the Leigh trustees. The Board thought this a favourable time for effecting an improvement in Lowerhouse-lane, and the trustees had given a considerable piece of land, which would enable that road to he made wider and straighter and of more uniform width. There were one or two other small pices of land which would have to be paid for, the amount being £5Ol, including fencing. The owners were Mr. Alcuim Cowley, Mr. Thos. Dennett,and the executors of H. Cowley. The Inspector would ob- serve that the upper part of the road was very zig zag, and the Board had agreed not to oppose the Leigh Trustees if at some future time they wished to divert that portion and make it straight. That alteration would be a great improvement and no responsibility would be cast upon the Board. Mr. Sinclair then gave details of the proposed sewer,which.he said,would ultimately drain 418 houses. The estimate for the sewering was £3,565 and for the road improvement £2,434.—Mr. Randle said

div.head: SOME AUSTRALIAN EXPERIMENTS.
div.p: SOME AUSTRALIAN EXPERIMENTS.

Speaking of " Australian Experiments in the Art of Government," Mr. Kinnaird Rose says in the " Juridical Review: "—Triennial Parliaments have not curtailed the usefulness of the Legislature,which has rather been brought into closer and more respon- sible touch with the electorate. Manhood suffrage by itself has not given strength to crude schemes of socialism, but has tried these with the unanswer- able logic of dear-bought experience. The ballot has become the main prop of personal liberty, and open voting shown to be the instrument of petty tyranny, whether in politics or trade disputes. The balance of plitical power has not been upset by equal electoral districts, nor has the payment of Members of Parliament degraded the standard of the representatives of the people in moral excel- lence, intelligence, or independence. The abolition of concurrent endowment of all ecclesiastical de- nominations has not strangled religion. The activity of the Churches is nowhere more manifest, or more aggressive, than in Australia. Free educa- tion for a quarter of a century has neither pauperised the community, nor introduced general intellectual snobbishness, nor weakened the power or the willingness of even the least rich classes for work with hands, while it has certainly raised the tidemark of mental culture, and imported healthier and broader views of life. We question whether there is anywhere among the English-speaking race a more general appreciation of literature, or more newspapers to the unit of the population, than in Australia. The principle of fixing rents by inde- pendent land boards, was established with benefit before it was ever dreamt of as a practical measure in Ireland and Scotland. It is, however, too soon to say whether a land-tax on unimproved land values introduced in Queensland. South Australia, and New Zealand, will secure all the benefical re- sults predicted for this scheme of taxation by its great advocate, Mr. Henry George.

div.head: SHOCKING SUICIDE IN LIVERPOOL.
div.p: SHOCKING SUICIDE IN LIVERPOOL.
HANGING FOR A WEEK.

Late on Monday night the police forced an entrance into the house 45, Copperfield-street, Toxteth Park, and there found hanging in the bedroom the body of the occupant, Thomas Robinson, who had not been seen by the neighbours since Tuesday lr Wednesday last. It ap- pears that Mrs. Robinson and the children are away in the country. The deceased, who was about fifty years of age, worked formerly as a van driver for a parcel delivery company, but he had for some time past been out of employment. On the kitchen table was found a note written in pencil as follows :—" 9,9, 92 (sic), 45, Copperfield-street, Toxteth Park,—l am sick and tired of this sort of living, sof bid adieu to all concerned, T. R." —Mrs. Skiffington, residing next door, handed to the police two` letters which she had taken in because no one answered the door. One of them was from Mrs. Robin- son, giving her address in Worcestershire and enclosing a postal order for ss. The police have conveyed to her the sad intelligence.

Mr. Brighouse, the county Coroner, on Tuesday held an inquiry at Widnes Accident Hospital, into the circumstances of the death of Ann Gordon,aged 39, wife of Thomas Gordon, who lives at 78 Pear- St., Widnes. It appeared that on Saturday night a " wake" will held at the house of a woman named Rimmer, of 15 Thorpe-st., where a man of the name of Christopher O'Brien had died. The deceased attended the wake, and was quite sober when she left home. A niece of the deceased named Anne Thompson, who was also present said it was a "respectable wake " only relatives being in attendance. There were five persons in the house. Witness left at two o'clock on Sun- day morning. At that time Mrs. Gordon had had some drink, but was not drunk, but she would not say deceased was sober. She was under the influence of drink, as were all the persons in the house. Before she left the house witness took a paraffin lamp from air' Jer and placed it on the mantelpiece, telling these present not to touch it. Witness did not see the accident, but she saw the deceased at noon on Sunday. The deceased told her that she raised the lamp from the mantelpiece, holding it by the bottom, and she was blowing the light out, when the top of the lamp fell upon her, and set her on fire. She remembered nothing more. The deceased was taken to the hospital shortly after- wards and was attended by Dr. McCarnbridge. She died at 8.30 the same night.—Patrick Burns 'another participator in the " wake," admitted Ithat he was under the influence of drink, and he could not tell what ccndition the other persons were in. There was a large quantity of beer brought into the house. He was on the sofa asleep when the accident occurred. When he awoke Mrs. Riminer was placing a rug round the deceased, who was carried into the yard. The witness made several statements as to the time of the accident, and the Coroner remarked "You are muddled. Yeu have not got over the effects of that quart of beer yet." (Witness smelt very strongly of beer.)—The jury returned a verdict of accidental death, and the foreman (Mr. W.) Farrant) remarked that it was a disgraceful affair.
