GIRLS BEATEN AND DRENCHED WITH WATER Some little time back, it may be remembered, a great deal of ' excitement was caused in France over the alleged ill-treatment of girls at the Reformatory of La Fouilleuse. The affair gave rise to considerable discus- sion, and M. Herbette—ex-Director of the Penal Depart- ment at the Ministry of the Interior, and brother of the French Ambassador atßerlin—was subjected to a great deal of criticism. On Saturdav(says the Paris correspon- dent of the " Telegraph), at the police court of Versailles came on the trial of two of the matrons who had been accused by some of the girls of ill-using them, and the case excited considerable interest. In the course of the proceedings M. Herbette—who, owing to his official position, had had no previous opportunity of replying to the attacks made upon him, though he was the founder of the institution—said that most of the girls were fearfully depraved—the very scum of the metropolis—and that the establishment had been erected in the hope of saving them from utter ruin. They were not unkindly treated, though they often gave great trouble, and all the fuss had been made through the utterly untrustworthy testimony of a score or so of vicious girls. The strait waistcoat, about which so much had been said, could not be used as a punishment, but only as a means of coercion. Then followed the doctor of the institution, who stated that he had never noticed anything wrong ; but a whole bevy of girls were now brought forward as witnesses. They told stories of how their fellow-inmates had been thrashed and then drenched with buckets of water, and a former porter of the establishment declared that he used to be called to brace the strait waistcoat tighter. Another witness said that girls were plunged into icy-cold water, and were beaten to make them go in. Finally the two matrons were condemned to imprisonm,-nt, the one to a week and the other to a fortnight, but with the benefit of the Berenger Law, which means that, as it was their first appearance in a court, the sentence will not take effect.

div.head: MR. KEIR HARDIE. M.P., AND MR.
div.p: MR. KEIR HARDIE. M.P., AND MR.
CARNEG EL

The " Daily Chronicle" says :—We learn that Mr. Keir Hardie has sent the £lOO which he received from Mr. Andrew Carnegie towards his election expenses as a contribution to the strike funds of the ironworkers at Homestead. Someyears ago the Ayrshire miners pre- sented Mr. Hardie with a substantial testimonial, which was invested in Mrs. Hardie's name. With her full consent the member for West Ham has drawn upon this fund in order to clear himself from all indebtedness to the author of" Triumphant Democracy."

div.head: I MP .E RIAL 4 PARLIAMENT.
div.p: I MP .E RIAL 4 PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MoNDAY. THE RESIGNATION OF THE MINISTRY. -FORMAL- ANNOIJAWKAIEDIT._ The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter past four o'clock. There were then about thirty peers in attendance. About half a dozen peeresses, including the Marchioness of Salisbury, occupied seats in the side galleries. Sir John Hay, Mr. H. Hibbcrt, and Mr. Courtney stood ort the steps of the throne, and there were two or three .pectators in the strangers' gallery. On the Treasury I,ench were the Marquis of Salisbury, the Earl of Latbom, Lord Kuutsford, and the Marquis of Lothian; ..nd on the front Opposition bench were Lord Herschell, rile Earl of Kimberley, the Earl of Aberdeen, and the Marquis of Ripon. Amongst the other peers present were Lords Stratheden and Denman._

MESSAGE FROM THE QUEEN. The Earl of Lathom read the following reply from her Majesty to the Address in answer to the Speech from the Throne :—" I have received with great satisfaction your loyal and dutiful address, and the expression of thanks for the Speech with which I opened this session of Par- liament." LORD SALISBUIPS STATEMENT AND SUGGESTION. The Marquis of Salisbury, who on rising was received with cheers, said :—" My fiords, it is my formal duty to announce to your lordships what your lordships have no doubt already heard from another source—namely, that, in consequence of the vote which took place in the House of Commons en Thursday, her Majesty's, Government have placed their resignation in the hands of her Majesty and she bas been pleased 0 accept it. We only hold our seats until our successors are appointed. It is not, I believe, usual for an out-going Minister to make any observations on an occasion of this kind, but I have known cases in which an incoming Minister has taken the opportunity of giving an account of his views on various subjects. (Laughter.) I am sure that if the noble earl opposite should think fit to follow that precedent, and give us an exposition of the intention of the incona- ing Ministry on domestic and foreign affairs, we should listen to him with a great deal of pleasure. (Renewed laughter.) The Earl of Kimberley: I am -extremely sorry I cannot oblige the noble marquis, for the one reason that I am not at present a Minister of the Crown. I should not feel able, without seeking an opportunity of consulting with my colleagues, to make any statement 'on the subject. _ . . _ .

fhe Marquis of Salisbury : Perhaps it would be more ' convenient if the noble earl should fix the time to which he desires the house should adjourn. The Earl of Kimberley : If the noble marquis would be kind enough to move it, I think it would be well the house should adjourn until Thursday next. . . .
The Marquis a Salisbury: I be to move that the house do now adjourn until Thursday noit. . . .
The motion was agreed to, and the'hodse adjourned at twenty-five minutes to five o'clock.
HOUSE OF LORDS.-THURSDAY.

When the house met at the usual hour, a quarter-past pour, there were only about a dozen pets in attendance, and they oceupied the opposite side of the house to that on which they have been accustomed for the past six years to sit. The Earl of Lathom took his seat on the woolsack, and on the Government bench *ere Lord Oxenbridge and Lord Sandhurst, the other other Liberal peers present including Lords Thring, Monkswell, Camoys, and Thurlow. On the Opposition side were Lord Stratheden and Campbell, who took his usual sea, and Lords Clinton and Waldegrave and the Earl of Galloway. Lord Abinger occupied a seat on the cross benches. No business whatever was transacted, and at half-past four the sitting was suspended till a quarter to nine.
THE PROROGATION.

At the latter sitting there were a few spectators, ladies as well as gentlemen, in the strangers gallery. Mr. Keir liagdie alone appeared in the Commons gallery. and in the side gallery to the left of the throne was seated the Dowager Lady Sandhurst. The Lord Chancellor (Lord Herschel!), the Earl of Kimberley, the Marquis of Ripon, Earl Spencer, and Lord Oxenbridge, all wearing their full peers' robes of scarlet and ermine, entered the house at nine o'clock, and took their seats as Royal Commissioners upon a bench placed in .front of the throne. The only other peer present was Lord Stratheden and Campbell. Captain BUTLER, the Yeoman Usher of the Black Rod, was directed to summon the Commons, and shortly afterwards the Speaker, accompanied by the Sergeant- at-Arms without the mace, and followed by about thirty members of the Lower House, appeared at the bar.
- By direction of the Lord Chancellor, the Hon. E. Thesiger read the commission for the prorogation, after which

The Lord Chancellor said :—" My Lords and Gentle- men,—By virtue of her Majesty's Commission under the Great Seal, we do, in her Majesty's name, and in obedience to her commands, prorogue this Parliament till Friday, the 4th day of November next, to be then holden.

The members of the House of Commons then with- drew from the house, the Commissioners retired, and thus ended the first session of the thirteenth Par- liament of the Queen—a session of exactly sb fortnight's duration.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-THIIRSDAY. SIDES CHAN GED.

The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three o'clock, and parties immediately ch&nged sides, the Liberals occupying the benches to the right and the Conservatives to the left of the chair. The only occu- pants of the Treasury bench were Mr. Marjoribanks, the Patronage Secretary to the Treasury ; Mr. J. T. Ilibbert Financial Secretary to the Treasury; Sir Ughtred Kay-Shuttleworth, Secretary to the Admiralty; and Sir W. Foster, Parliamentary Secretary to the Local Government Board. The Liberal party was well represented, among the more notable mem- bers present being Mr. Labouchere, who *occupied the corner seat on the front bench below the gangway. Next to him sat Sir C. Dilke, while on the third bench immediately behind the Ministers,was Sir Lyon Playtair. Scattered on the Ministerial benches were the familiar figures of Mr. Whitbread, Dr. Cameron, Dr. Hunter, Mr. Conybeare, Mr. Summers, Mr. Francis Stevenson, Sir J. Whitehead, Mr. S. Evans, Mt. Halley Stewart, Mr. Bol- ton, and Sir El. Roscoe. The front Opposition bench was occupied by Mr. Akers Douglas, Mr. .1. W. Lowther and Sir E. Clarke; whilst Mr. Talbot, the member for Ox- ferd University,temporarily took possession of Mr. Cham- berlain's old seat. The Liberal Unionists were represented by Mr. T. W. Russell, who occupied his accustomed seat on the Opposition benches ; and by Mr. Austen Chamber- lain, who, during the brief proceedings, stood at the Bar. Mr. John Burns was also on the Opposition benches, which gave rise to some surmises as to the future atti- tude of the Labour party, surmises which were accen- tuated by the appearance of Mr. Keir Hardie, first on the cross-benches to the left of the Speaker and immediately underneath the Serjeant-at-Arms, and afterwards on the front bench below the gangway on the Opposition side. The Anti-Parnellites.in accordance with their proclaimed intentions, monopolised the seats they have held for many years past, whilst the Parnellites were conspicuous by their absence. Writs were agreed to for the election of a member for Midlothian in the room of Mr. W. E. Gladstone, also for the other seats whose. representatives have to seek re- election in consequence of accepting offices of profit under the Crown. The Speaker explained to Mr. Keir Hardie that constitutional usage did not permit him at the present juncture to bring forward his motion regard- ing an autumn session. The Rouse was afterwards summoned to the House of Lords to hear the reading of the Royal Commission proroguing Parliament.

div.head: BRITISH FIREMEN AT HAVRE;
div.p: THE BRITISH FIREMEN AT HAVRE;
REMARKABLE
TOPULAR DEMONSTRATION.

The British firemen who have been attending the International Fire Brigade Congress at Havre set out upon their return journey on Wednesday evening, when they were the objects of a very remarkable popular demonstration. On the march from the Lycee to the Quay they were preceded by the Customs band and the "fanfare Gravillaise," another local instrumental band, and escorted by the entire force of the Havre fire bri- gade, carrying lighted torches, while the streets were filled with cheering crowds. The parting ceremony in- cluded complimentary speeches. While the men were embarking the British and French national anthems were p ayed, and asthe vessel moved out of the harbour the firemen were greeted with lusty rounds of cheering on the part of their French comrades.

div.head: LUTING FRODSITAM RAILWAY STATION.
div.p: LUTING FRODSITAM RAILWAY STATION.
A REMARKABLE UNDERTAKLNG.

The joint railway companies have succesafully COM.. pleted a remarkable undertaking at Frodsham Station. Complaints have been made for years of inadequate platform accommodation, and filially it was decided to remove the 6tationmaster's house, booking offices, and general wai•ing roam some six feet back. In order to accomplish the task without taking down the structures excavations were made beneath them until they were supported on large baulks of timber. Then came the crucial point, whether they would slide into their new situation. Eleven powerful jacks were brought into operation under the superintendence of Mr. Johnson, the companies' engineer. Although the mass to be moved weighed quite-400 tons,the work was accomplished with- out a hitch, save that a chimney stack, which cracked, bad to be taken down. This is stated to be the first occa- sion on which an English railway station has been suc- cess u:ij lifted on the American principle.

div.head: 'EXAMINER,
div.p: THE 'EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, AUGUST 20, 1892.

WE shall soon begin to feel the The New benefit of the result of the recent Government. General Election. The Salisbury Government have been turned out of office ami Mr. GLADSTONE has, for the fourth time, become Prime Minster of England. The Liberal chief was charged by her Majesty, on Monday, with the formation of an Administration. On Tuesday, he returned in triumph to London, and the same evening an official list was issued of the members of the New Cabinet as far as it had then been submitted to the Queen. Mr. GLADSTONE becomes first lord of the Treasury, and Lord Privy Seal. The latter office has not carried with it any oner- ous duties, and Mr. GLADSTONE'S post as first lord leaves him in a position to give thut general supervision of the business of the Government which is the prime function of the Prime Minister. The country has had experience of Lord HERS- CLIELL as Lord Chancellor, and can rest well satisfied that he will be more than equal to everything that will be required of him. He is recognised in his profession as one of the I soundest of living lawyers; and he was a Home Ruler of the most pronounced type, when some politicians had not made up their minds as to the best course to take. The Earl of Kimberley will have responsible duties as Secretary of State for India; but heis a man of wide experience in the affairs of the empire, and it ia not saying much to affirm that he will make a better secretary than Lord CROSS, whom he succeeds. He will also hold the post of Lord President of the Council but the duties of that office are, it is Well known, exceed- ingly light. Lord ROSEBERVS appointment to the post of Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs is one which is welcomed by Tories as well as Liberals. His lordship was Foreign Secretary in Mr. GLADSTONE'S previous Government, and the firm yet conciliatory manner in which he discharged his duties won golden opinions from all sorts and conditions of men. It was feared that the somewhat uncertain state of his health, would prevent him occupying a place in the new ministry, and it is therefore especially gratifying to find that his medical advisers have pronounced that he will, in all probability, be fully equal to the heavy task before him.

The Marquis of RIPON is the new Secretary of State for the Colonies; and this is an appointment to which it may be said that no objection can be made even by the bitterest Tory. Lord RIPON has served his Queen and country in various offices; and he is remembered in India with grati- tude as one of the best Viceroys who ever ruled over that great Dependency. Mr. ASQUITH, Q.C. receives sudden if not unexpected promotion in becoming Secretary of Stato for the Home Depart- ment. He is a fine speaker, as Liberals in this district know ; and, more than that, he is a most thoughtful and able politician. It is needless to say, that Mr. CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN, as Secretary of State for War, Earl SPENCER as first Lord of the Admiralty, and Sir W. HARCOURT as Chancellor of the Exchequer, are not likely to be in any respect lacking. They are important men, and they have been givan import- ant posts. Sir George TREVELYAN Will be the right man in the right place as Secretary for Scotland, while the Board of Trade will have an excellent head with Mr. MUNDELLA. as president. ' Mr. H. H. FOWLER, as President of the Local Government Board, Mr. Arnold MORLEY, as Post- Master General, and Mr. Arthur ACLAND, as vice- President of the Committee of Council on Educl- tion, are new men in the sense of receiving Cabinet

rank for the first time but they are not new to politicians, who know that they have special quali- fications for the duties laid; upon them. Lord HOUGHTON is the new Viceroy of Ire- land, but he will not have a seat in the Cabinet. He is a young man comparatively, but he is well known as a good speaker, an ardent ardent Liberal, and a nobleman of means. The ' general administration of the affairs of Ireland will, of course, rest with Mr. John MORLEY, who will be Irish Secretary, as in the last Liberal Administration, with a seat in the Cabinet. Mr. MORLEY, before he came to the front rank as a Statesman, had much to do, as one of the principal journalists of the day, in shaping the thoughts of politicians in the direction of Home Rule. His record as to Ireland is a clear and consistent one, and if Home Rule is to be granted, as we trust it will be granted by the present Parliament, it will be largely due to his labours. There is some reason to fear that he will have a hard fight for his seat in Newcastle, when he seeks re-election as the result of his appointment. The Tories are making the most of the fact that he does not see his way, as yet, to compulsory legislation in favour of an eight hours day, and that he has expressed the difficulties of the pro- blem with frankness and fearlessness. It should not be forgotten, however, that for the present, Horne Rule is the question of the hour. Nor can it be said by either party that Mr. MORLEY is wanting in sympathy with working men. On the contrary, he recently remarked that, Home Rule once out of the way—" for him the question of questions would be the labour question." It will be seen that we are especially anxious that he should retain his seat. It would indeed be a dis- credit to Newcastle, and a blow to the cause of Home Rule if he were to lose it. But we will not think of such a thing, for this is the era of the triumph of Liberalism and of Home Rule.

Nineteenth IVlessas F. WARNE and Co. have Century just published a volume of "Popular Poets. Studies of Nineteenth Century Poets" by the Rev. J. MARSHALL MATHER, author of the "Life and Teachings of JOHN RUSKIN " which we had occasion to commend in these col- umns some time ago. It is a bold thing to under- take a commentary upon the greatest of modern poets; but Mr. MATHER lets it be seen that he has prepared himself for the task ; and he must be congratulated upon the production of a work which is likely to prove popular. The studies are not of a kind to convey much that is new to thosw who are thoroughly familiar with latter-day poets.; but they cannot but be of great service to ordinary readers who find poetry either something of a drug, or something beyond them. It appears-from the preface that the essays were originally prepared for a class of working-men; and the fact that no material alteration has been made may account for the lecturing—not hectoring tone which is occa- sionally noticeable. Seven poets are brought under consideration in the following order and form.: Wordsworth, the Naturalist; Shelley,.the idealist; Coleridge, the Metaphysician; Byron, the Pessi- mist; Hood ,the Humourist; Tennyson,the Moodist; and Browning, the Optimist. This ticketing,. so to speak,of such writers has a tendency to narrow the view, but at the same time it must ba admitted that it has•been done felicitously. Mr. MATIIRR as might be expected, quotes freely,. thus letting each writer speak for himself, the essayist stepp- ing in to expound whenever he thinks it neces- sary. Ile shows himself dispassionate in his judg- ment, mentioning the weak as well as the strong points in each author; and explains some things which to the casual reader might either seem obscure-or be misunderstood. It is specially satis- factory to find a clergyman who can do justice to Shelley, whom he speaks of standing in "peer- less rank as a lyrical poet." He makes the most of Coleridge—so much that one cannot help think- ing he ought to have included Keats in his list. He hits Byron rather hard when he says the poet's " pessimism had its root in his lawlessness,, his lust, his rebellion; and his genius uttered his pessimism in song." It is, suggestive of Byron's weakness as a thinker and a ' moralist that, while he is the delight of youth, be is little in favour with. "age which brings the philosophic mind." As to Tennysoni., he regards" Locksley Hall " as the poet's master- piece, and describes it as a " swiftly moving panorama of moods." He is vigorous in defence of "the optimist ;" and roundly says that " Browning's vagueness is often mistaken for " Browning's mysticism. Heaven has a language as well as earth; and he who seeks to translate it must be content to be despised by the vulgar crowd." Admitting this, it must still be said that Browning's translation sometimes requires to, be itself translated; hence the Browning Society. These" Studies," it should be added, are as cheap as they are excellent, for the volume which con- tains them may be obtained for the modest sum of half-a-crown.

div.head: TERRIBLE FIRE AT TREDROAR.
div.p: TERRIBLE FIRE AT TREDROAR.
LOSS OF ELEVEN LIVES..

A terrible fire, attended with the loss of eleven lives, occurred early on Wednesday morning at the new model lodging-house situated in Red Lion-square, Tredegar. The building, which was lout storeys in height, was one of the finest of its kind in South Wales. It was erected last year by Mr. C. T. Lee at a cost of about £2,000, and was opened in December last. All the partitions and floors were red dealt, while the ceil- ings were constructed of match wood, There was ac- commodation for 120 lodgers, and the premises were fitted throughout with bath-rooms. At the time of the outbreak the building contained some 70 inmates. The fire originated in the fourth or upper storey, and so rapidly did the flames spread that it was with the greatest difficulty those who occupied the lower rooms were able to effect their escape. Many of those in the top storey found it impossible to descend the staircase and in their mad fright two at least flung themselves 'from the windows. One old man named Twigg fell with terrible force against an adjoining wall, breaking his neck, which caused instant death. Another man was so badly injured that he had to be carried to the hospital, where he lies in a very pecaricus condition. Police Constable _Evans and a young man named Thos. Thomas heroically entered the burning premises in order to assist the escape of any who might be unaware of their danger. They found four men in e stupefied con- dition from the volumes of smoke which by this time penetrated the whole of the rooms. Fortunately these were safely carriei into the street. Many others who were aroused from their sleep fled from the building in almost a state of nudity. The fire brigade, with a large contingent of police, were promptly on the spot, under the direction of Captain Parker, and every effort was made to extinguish the names, but in consequence of so much timber having beep used in its construction, it was found impossible to save the building. In less than an hour and a half nothing remained but the bare walls. Happily the fire was prevented from spreading to the adjoining premises. As soon as possible a search was made among the debris for the bodies of any who might have perished, and up to dusk the remains of seven per- sons have been taken from the ruins. The bodies were all frightfully charred, and it will be next to impossible 'to identify them. it is feared that other bodies may yet be found. The bailding is said to be insured. The latest statement of the loss of life is eleven. Ten bodies have now been reovered.

The Moorish Ministers who prevented the Sultan from concluding the sritish treaty are each reported to have received 10,000 dollars from the French agent. The Sultan is unwell from worry and apprehension. A New York telegram announces the death at Philadel- phia of Michael Harkins, who took a prominent part in the dynamite plot against the English Government some years ago,

In a poem in this month's " Centtyvy," on "Sea-longings, he says:— Sea-sounds, sea-odours, these were all my world, Hence it is that life languishes with me inland; the valleys stifle me with gloom And pent-up prospect ;in their narrow bound Imagination flutters fntile wings. If Aldrich had, like the friends who are with us here, lived for several years at Blackpool, he would, I think, have sung a dlferent tune on being trans- ported to this land of mountain and mead,. of winding valleys and gleaming lakes, and have be- come the latest addition to the lake poets," For my part, I find these surroundings stimulating to ' the imagination; for, until one gets familiar with every valley, it is unceasingly pleasant to imagine' ' the view which is to be seen from the next hill topr and then compare or contrast it with the reality.

The sea, like that school book which all boys an girls of course love, has its " moods and tenses ; but they are not, after all, so varied as those which, may be studied in the Lake District. When mist and cloud, are about—and they are never away for • " very long—they play the most" fantastic tricks • ' with "hill and steamily,. lake;" so that a single e vale may become a swift-changing panorania. The sea offers nothing, in the way of colour and variety, compared with the wonderful transforma- tions which akiddaw undergoes in the course of the day as we watch it from our eastern window, It is seldom, without its cap of clouds; and some- times to the cap is added a winding sheet, and there is nothing else to be seen. But when the sun is shining upon it in the evening every ridge and hollow is revealed ; and the last glow of purphi) light adds such colour as could only be surpasse" by that which the Pen i saw when she stood at Heaven's gate. _ -

div.head: WIDNES PR! MROSE LEAGIIE.
div.p: WIDNES PR! MROSE LEAGIIE.

liOn Thursday afternoon the first annual picnic was eld in connection with the Widnes Branch of the Prim- rose League, when a large number drove to Hale, in waggonettes supplied by Mr. J. H. Lee. A substantial tea was partaken of at the Wellington Hotel, and a stroll round the old village was much appreciated.

PROM^TION OF A WIDNES POLICZ SERGE ANT. We are pleased to record the promotion of Sergeant Clarkson, of Widnes Petty Sessional Division to the rank of Inspector. Inspector Clarkson joined the county constabulary 21 years ago, and after serving 14 years as constable he was made a sergeant. He has served the whole of that long period in Widnes, and it says much for his character and conduct that he pos- sesses the respect and goodwill of the law-abiding popu- lation in the town, He commenced his new duties at Bolton on Wednesday. Sergeant Carter, of West Derby Division, is his successor. If yen want your watch repaired by skilful workmen, take it to PAITCHARD'O.—Advt. THEFT OF BRASS AT RUNCORN.

Peter Brooks, of Windermere-street, Runcorn, was brought before Mr. Henry Reynolds and Mr. James Handley at Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, charged with having stolen 651bs. of brass fittings from the Run- corn Soap and Alkali Co's. Works of the United Alkali Company. The foreman, named Dwyer, identified the property, and said the prisoner had worked for the firm at Weston and Runcorn for 14 years.—A marine store dealer in Waterloo-road named Howard said the prisoner came to his place on Monday morning and offered him the brass. He was questioning the prisoner when P.C. Booth came in and apprehended him. The prisoner ad- mitted having stolen the brass, and said he did it be- cause he was in danger of being sent to prison for debt. Ha was fined 255., or a month's imprisonment. The money was paid.
JOSEPH PRITCHAE. has the best stock of ladies' silver and geld watches in the town.—Advt. DEATH OF MR. H. N. WHARTON, OF WIDNES:

Mr. H. N. Wharton, of Aloorside Terrace, Widnes, died somewhat unexpectedly at his residence on Wed- nesday morning. About twelve days ago Mr. Wharton became confined to bed with congestion of the lungs, which ultimately developed into typhoid fever, and though the best medical skill was obtained,he gradually sank and died as stated. lie was only 39 years of age, and leaves a widow and five children to mourn his loss. For 16 years Mr. Wharton had carried on an extensive grocery business in the town. During that time he had taken an active and prominent part in religious and philanthropic work. He was a staunch Churchman,and he had filled most of the offices in connection with the Parish Church, for which :he was charchwarden on several occasions. He was well known and respected amongst all classes. At a meeting of the Church Coun- cil on Thursday, a vote of condolence to the widow and family was passed. The remains of the deceased were interred in the churchyard of St. Mary's Church, yes- terday afternoon, in the presence of a large concourse of people. JOsigPl PEVICEiRT) keeps spectacles to suit all sights from a shilling a pain—Advt. ST PAUL'S WESLEYAN CHAPEL CHOIR, RUNCORN.

The members of this choir had their annual picnic on Wednesday. when they had a pleasant drive to Delamere Forest in a brake supplied by Messrs. Yarwood Bros. The weather was fine and the party spent a most enjoy- able day amid the rural beauties of the Forest. Eddis- bury Lodge was the head-quarters for the outing and here a capital dinner and tea were partaken of, a well- stocked hamper of edibles having been carried from Runcorn. On the return journey, a stoppage was made at Kingsley Hall, the residence recently acquired by Mr. S. B. Chadwick, J.P., of Cropton Lodge, Runcorn, and the choir, under the leadership of their conductor, Mr. Richard Morris, rendered several hymns and anthems. Mr. Chadwick cordially invited the party into his house, and most hospitably entertained them. Before leaving, the choir sang several other anthems and glees, and Mr. Chadwick pressed them to make him another call whenever they were it the district. On behalf of the choir, Mr. Morris heartily thanked Mr. Chadwick for his hospitality, and kind invitation. The drive to Runcorn was accomplished in good time, and all expressed them- selves highly gratified with the day's outing.

div.head: SAD ACCIDENT TO A NEWSBOY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SAD ACCIDENT TO A NEWSBOY AT RUNCORN.

The danger to which the young newsboys on railway stations are subject was illustrated at Runcorn on Satur- day evening. The victim was a boy named W. Summer- field, whose father is an engine driver living in Picow- street. As the 5.50 from Chester was leaving,' the platform for Liverpool, a passenger called out to Summerfield for a newspaper, and the boy in endeavouring to hand one up to him, was knocked down by the carriage,and, after rolling over several times, fell on the line between the platform and the train. Mr. Smith, the stationmaster, stopped the train as quickly as possible, and picked up the lad, who was found to be suffering from a fractured leg. His left leg was dreadfully smashed between the ankle and the knee. Harry Tarleton, the Mersey ferry- man, who happened to be on the platform at the time, utilized his knowledge of ambulance work to bandage the injured limb, and the boy, after he had been seim to by Dr. Carruthers and Dr. McDougall, was sent on to the Royal Infirmary at Liverpool. The surgeons of that institution thought it necessary to amputate the poor boy's leg, which was done, and he is progressing satis- factorily. The boy was acting against orders in supply- ing a newspaper to a person in a moving train.

When in want of a chaste and elewint wedding sr birthday present go ta reit ARD'S, 51. High-st.—Advt. DESEIMON OF A CHILD AT WIDNES. At Widnes Poließ Court, on Wednesday, Rose O'Neil, a young woman, 18 years of age, whose home is in New- town, was charged with deserting her illegitimate child, three months old, on the 12th of July. prom the evi- dence it appeared that the prisoner in order to get rid of her child, placed it in the care of a woman named Sarah Owens, in Caroline-st., and she at once left the town. Mr. liampson, the Relieving Officer, traced the prisoner to Ron on, and found her employed there as a domestic servant. under the name of Monaghan. She was arrested by the Rol t,,n police ad handed over to P.C. Thompson, of the Widnes Police. The Relieving Officer said when he took the child to the Workhouse it was much emaciated and appeared to have been neglected from its birth. The prisoner was remanded and brought before Mr. Dear n and Mr. Pilkington at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday. She pleaded guilty.—The Relieving Officer said the prisoner before she went away asked him to send the child to some institution, but he told her he could not unless she paid for its maintenance. She then admitted that she did not care what became of the child if she got rid of it. Three days afterwards she deserted the child. It transpired that Mrs. Owens was the mother of the young man whom the prisoner alleges to be the of the child—Mr. Hampson :aid there were man,- cases of tlegertion in this district. —The prisoner was s literwed to 14 days' imprisonment.
JOSEPH PRITCHARD, Watchmaker and Jeweller, 51, Highst., and 4, Bridge-st., Runcorn.—Advt. CHOKED BY A PIECE OF BEEF' AT RUNCORN. . _

On Sunday, a farm labourer, named Michael Holland, came to Runcorn, on a visit to some friends who reside in Back Mersey-st. At their invitation he stayed for dinner, and while eating the repast a piece of beef be- came fast in his throat. Although those present used their best endeavours to release the piece, they did not succeed, and he died in seven minutes. Dr. McDougall was sent for, but death had taken place before his ar- rival. He, however, extracted from the man's throat the piece of beef, Which was about an inch and a half long and an inch thick. The deceased had been in the employ of Mr. J. W. Baguley, of Stockham, and he was 48 years of age. He was a big, powerfully-built man. Mr. R. Dobson, the deputy-coroner, held an inquest en the body at Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday morn- ing.—Michael McDonald, of Back Mersey-st., said lie saw the deceased about one o'clock on Sunday, and de- ceased had two-pennyworth of rum with him. He in- vited him to have dinner, which consisted of beef and potatoes. The deceased seemed hungry, and ate his dinner very heartily. When half the dinner was taken, deceased commenced to cough, and John Coleman, who was present, said he was choking. Witness ran for the doctor.—John Coleman, labourer, said deceased had had too much drink. When he noticed deceased was chok- ing he struck him on the back and put his fingers in his mouth, but he could not get the meat out of his throat. The doctor came and took the piece out : it was a very large piece. Deceased was then quite dead.—William Duffy, Stockham, identified the body. Deceased was 55 years of age, and was a native of Cloonfaughtrin,County Mayo.—A verdict that deceased was " Accidentally choked' was returned.
JOSETE PRITCHARD'S MIS shop is 51,High•st., hie workshop 4, Bridge-st.—Advt. A LIVELY TIME IN A WIDWES PUBLICHOTJSE.

At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, David Johnson and William Paddock, of Lugsdale-road, were charged with being drunk and disorderly and with doing wilful damage to a glass panel in a door at the Railway Rotel. —Mr. T. Laws, landlord of the hotel, said that the two defendants came into the bar on Saturday night, and asked to be served with drink. As he thought they shad had sufficient he refused to serve them, but when he turned his back one of the girls in the bar gave them a glass of beer each. lie, however, took the glasses away from them, and ordered them out. They refused to go, and he sent for an officer. Paddock became very violent and used very abusive language, whereupon he (witness) had to forcibly put defendants .out. They returned, and therefore he again put them out. He could not say who had broken the glass.—Defericlant Paddock said that Mr. Laws would not return the money that had been taken for the beer, and also alleged that Mr. Laws kicked him. In answer to the Bench, Mr. Laws said that no mention was made of any money, and he never kicked either of them.—Dr. Saul said that about seven o'clock he was looking out through a window opposite the Railway Hotel when he saw the defendants ejectod by Mr. Laws. Be saw Johnson deliberately smash the glass with his fist. Be did not see Mr. Laws use any violence whatever.—Mr. J. Hatton also spoke to seeing Johnson smash the glass.—Mr. Deacon said the Bench were satisfied that Johnson had smashed the glass, and Mr. Laws was quite right in refusing to serve him. Pad- dock was fined ss. and costs, and Johnson ss. and costs for the drunkenness, and ss. and costs for breaking the glass, and also ordered to pay £3, the amount of the damage ; or seven days in default in each case.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 20. 1892
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 20. 1892
SUNDAY SCHOOL DEMONSTRATION AT WIDNES.

The first united demonstration of Nonconformist Seinday Schools in Widnes, took place on Saturday last. As originally arranged it was intended that the whole of the Protestant Sunday schools should take part, but from some unexplained reason the church party and several dissenting schools withdrew. Nevertheless a most successful procession was held. The weather being fine, there was a capital turn-out of scholars, it being computed that there were 3,500 present, repre- senting the following schools :—Lacey-st., Wesleyan, 560; Cromwell-st., Wesleyan, 130, Oakland-st., Wesle- yan, 764 ; Albert-read, Wesleyan 376 ; Moss Bank- Wesleyan 170 ; Lacey-st., Welsh Wesleyan 120 : United Methodist Free Church, 280 ; Hutchinson-st., Primitive Methodist, 200 ; Princess-st., Primitive 260, Baptist 135, Gospel Union Mission 100 : Salvation Army 50 ; Milton Congregation 320. The promenade was the place of assembly, and there the children sang several hymns, under the leadership of Mr. S. Lamb. The route taken by the procession was along Mersey-road,Waterloo-road, Victoria-road, Widnes-road, and Albert-road, to Milfield Recreation Grounds, where each child received a bun, and a bottle of aerated waters. More singing was engaged in under the leadership of Mr. J. C. Crawford, and afterwards games were indulged in until dusk. The procession was led by three bands, viz., Widnes sub- scription Band, I,Vidnes Soap works band, and Mill Brow band, Runcorn,' and a number of teachers acted as marshals. There were a number of banners and ban- nerettes displayed in the ranks. The demonstration was viewed by a large concourse of spectators. WIRRAL AND BIRKENHEAD AGUICULTUAL

div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
Br AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.
That the animal election of Runcorn Commis- sioners takes place on Thursday, September Ist., but if we are to take present indications there will not be a contest.

That last year at this time there were eight candidates in the field, with addresses issued and in full work ; now the affair seems as dead as Queen Anne, and perhaps the undermentioned five, who are retiring, may be re-elected unopposed :... Messrs. P. Speakman, Walter Timmins, William Hankinson, Henry J. Once, and Henry White. That maybe an eleventh hour surprise is in store, and we shall see the Temperance Federation—if it is yet in existence—and taking that qctive part in this election although the organisation held aloof at the General Election ; and possibly there may be an "independent " or two.

That large numbers of electors would be ex- tremely glad to see Mr. Imison emerge from his retirement nnd take that pnrt in the control of our local affairs for which hid character and abil- ity so well tit him.

Thnt the elevation of Mr. John Rigby, Q.C., M.P.. to the insition of Solicitor-General has given wide- spread sntisfaction in Runcorn, which is his native place. The position carries with it a salary of £6,000 a year and fees.
That it is unlikely that hiS re-election for For- farshire will be opposed.

That the Liberal; of Northwich Division have a warm corner in their hearts for Mr. T. E. Ellis, M.P., and were he to visit them congratulations would shower upon him in respect to his selection for the position of junior Lord of the Treasury, which they join in regarding as only the first step to greater things. The salary is £l,OOO a year

That there is no dQuht that Widnes Local Board will obtain the sanction of the Local Governint.nt Board to the loan of .£12,000, of which £6,000 is to he devoted to works of private iln pro cements, toad £6,000 to works of pubic impro,ement.

That a number of property owners from Warring- ton-road district opposed the application, on the ground that the streets in which they were inte- rested did not require making, and that the sewer already provided was quite adequate.
That they did not bring any of the tenants to make a similrir declaration, and the evidence of Mr. Sinclair disclosed quite a different state of affairs.
That there certainly are other parts of the town- ship that are in need of immediate attention, for their sanitary surroundings are something disgrace- ful.

That Mr. Potts, the clerk to the Cheshire County Council, was married at Aberyst- myth on Thursday, and the members of the Council and of the Standing Joint Committee showed their respect and esteem, for the chief executive officer of the county by presenting him with three pieces of valuable old silver plate.
That the presentation wa9 in charge of a small committee, of which Mr. P. Speakman, of Runcorn, aas the chairman.

FRODSHAM.

FIRE IN Mafir-Sr.—On Sunday evening a rather mysterious fire broke out at the house and premises occupied by Mr. Samuel Massey, fruiterer, Zicc., Main- St. Owing to the indefatigable exertions of a number of neighbours and others the -house was entered (in the absence of Mr. Massey) and the fire completely extin- guished before much damage had been done. The cause of the fire has not yet been ascertained.

Foster, Frodsham, Ist • J. Hitchmouth, Hale, 2nd ; J Houghton, Hale, 3rd :S Large, Widnes, 4th ;T. Woods, Hale, sth ;W. Woods, Hale, 6th. Mr. J. Large conducted. After service six members of the Lancashire Association started to ring 720 grandsire minor, and time not being allowed the bells were brought into rounds in 360 changes. The ringers were—S. Large, Ist ;J. Hitchmouth. 2nd ; T. Woodward 3rd ; F. Griffiths, 4th; J. Houghton, sth; T. Woods, 6th. THE LIBERAL Cr.nn.—On Saturday the Liberal Com- mittee and workers, to the number of fifty-four, drove to Willing ton Hall, the residence of Mr. James Tomkin- son, T.P. At the hall a splendid tea was pro- vided for the party by Mr. Tomkinson, to which full Justice was done. Afterwards several short speeches were made by Mr. and Mrs. Tomkinson and others. The beautifully arranged gardens and grounds were in- spected, and a nice game of cricket was indulged in— Married v. Single—in which the married members came off the winners. The picnic was thoroughly enjoyable, and will long be remembered with pleasure.

RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY COMMITTEE. The monthly meeting of the Runcorn Free Public Library Committee was held on Wednesday in the Board-room, Town hall, Mr. Thomas Riley in the chair. The librarian reported that 1,586 works had been issued during the month of July, classified as follows: Theology 15, philosophy 9, science and art 29, history, travel, and biography 111, poetry 5, prose fiction 1,286, miscellaneous literature 131. The annual report was read and adopted, which showed th t the number of volumes on the shelves of the library was 6,286. There had been added during the year 427 volumes, 27 of which had been presented* and 400 purchased. Fifty-four of the books added were in the French language, and had been purchased to assist the students in the French class, recently formed in con- nection with the Science and Art Classes. Seven hun- dred and thirty-five borrowers' tickets had been issued during the year. The library had been opened for the issue of books 151 days, and 21,757 works had been issued, being a daily average issue of 14-4. The reading room continued to attract large numbers of readers, and often the accommodation proved inadequate. The com- mittee, in conclusion, expressed their thanks to the donors of money, books, periodicals, and newspapers, whose gifts materially assisted them in the work of con- ducting the library.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO THE CLERK OF THE CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO THE CLERK OF THE CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL.

On the occasion of the marriage of Mr. Potts, the clerk of the Cheshire County Council, a beautiful album containing the address given below has been presented to him. The address was signed by each subscriber and contained pencil sketches of Heron Bridge House, Mr.Pott.s's office, the old Dee Bridge, the Chester Eastgate, the Shire Hall, the County Council Chamber, the Knutsford Courts, the county arms,and also a photograph of Mr. Potts and a copy of his crest. There has also been presented to Mr. Potts a silver tankard, which is a beautiful piece of old silver. The address reads as follows : "To Reginald Potts, Esq., Clerk of the Peace for Ches- hire and Clerk of the County Council. We, the under- signed officials and Magistrates' Clerks of the County of Chester, desire to offer you our united and hearty con- gratulations on the occasion of your marriage, sincerely wishing you and your bride every happiness, and pray- ing that a Gracious Providence may bless your union with the purest domestic felicity, and spare you both long to enjoy the greatest of earthly blessings. We also ask your acceptance of the accompanying Silver Tankard." The signatures appended are these of—John Ashton, magistrates' clerk, Runcorn and Frodsham ; J Carter Bell, county analyst ; G Boyden, maagistrates' clerk, Broxton ; R Bygott; magistrates' clerk, Middle- wich and Sandbach ; Stanhope Bull, county surveyor ; T Cawley, magistrates' clerk, Tarporley ; J H Cooke. magistrates' clerk. Over ; G 1-1 Cope, deputy chief constable; Henry Churton, county coroner, Chester; W Henry Churton, magistrates' clerk, Chester Castle ; Henry Greenall, magistrates' clerk, Daresbury ; J H Ilamersley, Lieut-Col., chief constable of Cheshire ; J Harris, magistrates' clerk, Altrincham ; John Flibbert, magistrates' clerk, Hyde and Dukinfield ; W D Laird, chief inspector of weights and measures; Charles E Lake, magistrates' clerk, Stockport; Walter Lewis, chief veterinary surgeon; William Mair, magistrates' clerk, Prestbury: James Newell, magistrates' clerk, Leftwich ; Francis Newton, county coroner, Stockport ; Henry L Reade, clerk of indictments and magistrates' clerk, Congleton ; Henry Roscoe, magistrates' clerk, Bucklow ; C E Speakman, magistrates' clerk, Nantwich and Crewe; Godfrey A Solby, magistrates' clerk, Wirral ; James Steen, sessions courts crier; J 11 Thomson, county treasurer; J L Trafford, magistrates' clerk, Eddisbury ; R P Ward, organising secretary for technical education ; James Williams, county accountant, &,3.; James E Worsley, county coroner, Halton Fee; El C Yates, county coroner, Knutsford.

div.head: SENSATIONAL AFFAIR AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SENSATIONAL AFFAIR AT RUNCORN.

The inhabitants of Runcorn vt ere thrown into a state of great excitement on Thursday afternoon, in consequence of the circulation of a most extraor- dinary story. It was alleged that for the past seven years a boy had been kept in close confinement in the house No. 18, Brunswick-st., and occupied by a man who earns his living as a bricklayer's labourer, and is known under various aliases. The story went that this poor piece of suffering humanity had been seen during the past few days peering out of the window of the upper room of the house. His face was described as most emaciated, his unkempt locks reached down to his waist, and his finger nails were said to he at least six inches long, and might have served for the talons of some bird of prey. His 1 attire was a woman's old pettiCoat and a woman's l bodice, and his condition was described as in the last degree filthy and disgusting. Brunswick-st. was be- seiged on Thursday afternoon with hundreds, anxious to catch a ell amps,. ro rhis allerl victim of parental neglect and cruelty. . Their curiosity was not gratified, but they remained t lwre for h00r.4, gazing at the unpreten- tious cotta:.e, an I as they 'salted, the stories with re- gard to tlas boy lo•eame more sensational. His hair in- creased in rent:l until it tonched the ground, and his nails grew in length as rapidly as the minutes passed by. The women present revelled in the gruesome details con- jured up by the morbid imagination of most of those pre- sent, and at last his appearance was pictiirati as like that of ail uncanny ape. As evening drew nigh the numbers in the street increased by hundreis,and many respectable persons of both sexes were to be seen in the street eagerly gleaning details of the rumoured horror. Execra- tions against the occupants of the hou,e began to be not only deep but lou I, and it w;i4 it one time feared that the house would ho stormed,hti, Superintendent Atherton and a force of core:tables were ,m the spat, and their presence had no little infieence in restraining any acts of violence. It appears that rumours of the C'onfinement of the bey had reached the ears of Mr. Atherton on the previous day, and in order to ascertain whether there was any truth in the allegations he visited the house and found the family circle were living on the same terms as in any other dwellink of a like description in the town. There was a youth there who is certainly seldom seen in the street, but this was ascribed to his delicate health, which rendered him unfit for much outside intercourse. In answer to tha Superintendent's inquiries, he said he spent his time in tnaking flower boxes and various nick- nacks,and that he was well fed and well cared for. He was attired in the same manner as a youth of his age and condition of life would be, and there was an utter absence of long hair and long finger nails. The police constables engaged in keeping order in the street endea- voured to impress those facts on the large crowd of persons who had assembled,but their veracity was ques- tioned,and it was not until a considerable time after dark 1 that a dispersal took place and the street resumed its normal appearance.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE,WARRINGTON.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE,WARRINGTON.

On Monday evening Messrs. Crozier and Milton's drama "Fair Play," which has previously been performed in Warrington, was produced at the above-named theatre, in tie presence of a large and appreciative assemblage. The pains which had been taken by the management to provide an adequate array of dramitc talent, rind mount the piece with becoming scenic accessories were abundently manifested in the happy results accomplished; and we must accord the credit for this to Mr. W. F. Tindell, the travelling, and Mr. H. Parrett, the local, stage manager. The representation of the comfortable yet handsomely appointed drawing room at Eastmount was a most realistic present- ment, as was also that of the quarry, in which one of the most melodramatic of the incidents occurs, and which was a truly artistic piece of rugged picturesqueness. The characters, generally, were admir- ably impersonated, and exhibited careful training and the true dramatic insight. Mr. Percy Milton took the humble part of Josephus Washington Grubb, pedlar and poet, but the part, though humble,was in the eyes of the audience and in the ability with which it was carried out, one of the most prominent. The humour of Grubb so refined and utterly free from coarseness and mannerism, which are such common faults with comedians, was delightful; and every point he made was a perfect hit. The part of Major Durston, squire of Eastmount,( Mr. W. Egerton) was well taken ; and his nephew, Lawrence Durston (Mr. George Mitchell) whose somnambulistic inclinations constitute largely the interest of the piece, acquited himself to great advantag,e,the sleep-walking scenes being striking- ly effective. As David ffedfarn Mr. Torn Wallace proves himself fully equal to the demands upon him, his acting of the more impassioned parts being commensurately fine. Dolores was excellently represented by Miss Daisy England; and the gipsy, Esther Redfarn found a good exponent in Miss Trissie Humphreys, while the ideal of the piquant and vivacious Patty was truly brought out by Miss Rosie Leyton. The last performance will be given this (Saturday) evening. We may mention that at the entrance to the circle there now hangs a fine portrait of Mr. Henry Irving, presented by the emin- ent tragedian to the proprietors of the theatre.
Thirty persons and a number of domestic animals have been bitten by a rabid wolf at Lodz, Rusgian Poland,and the village is full of. people suffering from raving mad- ness. _ . .

On Saturday morning some workmen employed in excavating a cellar at the rear of 63, Mostyn-st., Llan- dudno, discovered some human remains in a fair state of preservation. Patrick Gibbons, aged thirty-three, a labourer, was executed in Walton Gaol on Wednesday morning for the murder of his mother, Bridget Gibbons, at Royton, near Oldham. The prisoner acknowledged the justice of his sentence, and met his fate with unflinching fortitude.

div.head: FIRE AT THE TOWN HALL.
div.p: FIRE AT THE TOWN HALL.

An accident occurred at the Town Hall, on Tues- day, which might easily have had serious results. This was nothing less than an outbreak of fire in the Council Chamber. It appears that in former days, when the hall was the residence of the late Lord Winmarleigh, the present Council Chamber was divided into two compartments. The separat- ing wall was, of course, removed in making the present enlarged chamber,and with it a flue that communicated with a fire-place below. On Tuesday some workmen who were engaged about the building burned some material in this fire-place not knowing that the flue was stoped up, and as a consequence the floor of the Council Chamber which covers the upper part of the dislocated flue became ignited. This was pretty early in the morning, and, we are informed, that both the hall keeper and the workmen were at breakfast, unaware of what had taken place. Fortunately,another employe of the Corporation, who was in the Park at the time, noticed an unusual accumulation of smoke in the Council Chamber, and made all haste to inform the hall keeper of what he had seen. No time was lost in exploring the Council Cham- ber, with the result that the fire was detected before it had secured any great hold, and it was very quickly extinguished. Th,se who have been in the Council Chamber need not be told that it contains a considerable quantity of inflammable timber, and had the fire ob- tained much headway, it would most certainly not have been easily subdued. As it was, the damage was com- paratively slight. The decorations which were lately made in the Council Chamber have been injured to some extent, but this will be repaired at the cost of a few pounds.

div.head: WARRINGTON TRADES AND LABOUR. COUNCIL.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON TRADES AND LABOUR. COUNCIL.
The monthly meeting of the above Council was held on Tuesday at the llorsemarket-st. Cocoa Rooms.

After the usual business an appeal was made to the different trades on behalf of the widow of the late Mr. Brown, ironworker, at the DaHam Forge, who died recently and left ten children totally unprovided for,and for whose benefit the ironworkers are getting up a draw, hoping that the trades of the town will co-operate. A reply was read from the Sanitary Committee to a com- munication from the Trades Council complaining of boy labour employed in scavenging and other light work, whereas old men could dolt and so keep themselves off the parish relief fund. The communication stated that the number of scavengers employed by the Corporation was 26,19 whose ages are from 40 to 74 years, 5 between 21 and 40, and 2 under 21 years. The Trades Council was of opinion that there was cause for complaint, and had communicated to the Town Clerk to that effect.

The Parliamentary Committee of the Trades Union Congress, sent their final notice of Congress to be held in Glasgow, on Monday. September sth and five follow- ing days, and an invitation to send a representative, when it was unanimously resolved, that Councillor Thomas Flood do represent the Warrington Trades and Labour Council at the forthcoming, Trades Union Con- gress, in conjunction with his own Society the Operative Stonemasons. There are some very important resolutions to be brought forward at this gathering of Trade Uni,m- ists, among which are the Employers Liability Act, Labour representation, Co-operation and Trades Unions, Government contracts, Marking of files, Royalty rents and Wayleaves, sub-contracting and bakers and night work.

div.head: DEA.TH OF MR. JAMES MA.TtSON.
div.p: DEA.TH OF MR. JAMES MA.TtSON.

The death of Mr. James Marson, J.P., took place suddenly at his residence, Hill Cliffe, on Sunday night. It appears that it was Mr. Marson's habit before retiring to rest to walk round the house and put out the lights. On Sunday evening he had partly :lone so when Major 110 l well, a guest, heard him call for help. He went to Mr. Marson's assist- ance, and was surprised to find him holding a candle ;in one hand and grasping the banisters with the other. The Major called for his son, Mr. Charles Matson, and with their joint assistance Mr. Marson, sen., walked into his bed-room. Stimulants and restorative.s were applied, and no time was lost in sending for Mr. Charles White,his medical adviser. For a thne Mr Matson seemed relieved, but in a short while he began to grow worse, and death soon resulted from distension of the bowels. Mr. Marson had been intimately connected with the firm of Messrs. Peter Stubs and Co. most of his life, and for many years was an active partner, but for the past ten or twelve years he had not taken any part in the business. He was appointed a justice of the peace for Lancashire in 1863, and was also on the commission of the peace for the county of Cheshire. Mr. Marson took a great interest in local musical affairs, and was one of the promoters of the Warrington Musical S,-)ciety some 50 years ago, the Society having in him one of it warmest supporters. For many years lie lived at Northfield, Bewsey-road. Amongst the latest of his gifts was £lOO to the building fund of St. Luke's but he expressly stipulated that his name should not be advertised, a condition which he made of most of his benefactions. In politics he was a Conservatives Ile was a land and tax commissioner for Warrington. and the West Ilucklow division for Cheshire. He was 73 years of age, and leaves a widow and one sun, Mr. Charles Marson, who is a captain in the Militia, to mourn his less. _ . _

..... At the Warrington County Sessions on Wednesday, Captain Withington, the chairman,said before taking his seat on the bench that day he wished to say a few words aboitt the loss thy Mae sustained, in the death of Mr. Janie; Marson. He was a most painstaking man, and as long as he was a magistrate there he did his very best. —The magistrates' clerk, Mr. H. Greenall, said he echoed what Captain Sirithington said. The Bench had lost a very valuable magistmto mude.l, because nobody was more ready to come f.n.ward, And do that part of a magistrates' work which •,.is perhanN the most tedious part of his duties. He wai wayo at hand with his assistance when it was called for.

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: FUNERAL.

_ _ ....... The remains of the deceas d gentleman were interred in the Warrington Cemetery on Thursday. The funeral cortege left Hill Cliffe at a qusrter past eleven, and reached the Cemetery shortly before twelve o'clock. In the first carriage were the Revs. S. Wilkinson (vicar of Timperley,'and formerly vicar of St Paul's, Warrington), and T. Pym Williamson (vicar of,Thelwall), Mr. Charles White (the deceased's medical attendant). The second carriage contained Mr. Charles Marson (son), Major Hollwell, Major Fenton ; the third, Mr. Hawley and Mr. Stubs ; the fourth, Major Linton and Mr. Colin Maclver ; and the fifth, Mr. Robert Davies and Mr. Henry Greenall. In other carriages were Mr. T. H. Lyon, Alderman Chandley, Mr. James Tinsley, Mr. J. T. Picton, Mr. Alfred Greenall, and Mr. Frost. Several unoccupied carriages which had been sent in expression of respect for the deceased's memory joined in the procession. The services were conducted by the Revs. S. Wilkinson and P. T. Williamson.

div.head: SHIP CANAL TRAGEDY
div.p: A SHIP CANAL TRAGEDY
ATTEMPTED MURDER THROUGH JEALOUSY.

The village of Ship Canal huts on Frodsham Marsh, near Runcorn, was the scene of a determined attempt at murder on Monthy. Last a navvy, named Charles Bundle, was working at this plao, but in the spring he obtained employment on the EAst Coast Railway, at chesterfield. On Monday he unexpectedly turned up at F.-odsham, and went to the hut of Mary Dukes, where lii- had previously lodged. She gave him a breakfast of ham and eggs, in company with the lodgers. In the middle of the repast he left the room, closing the door after him, and shortly afterwards piercing screams of" Murder" were heard proceeding from the kitchen. An engineer, named Henry Taylor, was first in the apart- ment, and saw Bundle fiercely striking Mrs. Dukes with a heavy poker. Taylor shouted "Good God, what are you doing this for ?' and Bundle replied "I have come this morning for the purpose of murdering her." He then ran away and attempted to escape but another lodger went in pursuit, and a blow on the head with a wooden mallet effectually stayed his progress, and he was then kept a close prisoner until the arrival of Police-sergeant Doyle from Frodsham. In the mean- , time the women of the place had take charge of Mrs. Dukes, who was unconscious, her head having been battered in. As quickly as possible Dr. Bryant, of Ilelsbv, was snmmonid, and shortly afterwards Dr. McDougall, of Runcorn, arrived, and together these medical men attended to the woman's injuries. Her skull is dreadfully fractured, and her body otherwise bruised. The doctors have small hope of her recovery. After several hours the woman re- gamed consciousness and Mr. Alfred Thomas, J.P.. took her depositions. She said the prisoner suddenly at- tacked her, and struck her several times on the head with a poker, and she remembered nothing further. Sergeant Doyle had considerable difficulty in conveying the prisoner from the spot. There was a large crowd of navvies and women present, who made a hostile demonstration, and threat- ened to lynch the would-be murderer. On being charged with the attempted murder of Mrs. Dukes, the prisoner said, "I was lodging with her last winter, and 1 upholded her, and then I went away for a bit ; and she had another chap, and I came back this morning." When the prisoner was living at Frodsham, he was know 's as Mrs. Duke's " boss lodger," and his murderous attack is put down to jealousy. Mrs. Dukes only buried her husband on Saturday. The prisoner was brought before the Frodsham bench of magistrates on Wednesdaf morning, and remanded. On inquiry yesterday our reporter was informed that the injured woman was progressing fairly well until Wednesday night when she had a serious reladse. On Thursday evening she had rallied somewhat,but her con- dition is extremely critical. Another relapse will be fatal. The prisoner will be again brought before the magistrates on Wednesday week.
A woman named Alice Howarth, who lived alone, was burned to death at Bolton on Tuesday, owing to her house catching fire. l-.. 4.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEE N
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEE N
AT WARRINGTON.

The stone which the builders (the constituency of Warrington) rejected, has, it appears, come very near being a corner-stone of the edifice of Irish political administration. According to the " Man- chester Guardian ' the choice of Mr. Gladstone for the appointment of Irish Solicitor-General lay be- tween Dr. Houston and Se.rjeant Hemphill ; though ultimately the latter was selected. The mere fact of Dr. Houston being chosen as the alter- native holder of the office Is a high distinction in itself; and will furnish additional consolation to the Liberals of Warrington, for his defeat here, in that it is another proof that their selection of Dr. Houston was amply justi- fied by his capacity. I fancy the Tories and many of the Liberals in Warrington have never realised how high he stands in his protession in Ire- , land. The Tories of IVarrington were very fond of asking—Who is Dr. Houston ? as though he was some exceedingly obscure individual, who had never been heard of—whereas he was- he now is so to a greater extent—a man of considerable eminence at the bar—and indeed stood in his own country on a level with Sir Charles ltu!sell in England. But surely after this no Tory in any constituency betore whom the Doctor may appear, will have to ask—Who is Dr. Houston ?

There is another aspect of the matter that pre- sents itself to me. ldo not know whether the pre- sentation to Dr. Houston by the Warrington Libe- rals, which was talked of recently, is to come off, and 1 don't know whether his candidature for War- rington has had anything to do with his having been under consideration as eligible for the solicitor- Generalship. It is probable that it has had,and per- haps this, combined with his meeting with Mr. Gladstone at Warrington, may have directed the attention of the Liberal leader upon his great at- tainments, with a view to his appointment. But supposiiag this to have been the case, then, indeed, ' his candidature has not been thrown away,consider- , . ing the very substantial advantages likely to result to him from so conspicuous a recognition in high quarters, of his ability. Dr. Houston, I believe, has a career of great Parliamentary distinction before him, and may yet be Solicitor-General to an Irish, if not to the English, House of Commons.

I am sorry to bear that there is any danger of the new and excellent custom of closing the Warring- ton shops all Thursday afternoon falling into desuetude. I fervently hope that that excessively hard-worked class, the shop assistants, are not go- ing to be deprived of this privilege so soon after having obtained it. If even it be looked upon as a mere experimental matter, surely the experiment has not been tried long enough yet to justify a reversion to the bad old state of things. But un- fortunately it is not the majority but, the minority which controls matters in this case. and even the smallest minority—one—may determine whether tile good custom is to stand or not. A chain--no matter how strong it is in all its other links will break if there be but a single one in it that does not hold good, so this early closing movement, if there be hut one shopkeeper that fails to stand firm, will collapse, no matter how ardent the others are in the cause.

The Warrington Trades and Labour Council, I think were quite in their province, when, recog- nising that principle, which is becoming more and more accepted, of the unity of all labour, that is, labour in all its diversities, whether physi- cal or mental, they lately published their appeal to the public to co-operate with the shop assistants in endeavouring to maintain the half-holiday. I was much pleased to see this indication of the new spirit of the brotherhood of labour,a brotherhood not to be confined among merely the various sections of that class who blacken their hands and wear mole- skins, but that ought to exist between them and all other classes of workers, physical or mental or both, who have to earn their own living. This new brotherhood of labour is a far more comprehensive thing than the old one ; and I am glad to find that the Trades Council have hearts and minds big enough to take that broader view of their province, which, animated by the new spirit, they have done. It is to be hoped their appeal, which the shopping , public have now had time enough to digest,has pro- duced, in conjunction with that of the shop assis- tants themselves, the desired effect, and that we shall not see a resumption of the Thursday after- noon opening.

It seems to me that, judging from the police cases, there are a number of men and women about Warrington who are practically mad, and it would be much safer for the pallic if they could be per- manently locked up somewhere. It is marvellous to me that with such characters constantly at large we have not one murder at least every six months in the town. I do not mean to say they are all IVarringtonians. Indeed, the facts seem to show that the majority of them are strangers. Many of the males among the desperadoes I refer to are ship Canal labourers, and the disrepute they bring upon the borough and the annoyance they cause to it are additional arguments for desiring the speedy completion of the great undertaking. But I fear the clearance of the town of this bad element will far from remedy the evil, for they will have left their contamination, which will not be soon done away with. MERLIN.

. . THE AVERAGE ATTENDANCE A ELEMENTARY SCHOOLS. THE WAY THEY DO AT ST. HELENS.

lAt St. Helens Police Court, yesterday week, before Mr. A. Sinclair and Dr. Gaskell. several ad- journed cases under the Elementary Education Act were down for hearing. At the outset Mr. W. J. Jeeves (town-clerk) stated that he appeared on behalf of the School Attendance Committee, and he wished to draw the attention of tile beneh to a certain amount of reorganisation which the com- mittee had found it necessary for improving what they had found to be a decreasing average attendance throughout the borough. In 1888 the attendance was , 77.9 per cent, and in 1891 it had gone down to 75.9 per cent., whilst in Liverpool and Widnes the attendance I was 85 per cent. The Committee's attention had been frequently drawn to the decrease by the school mana- gers, and more especially so since the new grant by Government came into force, and which was regulated largely by the average attendance. Mr. Jeeves then de- tailed the faults which the committee had found, after careful inquiry, and spoke as to the app)int- ment of more school officers, and weekly sittings by the committee instead of monthly sittings as previously, when the parents would be bronght up and, if necessary, summoned, by which they hoped to have a more direct relation between the offence and the punish- ment. It would at first result in a larger number of cases, but they hoped ultimately to be able to secure a better average attendance with a less number of sum- monses. The chairman said that he had seen many reports from other towns, in which the magistrates had been unwilling to assist the School Attendance Commit- tee. That bench, however, had always been well disposed to support the action of the committee. But, he continued, though they had in many cases reversed their judgments in the hope of inducing the offenders to improve their attendances, he might say that in fully three quarters of those cases there was no instance in which any of the magistrates had not tried to support the action of the School Attendance Committee as much as they could, and he trusted they would continue to do so in the future. Mr. Jeeves said that what he had said was not intended to be any reflection on the bench, but the committee, feeling that the magistrates had sup- ported them in the past, felt it their duty to inform them what they were going to do in the future, so that they could rdy upon the bench for their continued support, without which it was impossible that their work could succeed. I The Chairman replied that the committee could rely upon the magistrates' future support.
HOT WEA.THER IN FRANCE.
FATAL CASES OF SUNSTROKE.

The weather in Paris is still exceedingly oppressive. On Wednesday a fternoan the meteorological bureau re- gistered 96.8 Fahrenheit in the shade. Five cases of sunstroke, of which two terminated fatally, and one was followed by insanity, were reported in Paris. The " Radical" reports that while the 16th Battalion of In- fantry of Reserves were marching to Fontainbleau, three of the men were struck down with sunstroke, one of these cases proving fatal. a
FATAL ACCIDENT IN A ST. HELENS COLLIERY.

Peter Prescott, 29 years of age, a colliery fireman, of 48, Parr Stocks-road. St. Helens, died in the Providence Hospital, in that town, on Sunday morning, from injuries received in the Ashton' s Green Colliery, belong- ing to Messrs. Bromilow, Foster, and Co., on the 18th ult. Prescott was carrying out some repairs to the ventilating arrangements of one of the brows of the pit, when, by sf,ine means, a waggon of coals broke away and rushed down the brow. P'res,ott was knocked down, and badly injured about the head and leg. He was subsequently attended by Dr. Jackson, and left the hospital, after a week's detention therein, on account of the improvement he seemed to have made. Last week, however, he suddenly became worse, and was again removed to the hospital, where he died as stated. THE INQUEST.

Mr. S. Brighouse, coron2;, held an inquest at St. Helens Town Hall, on Tuesday, touching the death of Peter Prescott, 29 years of age, colliery fireman, of 48, Parr Stocks-road, St. Helens, who died in the Providence Hospital on Sunday, from injuries received at Ashton's- green Colliery., on the lath July. Mr. T. Pennington, certificated manager, represented the firm, and pro- duced a tracing of the working plan of the spot where the accident occurred.—The Coroner remarked that the plan was very unsatisfactory. It was customary to pro- duce a plan on an enlarged scale, showing all the neces- sary details, and it was very important that a jury should have such plan before them. Mr. Pen- nington said an enlarged plan would have been prepared had the firm considered it necessary.--laron Dixon, a drawer, deposed that on the 18th July he was taking a box of coals down one of the brows when it broke loose and rnshed down. He attempted to stop it with a wooden " scotch," but the " scotch " broke. The deceased was knocked down and seriously injured. It was usual to see an iron "scotch," but witness could not find it on the occasion in question. —The Coroner stated that he had a letter from the Government Inspector of Mines stating that from what he had heard he did not think it necessary to attend the inquiry. Ile (the coroner), however, thought it was a case where the inspector should be present to hear the evidence. Here the men ought to have used an iron "scotch," while they used a wooden one, which broke, and allowed a box to run away and kill a man. He suggested that the inquiry might be adjourned to give the colliery people an opportunity of drawing suitable plans.—The jury ultimately decided to adjourn.—A Juror asked if the firm were in the habit of allowing wooden "scotches "to be used.—Mr. Pennington replied that they were not in the habit of using wooden "scotches." They had always used iron " scotches" in that particular brow.—The proceedings were then adjourned. At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Wednesday, Mr. Brig- house resumed an inquiry touching the death of Peter Prescott, the colliery fireman who died through injuries received at the Asliton Green Colliery, on the 18th July. Mr. Pennington, manager, to whom the Coroner com- plained on Tuesday of the insufficiency of plans, pro- duced a new plan showing more details. Mr. Matthews, assistant Government inspector of mines, was also present.—Dr. Jackson stated that deceased really died of blood poisoning, but the accident was the primary cause, Aaron Dixon,whose evidence was given fully on Tuesday, added that he had not worked on the brow before. The scotch they used for the box was a wooden one. Previous to the accident the deceased man had told him that it was the proper thing to use an iron scotch, but as they made inquiries for and could not find one a piece of wood was used, about a foot long and three or four inches thick. The iron scotches were about a foot long and an inch and a half thick.—The Coroner remarked that it was his opinion that Dixon knew very well that they had no right to use these scotches. Martha Hall, married woman, stated that, in company with her husband, she visited the deceased at the hospi- tal a few days after the accident, and in the course of the conversation Prescott stated to her husband that it was a wonder he was not killed outright. He did not hear anyone calling to him, nor did he hear the box approaching. They should have used iron scotches, but he believed none were used. Mr. T. Pennington, the manager, said that in all cases where the men applied for iron scotches he supplied them. He considered a good wooden scotch safe enough. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death," and added that they considered proper scotches had not been supplied.
Mrs. C. Williams, a Liverpool lady, was on Monday afternoon knocked down by a passenger train when crossing the line between Bangor and Aber, and almost cut in two.

div.p: THE BALE OLD MAN.

THE QUESTION. " You are old, Father William." young man said, " Your locks and your whiskers are grey; But you're hearty and cheerful and stronger than I, Now tellme the reason, I pray. My nerves are quite shattered, my appetite's gone, I'm afraid I'm ju.t wasting away, Yet though double my years, your strength still appears, As though it would never decay. I am lonely and sad when I'm eft by myself, Though with friends I can never be gay; But you are quite lively and joyous and free, Please tell me the lesson, I pray. I can't get a partner to share my sad life— The ladies all answer me" Nay." I'm always depressed when they're at their best. Oh, tell me the reason, I pray. I've swallowed vile nostrums and pills beyond count, My vitals seem eaten away, But still I am sickly, while you are quite blythe. As lively and brisk as the day. There must be some cause for your excellent tone, Some cause why I'm wasting away, I'd give half my wealth to possess your good health, Oh, tell me your secret. I pray."
