div.head: BEFORE THE AIAGLSTRA'eE6.
div.p: BEFORE THE AIAGLSTRA'eE6.
TRANSFER OF LICENCE.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednes- day, Edward Lee Bent, applied for a transfer of the licence of Mrs. Ann Bent, Vulcan Inn, Newton, to him- self. The application was acceded to. SMOKING IN A PARK SHED.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Saturday, William Wych, 100 Manchester Road, and Robert Fair- brother, son of Thomas, 6 Porter-st., were charged with smoking in a shed in the Park on Sunday last. There was another man smoking with them, Joseph Stanley, but it appeared that he was not a Warrington man, and having finished his work in the town had left it. It was stated that he would be apprehended if possible. The charge having been proved against the others, the Chief Constable said this practice had been growing during the summer months, though there had been warning enough against it.—ln reply to the chairman the magistrates' clerk said the defendants were the first persons sum- moned for such an offence this year. The restriction only applied to the sheds, not to the open air.—The defendants were fined is. each.
A SWINDLING DEALER IN BLANK CARDS.

At the Warrington borough police court, yesterday, Henry Brown was charged with frequenting Butter- market-street with intent to commit a felony on the previous night. Inspector Spinks said about 8 o'clock on Thursday night he was at the entrance of the show ground, and saw several strange characters about. In consequence of what he was told he watched the prisoner for some time; and he repeatedly tried to get into the ground, and ultimately witness put him away. Shortly afterwards he saw the prisoner jump on to a lurry and try to get into the ground again. Witness then told a constable to keep an eye on him, and ulti- mately he was brought to the police station with a num- ber of blank cards in his possession.—P.C. Woods said on Thursday evening he was in Buttermarket-street when a young man complained to him that the prisoner had sold him for 9d. some blank cards purporting to be tips for the St. Leger. Witness arrested the prisoner, who gave ed. back to the young man. He was sent to jail for 14 days. MALTREATING A PONY AND PISTOL FIRING IN TIIE STREETS.

At the Warrington Magistrates' Court, on Saturday, Frederick Bennett, groom, 53 Finners' Brow, was charged with cruelty to a pony, by kicking it, on the 7th of June, and with discharging a pistol to the danger of passengers on the same date.—P.C. Cooper, 20, said he saw the defendant behind Orford Barracks with the pony and a spring cart. He kicked the pony in the belly several times as it was eating from the hedge, into which it had got with its front legs. He fired a pistol towards the barracks. Witness asked him what he had got in his pocket and what he had been firing, and he produced the pistol, some powder in a tin, some stone, which be had been firing, and some caps, from his pocket. —The defendant said he did not shoot stones. He only
kicked the horse once. He was shooting for the sake Of

shooting, and making a noise. He enliiied on the Mon- day following, as he did not lige to face out the proceed- ings.—The Chief Constable said he believed the reason the defendant was there now was that his father,at con- siderable expense and trouble,had bought him out of the army. He had surrendered that morning.—He was fined Sc. and costs, £1 is. in all. CHARGE OF SHOOTING NEAR THE HIGHWAY.
Isaac Ashcroft, son of Isaac Ashcroft,. Long Lane

Farm, Orford, was charged at the Warrington sorough police court, on Monday, with firing a gun less than 50 feet from the highway, on the 4th inst.—Mr. Ridgway appeared for the defence. The constable said the de- fendant was inside a gate in a -field off Winwick-road, and he was told that he shot a fowl.—lle had his back towards Winwick-road, and was 32 feet from the high- way.—The killing of the fowl was deposed to by an- other witness.—Mr. Ridgway contended that there was no breach of the law, and cited a case in which it had been decided that if from the position of the shooting the people entitled to use the highway had not sustained any damage from the shooting there was no offence. Lord Winmarleigh was the owner of the land and the defendant was simply the son of the tenant. As to shooting the fowl, fowls did enormous damage just at this time to crops, when oats were ripening.—Alderman Harrison : Supposing somebody had driven a horse past, and just at that particular moment, the horse had taken fright, and bad consequences ensued.—Mr. Ridgway said in that case he would not have contended that the defendant was not amenable. —The case was dismissed. DASTARDLY ASSAULT ON A COALYARD LABOURER.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Thurs- day, Frank Walkden, coalyard labourer, of 17, Erwood- st., was brought up on remand from the preceding day, charged with assaulting Martin McCue, coalyard la- bourer, employed by Mr. Francomb, and living at 53, Hoyle-st. On Wednesday he was charged with cutting and wounding McCue, but as the cut proved to be only slight, the charge was reduced on Thursday to that of assaulting and beating merely. The Chief Constable said the complainant,who was notoriously a very simple, inoffensive man, was at work emptying a coal wagon, and the prisoner came in a very boisterous manner, and began to call him names, for, as he said," working under prices." The complainant went on with his work for a considerable time, and ultimately the defendant sent a brick at his head, which missed him. McCue came out of the wagon for a bar, and the defen- dant hit him right and left about the head and face, and kicked him violently, and, as the complainant said, stabbed him in the hand with a knife. whcia brought to the Police Station, the prisoner said he had hit McCue and would hit him again, but denied using a knife.—Dr. Bowden,senior house surgeon at the Infirmary, deposed to dressing there a slight lacerated wound on the complainant's hand, and said anything with a sharp point would have caused it.— McCue repeated a statement made the previous day, corroborating what the Chief Constable had said, ex- cept that he denied that the prisoner had said anything to him about working under prices. In reply to the Bench he Said he was working for is. a waggon, but could not say whether that was the usual price.—James Turner corroborated, and said Walkden took a running kick at McCue and with an oath called him an Irish pig, and said he would be locked up for him.—William Ley also corroborated as to the striking.—The prisoner denied using a knife or mentioning about working under prices, and said McCue had thrown a piece of coal at him. This McCue denied.—The Chairman said the prisoner had committed a most dastardly assault on McCue, and it was only by a narrow chance that he did not stand there charged with a very much graver offence. lie would be committed to prison for two months with hard labour.

div.head: MINOR. CASES.
div.p: MINOR. CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATIIRDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Garnett (chairman) Geddes, and L. Voisey. ARMY DESERTlON.—Frederick Brayne was charged with being a deserter from the Bth Hussars at Norwich in March last. A colour sergeant from the barracks proved the case. He was sent to Strangeways jail to await an escort. .

TEBrr OF A lumen—Frances Ellis, wife of Joseph Ellis, wire works labourer, residing at 37. Guardian- street.was bought up on remand charged with stealing, the previous Wednesday night, a lady's jacket, value 255. to 305., the property of Sarah Jones, of Stockport, from

a stall in the Warrington Market. The prosecutrix missed the jacket between 6 and 7 pm.., and informed the police, and D.S. Monaghan learnt that she had offered it for sale at Gibbon's, old clothes' dealer's, in Mersey-street, and in pledge at another place. Mrs. , Gibbon was suspicious, and would not buy the jacket. Be saw the prisoner and went to her house, and her hus- band handed it up without hesitation.—Mrs. Gibbon and D.S. Monaghan confirmed this statement, and the former identified the jacket.—The prisoner said a woman gave her the jacket.—She was fined 10s, and costs, £l7s. in all, in default a month with hard labour. STREET GAMBLERS.—Bernard McNamee, son of John, 27, Dolman's-lane, Michael Mitchell, son of Bridget, 3, Ship Yard, Patrick Fallon, labourer, 9, Ship Yard, James Costello, son of Timothy, 17, Dolman's-lane, and John Glaven, son of John, 17, Bank-st., all youths,were charged with playing with cards for money on Sunday last in Ship Yard.—P.C.'s Lewis and Dale proved the charges, and the latter said they had a watcher, who, having his back to the police, failed to see them.—They were fined ss. each MOYDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Greenall) and Aldermen Francomb and Harrison. _ .

_ TRANSFER OF LICENSE.—SamueI Baxter applied for the transfer to him of the license of the Higher Seven Stars Inn, from the executors of the late Wm. Leigh.— Granted. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Thomas Pannell, in Bank- st., on the 6th inst., ss. and costs.—John Coleman, in Buttermarket-St., on Saturday afternoon. Ig.—James Doyle, was charged with being drunk and di3orderly in Ship Yard, the same afternoon. He had been fighting with the previous defendant and had injured him very much in the face. The defendant said the man struck him because he would not stand him some beer. Fined ss.—Wm. Aylward, an army reserve man, and a ship canal labourer, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly on Saturday night, also with assaulting P.C.'s Dean and Jones. He struck and kicked P.C. Dean and they rolled about and wrestled for some five minutes. A gentleman blew his whistle for him, and P.C. Jones came up. While they were taking him to the Station he put his leg round Dean and threw him down. He also kicked Jones during the struggle.--The defendant had been up previously for assaulting a man with a hatchet.—He said when he got drunk he always got excited, since he came from Egypt.—He was sent to jail for two months with hard labour.— Joseph Hares and Patrick Shaughnessy were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Fennell-st., about 10.45 p.m., on Saturday, and Hares was also charged with assaulting P.C. Rylatt. The officer said the men were drunk and fighting like two dogs, and on his ask- ing Hares for his address he gave him a blow in the face and tupped him in the chin. Inspector Bowen and a constable came to his assistance, and they took the man to the station. Witness could not say whether Shaugh- nessy struck him or not.—The other officers gave corro- borative evidence, and Hares was sent to prison for two months with hard labour, while Shaughnessy was fined 10s. and costs, in default 14 days' imprisonment.— Thomas Hennessy. drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st., at a quarter to twelve o'clock on Saturday night, was discharged on promising to leave the town.—John Mannion was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bold-st., on Sunday morning, about two o'clock. A constable found him lying on the footpath, with a new cap and vest lying beside him. The officer picked them up and gave them to him, but he threw them down, and refused to go away. 53.—Catherine Mann, of Middlewich, drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st., on Sunday night, was discharged on promising to leave thei town. DIU/MC—John Grounds, drunk in Allen-st., on Sunday evening, 2s. 6d. FIGHTINO.—James Rooney, was charged with fighting in Union-st., on the 18th inst. The defendant was fight- ing with another man, Pannell, already dealt with for being drunk and disorderly, and now said that this man asked him whether he thought there were more English- men or Irishmen employed on the Ship Canal, and be- cause he replied more Englishmen, was not pleased and struck him, hence the fight.—The defendant was bouad over in £5 for six months, and had to pay 7s. costs. STREET OBSTRUCTION. —Joseph Matthews, contractor, 33, Marsh House-lane, was charged with obstructing Buttermarket-st., on the 10th inst., by leaving bricks, mortar, Sze., there for over two hours.—He was fined ss. and costs.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Aldermen Wright (chairman) and Holmes, and Councillor James Fairclough. WIFE Assauvr.—Thomas Tully, employed at Greenall's bottling stores, Horsemarket-street, and living in Cropper's Brow, was charged with assaulting his wife, Margaret. Two constables proved the offences and said the prisoner was drunk and beat the woman, and threatened that if she was left with him ten minutes he would kill her dead and hang for her.—lnspector Uphill said the prisoner had a child badly clothed, and he went to see it, and deposed to witnessing the assault.—The prisoner denied assaulting her and said she was a drunken woman.—The Chief Constable said the woman was any- thing but what she ought to be, and the prisoner was harmless enough except that he did get a little drink sometimes. He was bound over to keep the peace, and had to pay 83. costs. TRURSDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley (chairman) and _ _ .

Councillor James Fairclough. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Thomas Pennington and Wm. Griffiths, drunk and disorderly at Market Gate, on Wednesday night, ss. and costs.—James Smith and Thomas Day, in Mersey-street on Wednesday afternoon. The defendants were begging, and Mr. Melia stated that Pennington came to his house begging of his wife, and was very abusive to her, refusing to go. Witness came out to him and asked him what he wanted, and he said bread, then that he wanted work. Witness then thrust him away—They were fined 10s, and costs each.— Catherine Elliott, drunk and disorderly in Wilderspool- road, about 25 minutes to on that morning, ss. and costs. -

ANOTHER UNSEEMLY FEMALE.—Annie Johnson, was charged with being guilty of unseemly conduct in River- road, on Wediaesday, and sent to jail for 14 days with hard labour. She had just finished 7 days in jail. SCHOOL CASES.—The following persons were dealt with, on the prosecution of Mr. George Riley, on the charge of not sending children to school.—Mary Bennett, 120, Pierpoint-st., ss. In this case the Chairman threatened the child, a boy' with a birthing if he continued to absent himself from school. The mother was fined 53.—John Buck, brick- setter, James-st., James Fogg, 3, Rooney-Bt., Joseph Gleave. Back Stamford-street, George Jaundrell, forgeman, War'ourton-street, Bridget Lennardy, 23, Warburton-street,Henry Macmahon, tanner, 28 Dannett- street, William Moran, forgeman, 40 Warburton-street, Arthur Pagett, 64 Howard-street.—Mrs. Pagett said the school mistress had sent her child a girl, home for 6d. back money, and asked why it was not paid,replied that work was so bad.—The Chairman rejoined that that was not the case, as work was most plentiful—The defendant was fined 2s. 6d.—John Whalley 63 Haydock street.

FSlDAY.—Before Aldermen Harrison (chairman) and Wright. Cm;Er.TY TO A HORSE.—James Beef,carter, 93,Tanners- lane, was charged with working a horse while in an un- fit state,on the 10th inst.,and Francis Robinson, lodging- house keeper, was charged with causing it to be so worked. Inspector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A., prosecuted, and Mr. Peace, solicitor, of Warrington, defended. The horse was proved to have been very lame on the near fore leg, from a strained fetlock, on the day in question. Mr. Peace pleaded guilty on behalf of Robinson, but urged that the offence was a light one, and asked that the cases be dismissed on payment of costs.—Keef was or- dered to pay costs, ss. 6d., and Robinson was fined 103. and costs.

THEFT BY A SOLDlER.—Patrick McDermott, a soldier stationed at Orford Barracks was charged with stealing two pairs of socks, value ls.,from the shop door of Wm. Richardson, Irlam-st. He was seen by a man named Henry Rigby to take the socks from the door, and Rigby seized him and gave him into custody. He was sent to jail for 14 days. DRUNK AND REFUSING TO QUIT.—JOIIII Gandy was charged with being drunk and refusing to quit the Lower Angel Inn, the previous night, and fined ss. and costs. _

ABiENTEE APPRINTICES.—The following apprentices to Mr. Platt, fustian cutter, were summoned for leaving their work on different dates, and putting their em- ployers to expense; and were ordered to return to work and pay of the damages by weekly instalments :—Mary Ellen Cain, 21, Friars' Green, Elizabeth Newton, William st., Fanny Jevons,Elizabeth-st.,Sarah Ellen Jones Chorley st., Amy Shaw, Wakefield-st., Catherine Melia, Carlisle- street, Ellen McCarthy, Warburton-st. Elizabeth Ann Hart, Watkin-st., and Bodelia Towey; Oliver-st., were summoned for not obeying a magisterial order to return to their work. Their cases were adjourned for a mouth, they to go to jail for IA days each if they had not in the meantime resumed work.

WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. TVESDAL—Before Mr. James Tinsley. DAMAGING WHEAT.—Daniel O'Reilly was charged with committing an act of vagrancy. He had been found sleeping in a wheat field at Poulton early on the morn- ing of the 15th inst. The defendant walked about 30 yards into the field and then lay down, doing damage to the wheat to the extent of 3s. P.C. Fleming proved these facts, and prisoner was committed to gaol for 14 days with hard labour.
WARRINGTON COUNTY S/MIONS. WZDNESDAL—Before Captain Vlithington (chairm an,)

and Mr. :Tames Tinsley:: Datma.—Michael Gann, drunk and disorderly at Sankey, on the 31st ult., ss. and costa.—John Thomp- son drunk and disorderly at Sankey, on the 11th inst., ss. and costs.—Richard Walters, on the same date, ss. and costs.—Abraham Kinder, on the 7th inst., is. and costs.—Renry Thomasson, at Sankey, on the 14th inst., ss. and costs.
A CYCLIST WITHOUT A LlGHT.—Albert Walker VIM charged with riding a bicycle without having his lamp lighted, on Saturday night. He was tined Is. and costs.

NON-MAINTENANCE OF A WlFE.—Matthew Littler, of Haydock, was charged with being in arrears £32 10s., due under a magistrates' order for him to pay 12s. ed. a week, for the maintenance of his wife Harriet. The complainant said the defendant was living with another

woman near to her home, and threatened continually to take her life, and she was afraid of violence from him. The Magistrates' Clerk said he had been committed to prison four times already for non-payment of arrears to his wife.—Fie said he could only pay 10s. towards the arrears, and ss. a week in fature, and she consented to accept the latter, but as he would make no better propo- sal as to the arrears, he was sent to jail for three months.

DAMAGING A FENCE AND ROSE TREES.—Edward Welsh, aged 20,was charged with damaging a fence and a quan- tity of rose trees, at Poulton, the property of Mrs. Sarah Griffiths, on the 24th ult. He was fined 10s. and costs, and half the damage, 7s. ed. ; in default 14 days.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY. AUGUST.O. 1892
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY. AUGUST.O. 1892
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.

Moenay.—Before Mr. Jas. Handley, and Dr. Steele. ALLEGED STREET ORSTRUCTION.—MendeI Blank, furniture dealer, Bridge-st., was summoned for having obstructed that thoroughfare by allowing a handcart to remain thereon an unreasonable time.—P.C.'s Ridgway and Pettinger, gave evidence in suppert of the charge, and Mr. J. Burton, solicitor for the defence, contended that the cart was not left on the road longer than the conducting of business in an ordinary manner required. Mr. Itaudley said the magistrates considered there was not sufficient evidence to convict, but the police had done their duty in bringing the case before them. They hoped the defendant would take notice of the proceed- ings and nvt give them further trouble.—Supt. Atherton said the defendant had been four times prosecuted for the same thing, and he had been twice convicted. STRAY Doos.—Geo. Colson, a ship canal navvy, was fined 6d. and costs Sc. 6d. for allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled and without a collar. TURNIP STEALING.—Three boys named Chas. Lowe, Enoch Walker, and Chas. Price,were charged with steal- ing five turnips value 6d., the property of William Dun- babin farmer, Weston Point.—Lowe and Walker were ordered to pay costs, and the case against Price was dis- missed.
DRUNK.—Jno. Brown and Flenry Wright were each fined for drunkenness.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THIIRSDAY.—Before Mr. H. Wade-Deacon and Mr. G. Pilkington. WrrunnawN.—Andrew Carrogher and Robert Bond, boys, Were summoned for damaging a field of turnips belonging to Peter Hodgkinson, farmer, Milton-road. The case was withdrawn.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.--Patrick Fallon, Cromwell- st. ; Wm. Crotnpton Penny-lane ; Thos. Fallon, Wilson- st ; Patrick Moran, Crom well-st. ; John Brian, Walmsley- st. ; John Wynne, Pepper-st. ; were each fined for being drunk.—Norah Redmond, Marsh-st., and T. Mitchell, Waltnsley-st., were each summoned for committing a breach of the peace, and they were bound over to be of good behaviour, in the usual sureties. A STRAY HORSE.—John Murphy, Chatham-street, was summoned for allowing a horse to stray in Cross-street, and he was fined is. and costs. I OBSTRUCTION BY A BurcrrEa.—Samuel Johnson, Elliot. street, was summoned for obstructing the footpath in Widnes-rd. on the 6th August. The defendant is manager of a butcher's shop, and he and his assistants were attracting people there in such numbers that the foot- path was obstructed for hours. A thousand people would be obstructed. One of the assistants had on a grotesque cap, and all were shouting.—The defence was that they sold cheap beef and they could not help people flocking there. They tried to shift the meat if they could.—Superintendent Keighley said the practice of "yelling and howling " by foreign butchers had become an intolerable nuisance.—Mr. Deacon said the defend- 1 ant was quite right in trying to sell his meat, but he had no right to block the footpath. As this was the first case, a fine of ss. and costs 4s. 6d. only would be im- posed. _. . . _
RIDING ON THE FOOTPATH.—Christopher Halligan, of Liverpool, was summoned for riding a horse on the foot- path, in Warrington-road, Bold. He was fined 28. 6d. and costs.

NOT BONA-FIDE.—EIi Boardman, of Abbots Hall Farm, was summoned for falsely rapresenting himself to be a traveller to William Byroin, landlord of the Bold Arms, Bold, on Sunday. The defendant said he came from the bottom end of Sutton, and he was served with a pint of ale. It was afterwards discovered that he only lived a mile and a half away. The defendant's wife appeared, and said defendant only earned 18s. a week, and there were eight children to keep.—A fine of ss. and costs 125., was imposed. It appeared that there was a family quarrel, and both defendant 3 thrashed the women.—Mrs. McMullen was bound over to keep the peace for two months, and Comisky was fined 10s. and costs 7s. 61 or 14 days.

div.head: EARTHQUAKE IN WALES.
div.p: EARTHQUAKE IN WALES.
EXCITING SCENES.

Distinct shocks of earthquake were felt between twelve and one o'clock on Thursday morning at Milford Haven and Carmarthen. One shock lasted twelve seconds, and many persons were so terrified that they rushed out of theft houses. Some men at work in the docks at Milford imagined that the dock wall was col- lapsing, but the shocks were not felt on board vessels in the harbour. Early on Thursday morning severe earth- quake shocks were felt in Pembrokeshire. The first shock occurred about 12.30, and quite terrified the in- habitants, hundreds arising from bed and gathering in the streets. The vibrations were severe, the windows and articles in the houses being violently shaken. Cage birds, fowls, horses' mid cattle were terri- fied. There were two further shocks, the last one about two o'clock, but these were less severe. Two distinct shocks were felt at Tenby, where crockery was smashed and furniture was shifted. The first shock was at 12.27 and was most pronounced, and the second occurred at 1.45. Shocks were also felt at Saunders, Foot, and Amroth, near Tenby. The weather in the area affected was last night most oppressive. Earth- quake shocks were also felt on Thursday night at Wor- cester. At Bridgend a sharp shock of earthquake was noticed at 12.20. In the Nearh district many persons were awakened by their houses shaking and a low, rumbling sound.

div.head: DROWNING CASES NEAR WAR-
div.p: DROWNING CASES NEAR WAR-

RINGTON. The body of a young man, aged between 16 and 20, was found in the Bridgewater Canal, enear Lon- don Bridge, Stockton Heath, at half-past ten on Monday. He was very poorly clad, and had no money in his possession. When taken out of the water there was a deep gash found on the back of his head. It appears that whilst two canal boats were passing one another one of the boats, as usual, allewed its tow line to sink in the canal, and when the passing boat bad gone, the horse pulled it taut and pro- ceeded oa its way. It was whilst the rope was being pulled tight that the corpse came te the surface, it evi- deatly having become entangled with it. The bdy was removed by a flatman to the London Bridge Inn, where the inquest was held on Tuesday. The wound on the back of the deceased's head is believed to have been caused by the screw of a passing steamer. —Mr. R. Dobson conducted the inquiry into the circum- stances attending the death.—The first witness, Mr. S. W. Dallow, Stockton Heath, stated that he was walking along the canal bank, on Monday, between London Bridge and Red-lane Bridge. when he saw a body in the water. He procured assistance, and the body was taken to the London Bridge Ism.—P.C.Shatwell stated that the youth appeared to be about 18 years of age, and was, he should think, a farm labourer. He was sft. 10in, in height, had a full face and blue eyes, and dark sandy hair. He should think that the body had beau in the water for eight or nine days. He (the lad) was dressed in narrow cord trousers. No report had up to the pre-' sent come to hand with regard to the name and occupa- tion of the deceased.—The jury returned a verdict of "Found dead."

Joshua Mason, 50 years of age, a native of Derby, described as a boiler maker, but latterly employed on the Ship Canal, was found drowned in the canal at Rixton on Monday morning. The deceased and others were returning frem the village of Rixton, on Sunday night, when the fbrmer disappeared from their view. A splath was heard,but the men appeared to take no notice of it, and proceeded to the huts where they lived. On their arrival they found that the deceased had not ar- rived. They commenced to search for the body at the spot where the splash was heard, but were unable to find it. The search was resumed the following morning, when the body was discovered at about seven o'clock in 22 feet of water. It was removed to the Boat Inn public-house to await the inquest.—The inquest on the body was held on Tuesday afternoon, when a verdict of "Found drowned" was returned.

A whaling party is being fitted out at a Massachusetts port with a view of obtaining a live *hale for exhibition In the fisbe;ies department. If captured, the whale will be confined ia a tank and towed to Chicago by way of the St. Lawrence river.

WARRINGTON T. SEFTON.—Rarely has a match on the Warrington ground excited so much enthusiasm as was the case on Saturday, when the Sefton Club were met in their return engagement. The match was looked upon as a foregone conclusion for Sefton, it being confidently anticipated that the Liverpool combination would again account for the local club, seeing that they were without such a trio as Messrs. S. M. and J. J.Crosfield and Capt. Manson. But the unexpected happened, and when Sef- ton were dismissed for what was apparently the poor score of 51, the favourable expressions made of Warring- ton's chance of victory were indeed many. It was,how- ever, only just managed, and credit is due to the "tail end" of the team, it not being found wanting at a critical juncture of the game. Sefton batted first on a treacherous wicket, facing the two Smiths. Jones got the amateur away to the boundary, but nothing could be done with the professional, and, with the total at eight, Overton was thoroughly beaten by an extra fast one. Jones continued to do the balk of the scoring, and runs came freely from R. Smith. The latter made two confident appeals for lbw, which were answered in the negative, and after the partnership had realised 18 runs Jones was cleverly taken at point. At the same total Stubbs was beaten, whilst only six more runs had been chronicled when the professional got at Rees's wickets. Champion tried the forcing game, and after running eight up, and with the total at 38, he fell to a clever catch by that smart fielder Podmore. Roper was never "at home" with either bowler,and after the amateur had experienced hard lines in not getting his wicket, Smith bowled him with a beauty. Sprott failed to survive the first ball, whilst F. Jones and Oakley were also dismissed with successive balls, H. Ratcliffe taking out his bat for seven. Warrington commenced their venture with Messrs. R. Smith and J. Yonge. The start did not augur well for Warring- ton's success, as at four Yonge was taken by the wicket- keeper standing back. Smith was bowled three runs later, whilst an additional run saw Bell dismissed, the board reading as 8-3-1. George Clarke and Clark (pro- , fessional) improved matters, and steady batting gradu- ally raised the score. Every run was applauded, but at 24 the amateur played one hard on. Voisey opened his account with a boundary hit, but at 31, the professional was sent back with a grand ball from Jones. Dutton and Voisey batted vigorously, and another boundary hit by the last-named closed his career, the score then stand- ing at 47. Dutton went at the same total, having also contributed eight, and the excitement of the spectators was indeed now something to be remembered. Smith drove Oakley for a couple, and then Williamson was run out. Pocimore stayed with Smith, and made the win- ning hit, but the Sefton score had only been passed by five runs when Smith was caught and bowled, and War- rington had won a good match as already stated. Both sets of bowlers displayed remarkable form with the ball, but the fact must not be lost sight of that they were greatly assisted by the state of the ground. Score : SEFTON. WARRINGTON. WARIIINGTON HIGHWAY BOARD.

The quarterly meeting of this Board was held in the Surveyor's office, Masonic Buildings, Sankey- street, on Wednesday afternoon. There were pre- sent, Captain Withington (chairman), Messrs. Thos. Blackburn, P:J. Bate, J. Houghton, J. Millington, W. Royston, J. Grounds, Walker, S. Kerfoot ; Mr. White, assistant clerk; and Mr. John Thompson, surveyor.

div.head: TELEPHONIC ENTEUPRISE.
div.p: TELEPHONIC ENTEUPRISE.

The Assistant Clerk read a letter received by the Sur- veyor from the National Telephone Co., asking if the Board would allow poles to be erected for telepbome wires along Kenyon-lane, near Kenyon Junction. If the Board consented, the company would enter into an agreement to pay a shilling per annum per pole.—The Surveyor re- ported that he had considered the matter, and found it would not be advisable to grant permission, as the nar- rowness of the road would, if the poles were erected, in- volve an obstruction. The company had better apply to the land owner for permission to erect the poles on the field side of the road fence.—The Board decided not to accede to the application, the Surveyor remarking that it was very likely that an application would be made to Mr. Bate, as agent for Lord Wilton.

div.head: CONDITION OF GLAZEBURY BRIDGE.
div.p: THE CONDITION OF GLAZEBURY BRIDGE.

The CHAIRMAN drew attention to the condition of th railway bridge at Glazebury asking if anything had been done about it.—The Surveyor replied in the nega- tive.—The Chairman said it was a most dangerous place. People were in the habit of taking shelter under it, and the doctor from Leigh always put his carriage up there ; and such was the condition of the bridge that that there would be a frightful accident tome day. The bridge was an old one, and wanted rebuilding. He wondered that the Railway Company let their express trains go over it so fast.—The Surveyor in reply to the Chairman : I have known it more than 30 years, and nothing has been done to it.—The Surveyor said the County Surveyor was there about three months ago and took a number of notes, and he thought that perhaps when the road became a main road something could be done to it.—The Clerk was directed to write another letter to the Company on the subject.—Mr. Walker observed that such bridges would not be allowed to be built now.
FINANCIAL MATTERS.

It was resolved that an agreement with the County Council by which they allowed the Board for repairs of main roads from March 25th, 1892, to March 25th,1893, a sum of £1,660, be sealed.—The clerk said Winwick conversion was not included in that, and for this the County Council allowed £2oo.—The 'surveyor said the total sum,with this £2oo,was £1,860, £lOO less than last year. WIDENING OF A MAIN ROAD. . _

A letter was read from the Deputy-clerk to the County Council stating that the petition of the Board with reference to the widening of Warrington and Widnes main road, near Sankey Bridges, had been again con- sidered by the Main Roads and Bridges Committee, and the application unanimously refused, the whole scheme appearing to be far too expensive and there being no offer by any of the local authorities interested to con- tribute towards the cost. rho treasurer's account showed a balance in hand of £6ll 16s. 4d. there was no other business of importance.

div.head: SERIOUS RAILWAY COLLISION AT ST
div.p: SERIOUS RAILWAY COLLISION AT ST
HELENS.

- An alarming collision occurred at St. Helens Station on Ttlesday morning. A passenger train from Widnes to Rainford Junction arrived in the station about a quarter to eight o'clock, and a few minutes later the driver, named Wilson, observed a pointsman signalling for his train—as he thought —to be mwed higher up the platform. He started the train for this purpose,and directly afterwards the engine ran into some waggons which were being shunted across the lines into the goods warehouse sidings. Two of the waggons were knocked clean over and consiaerably daiyaged, while several others were thrown from the rails. The passengers in the Rainford train were greatly alarmed, but fortunately none were injured. The buffer plank of the engine was smashed, and the footboards of the first carriage were Wrenched off. The permanent way was slightly damaged. Both lines were blocked, and the traffic between Liverpool and Wigan was interrupted for about half an hour.

div.head: ATHLETICS.
div.p: ATHLETICS.
NOTES ON GAMES AND
FOOTBALL.

The eruption at Etna I;no—t-111;;;,; to the eruption which has taken place in Yorkshire Rugby Football circles, On Saturday evening the ten clubs who proposed to form the Yorkshire Alliance held a meeting and considered the negotiations which have taken place between the Alliance and the sub-committee of the Yorkshire Rugby Union, and, in view of the fact that the latter body had given no authoritative answer to the request that such Alliance scheme be formed, it was unanimously resolved to secede from the Yorkshire Rugby Union. Great Scott ! What a mighty slap at the bombastic brethren of the Union !

Among the many important football matches that will be played on September 3, that in which Stockport and Runcorn are interested will no doubt furnish a splendid struggle. Both teams possess players of very high class, and the closeness of their engagements last season makes the prospect of this encounter all the more exciting. Stockport think th .y were overlooked by the Cheshire County Committee last year, and if they can play a tight game with Runcorn,they think they deserve some official recognition. They intend doing something on September 3, and they hope football enthusiasts will keep their eyes on Stockport.

The members of thri newly-formed football club to be known as the Leeds Northern are evidently determined to steer clear of any taint or suspicion of professionalism. The modern footballer is supposed to play for nothing, but is well looked after in the matter of expenses. Now the Northerners are striking out on a new line, and each player will provide himself with the necessary togs, &c., at his own expense; likewise he will pay his own railway fare, and, what is more, stand his own drinks. Wonder what they'll do with the gate-money ?

Yorkshire County football players will have special jackets presented to them in future by the County Com- mittee, in addition to the caps they have hitherto received. The jackets will be of blue serge, piped with white-corded silk and decorated with the White Rose badge, which is the time-honoured insignia of the House of York. They are of neat and tasteful appearance, and will no doubt be highly prized among Yorkshire football men.

The Sunderland Aibion F.C. is now dead, and will be respectably interred when the unlucky shareholders have paid something like £2OO between them. The Albion was a fairly managed club, but had to contend with a superior organisation in a superior competition, and the result is shown in the fact that during the season of 1890-1 they lost £248 10s. 11d., and last season £843 13s. sd. This swallows up the whole of the capital, and the shareholders are called upon to supply the rest.

div.head: eItICKET.
div.p: eItICKET.

Wainwright is the first nsan to reach 1,000 runs in all matches for Yorkshire this season, his figures during the last week having been brought up to the twelfth century. In first class cricket for Yorkshire he heads the averages with both bat and ball up to the present, and in all matches he is at the top of the batting list and second to Peel in howling. In first-class county matches he has scored 200 runs more than any of his colleagues, and 300 more in all matches.

S. M. Crosfield is an invalid—or rather, he is suffering from a bruised hand that prevents him from playing cricket,which is the same thing. He could not, says the " Athletic News," however, resist journeying to the picturesque ground of Clifton College last week to see Lancashire face the mighty men of Gloucester, and it is recorded that the invalid made a complete tour of the cricket field no less than 1,745 times during the game. It is also written down with due solemnity that the injured captain stopped every eighth pace to look at the game. The figure fiend had gone home, or we intended to ask him how many times the convalescent cricketer paused during the whole of his circus-like touring. We might mention, by the way, that S. M. Crosfielci was under strict orders from the doctor to keep quiet, and not to evcite himself. The above will give an idea how some men keep quiet.

The inconstancy of the moon made sweet Juliet deride fair Luna, but the inconstancy of the Warrington cricketers has says the same paper, caused a borough full of Juliets to speak in slighting terms of their erratic and uncertain way. Why is this thusness ? Who can explain the reason of Warrington's woeful downfall before the select of Wigan, and then expound the reason of their victorious display against Sefton ? Truly cricket is an uncertain thing, or perhaps it is the cricketers. Who knows ! At any rate, facts are stub- born and explanations fleeting.

The Nottingham men, with the exception of Shrews- bury and Gunn, who are not very conspicuous, and only five have distinguished themselves sufficiently to come within the jurisdiction of the average manufacturer. Surrey, however, are well to the fore, and Lancashire have a fair show, the former having the best in the matter of position, and the latter with regard to number of representatives. Wainwright sticks well in front, , and, as Yorkshire's best man, stands a long way ahead of any colleague from the same county.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

At the Hoo Green annual athletic sports, held on Saturday, the half-mile flat race was carried off by W. Price, of Warrington • and the first prlze in the mile al- so went to a local athlete, J. H. Fair. J. Buxton, entered for the half-mile bicycle (open) at the annual gathering in connection with the Southport Cycling Club, on Saturday, and succeeded in capturing the first prize. At Cong,leton on the same day Rollins Allen won the two miles bicycle handicap, with another local, T. Hope, third, the latter also being second in the one mile handi- cap.

div.head: AMERICAN LABOUR WAR.
div.p: AMERICAN LABOUR WAR.

So far there is no apparent prospect of the labour dispute on certain American railways being amicably• settled. Three Erie trains were on Wednesday blocked at the Seneca-st., ciossing in New York, owing to the strikers having tampered with the switches. Two com- panies of militia have been ordered to proce3d immedi- ately to Buffalo. On Tuesday evening some armed miners captured a train passing over Coal Creek, and near Oliver Springs dynamite was placed under the railway to prevent the militia from approaching. Judging from Thursday's telegrams, the labour war in America is assuming a still more serious phase. The National Guard has been ordered to the scene of the dis- turbances in Tennessee, and the deputy-sheriff is enrol- ling citizens as volunteers to assist the troops. Later intelligence reports a battle at Knoxville, in which the troops were driven back by the miners. Major Chandler, in charge of the troops, surrendered on terms of non- molestation and safe conduct for the captains, and after this the miners burned the convict stockade and build- ings. With regard to the railway strike at Buffalo, a telegram of Thursday states that the city is under mar- tial law, and the loyal military of New York have been , ordered to hold themselves in readiness.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF THE DUKE OF DEVONSHIRE.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF THE DUKE OF DEVON- SHIRE.

The Duke of Devonshire was married at Christ Church, Mavtair, on Tuesday morning, to the Dowager Duchess of Manchester. By his marriage the Duke of Devon- shire becomes stepfather of his Grace, George Victor Drogo Montagu, eighth Duke of Manchester, and better known as Viscount Mandeville, who was born in 1853, and who in 1870 married Consuelu Yznaga, daughter of a Louisana gentleman. The new Duchess of Devon- shire is the daughter of the late Count von Alten of Han- over, and was married in 1852 to the seventh Duke of Manchester, who died two years ago. It was recently pointed out "that when the wife of Mr. Victor Cavendish becomes Duchess of Devonshire, as in &Gillman probability she will, she would be the first Duchess since the year 1806. In that year died the famous Duchess Georgians, of Gainsborough fame. It was she who intro- duced the Devonshire romance into the peerage. Fifteen years after marriage it was announced that a son and heir had been born. According So the legend the son was a girl, and the Duchess, anxious for a son, changed children with a friend. The son' became Duke, but in accordance, it is said, with a private ar- rangement, never married, and simply held the title for life. On his death it passed to the kinsman, the Earl of Burlington, who became seventh and last Duke. The present Duke's mother died Countess of Burlington." In regard to the above prophecy as to the next Ducbess of Devonshire, it has been speedily doomed to non-fulfil- ment. Louisa Frederica August, once Duchess of Man- chester, is to take Duchess of Devonshire,and Chatsworth, has a fully reigning mistress for the first time for many long years. The Duke of Devonshire, it is stated, went down to Osborne, to see her Majesty and acquaint her of Ins impending marriagn. Her Majesty gave her approval to the union.

div.head: Zttters to Um Obitor.
div.p: Zttters to Um Obitor.
T-H-"i JOLLEY MEMORIAL.

_ Sir—l and my wife, desire blender our thanks to the Committee, who arranged for, and to all the friends who subscribed towards, the handsome memorial to my son which has been placed in the cemetery. We are all much pleased at the way in which the work has been done, and at the kind feeling which has been shown by all connected with it. If you will kindly insert this in your paper you will oblige, as it seems to me the most suitable way in which I can acknowledge the kindness which so many have shown to us in our trouble.— Yours truly,
ORGE JOLLEY.

div.head: MR. MATTHEWS'S QUOTATION FROM SATAN'S
div.p: MR. MATTHEWS'S QUOTATION FROM SATAN'S
SPEECH.

Sir,—Was it not an infelicitous quotation for Mr. Matthews to make at the Tory Unionist banquet at Bir- mingham on Wednesday night? The quotation which was " What though the field be lost all is not lost, the unconquerable will to submit or yield," is part of the speech of
The apostate angel, though in pain Taunting aloud, but racked with deep despair,"

when having been cast out of heaven he was plotting " in a place of utter darkness, fitliest called chaos," with his fallen spirit-lieutenant for revenge. As a poetical effusion Milton's lines are of acknowledged grandeur, but used as a political attack they are apt to rebound to the discomfort of and are not very flattering to the speaker, his applauding hearers, or the party he embraces as his allies.—Your Stc., FM NOT ONE OF THEM.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Sir,—l read Mr. Brandreth's remarks at the last meet- ing of the Runcorn Board of Guardians with great as- tonishment, because I have always understood it to be an elementary qualification in a person who occupies the position of Chairman of a Finance Co:nmittee,to have at least some knowledge of the accounts which ceme under his supervision, and especially when such an individual claims to enlighten his fellow-members and the public generally. Well might Mr. Taylor say "it pleases him and harms nobody else." Mr. Brandreth says "Runcorn contributes £1,500 a year to the union, and they take out more than £1,500 a year in their poor alone." Now, Sir, what are the facts? For the year ended Lady Day, 1892, the overseers of Runcorn paid to the treasurer of the Guardians £3,895, £1,624 of which was for county and police rate, and £2,271 for poor's rate. With regard to the disposal of these sums I have nothing whatever to do. The absurdity of the supposed comparison has al- ready been demonstrated in the columns of the " Exami- ner" of Saturday last, and with the above additional exposure of Mr. Brandreth's inaccuracy, I venture to think his discomfiture is about complete. The public await with interest Mr. Brandreth's explanations of his supposed facts.—l am. tec., WILLIAM SUTTON, Assistant Overseer. August 18th, 1892.

div.head: BREWSTER SESSIONS.
div.p: THE BREWSTER SESSIONS.

Sir,—The Brewster Sessions are again at hand involv- ing our magistrates in weighty responsibilities. On the one hand will be the brewers and their allies, pleading for the development of their ruinous traffic. " Vested interests," is the cry of all such promoters and defenders of the drink trade. The freedom they claim in the inter eat of the people is but the freedom of the spider to catch its victims as prey. "Oh !" says Archdeacon Farrar, " when those who are most guilty of this massacre of souls stand before the judgment seat of God, will not the angels of those lost little ones " plead trumpet- tongued against the 'deep damnation of their taking off ?" Whether the curse and guilt of the drink business is to increase or decrease in our town, rests largely on our magistrates. They have the power to increase or de- crease drinking facilities and the inevatiable consequence on all those whose present deplorable condition pitifully plead, for deliverance from the abounding tempations to drinkers. lam glad that our town is blessed with some few magistrates who do their duty from a love of hum- anity, and not of the drink trafic. We need more of this class on our Borough Bench. Surely we need no more new drinking places to curse those parts of the town where the brewing interest now are endeavouring to plant their plague spots, as they want to do in Battersby-lane and Bewsey. "We want, in the words of Archdeacon Farrar "freedom for the right, which means suppression of wrong; liberty for virtue, which means prison bars for crime. eive us this, and in ten years' time, with the drink fiend hurled from his throne, England would be such a paradise that you would hardly recognise her from what she now is."

IQ the Interest of hellthi happy hoe, and the Tlibrals of the people, we hopefully plead that ne ntw drink licenses will be granted in our already drink- cursed town of Warrington.—Yours truly, R. STOREY. Warrington.

div.head: -- THE LINCOLN JUDGMENT.
div.p: -- THE LINCOLN JUDGMENT.

Sir,—Kindly allow me a little space to enter my pro- test against the decision of the Privy Council, and give tuy reasons for so doing. First, Bishop King is a mem- ber of the E C U whose object is to bring the Church of England back to the see of Rome. I would ask how many of the Privy Council are in touch with this society? By their fruits we shall know them. When professor at Cuddesdon College he taught that prayers should be made for the dead. He thought that confes- sion and absolution should become" a substantial part of elementary education." Ile recommended many ritualistic books one of which Charles I directed to be burnt as popish. No marvel then that out of 160 students, who were under him during the ten years he was principal, 129 are stated to have become ritualistic priests, and eight to have openly joined the Church of Rome. The last clause of article 28 condemns Bishop King ; article 35, third part of the homily on idolatry, also condemns him, viz.," For in the day it needeth not but was ever a proverb of foolishness, to light a candle at noon time. Seemeth he therefore in his right mind who offereth up to the Giver of light, the light of a wax candle for a gift ? God requireth another gift of us, which is not smoky, but bright and clear, even the light of the mind and understanding." The same article on prayer says: " Oh that all men would studiously read and I search the Scriptures ! then should they not be drowned I in ignorance, but should easily perceive the truth, as well of this point of doctrine as of all the rest." Turning the back upon the congregation during divine service is an insult. It does not in all cases mean eastward, because many churches are built north and south, and south and north, butit means according to these Roman- izers. " the position of a sacrificing priest." Of such an official the N.T. is silent. We read of " apostles, prophets evangelists, pastors, and teachers," but in vain do we find " sacrados." It comes from paganism or sun-wor- ship. The ritual means that after the prayer of conse- cration, these would-be priests have brought Christ down from heaven, and put Him inside a bit of bread, and they thus practically deny the presence of the Holy Spirit. I venture to say that the spiritual administra- tions of such men are practically nil. ROBERT FOULKES. Frodsham, August 17, 182.

div.head: WAS SHELLEY AN ATIIIEST ?
div.p: WAS SHELLEY AN ATIIIEST ?

Sir.—l have read with much pleasure your graceful leader on the subject of the Shelley centenary, and also the brief report of the Rev. F. K. Freestcn's sermon on " Was Shelley an Atheist ?" Great men are generally misunderstood by their generation, and Shelley was,pro- bably, no exception to the rule. For his poetry I have the greatest admiration. lam prepared to say there is but one Shelley. But he is an apostle of despair. Whether Shelley was an atheist or a pantheist is a question of comparatively no importance. To the theistic thinker, for all practical purposes, there can be but little difference between their speculative positions. If their advocates are logical, both systems alike are fatal to human aspiration and human endeavour. Human freedom is a mockery, and life beyond the grave a delu- -Won. It does not heishten my appreciation of Shelley to

think of him as a pantheist. There is a kind of Chris- tian pantheism current in certain quarters—Prin- cipal "Caird, I think, is its chief exponent—but that is not the pantheism of Shelley. Might we not say that Shelley's pantheism was a poetic atheism? " Given an extreme sensitiveness, a dominating passion for the beautiful in all its forms, a keen perception of the ideal, and along with these positive powers the utter absence of any faith in a Supreme Presence at once lov- ing and just, and you have the perfect condition of a perfect pessimism. Pessimism flows from such a con- stitution as naturally as streams the lightning from some thunder-laden cloud. Poor Shelley! Poor faithless Shelley ! God be merciful to thee in that day when the Great Book of Life is opened. Of his power as a poet I say nothing ; he needs no words of mine. And, besides, pages could not give a orrecter view of his power and of its scope than the glowing brief passage from Macaulay :--" Out of the t }Uncle:Ate terms of a hard, cold, dark metaphysical system he made a gorgeous pantheon full of beautiful, majestic, and life-like forms. lie turned atheism itself hsto a miythology rich with visions as glorious as the tods' that live in the marble of Phidias, or the Virgin saints, that smile on us from the canvass of Murillo." Quite true every word of it ; but by no effort, however successful, and by no creation of his genius, though ever so splendid, could Shelley dispel the gloom so natural to atheism, or dethrone pale melancholy from sitting in the place of God. Singer of a glorious, if baseless, liberty ; a splendour among shadows ; a bright blot upon this gloomy scene ; unequalled melodist of Nature's sweetest music ; he was all these and more beside,yet terribly sad of soul. Nor was Nature so bad in all her Southern beauty able to stem back the confession which bubbled from his heart-depths at Naples : I could lie down like a tired child And weep away the life of care Which I have borne and yet must bear.

Never a style so orphic:as Shelley's. Mountains and stars and suns, rivulets, mossy banks,and winding dellq, day and night, summer and winter, grey rocks, blue waves, and forests green are clothed upon with an en- trancing loveliness. Under his creative touch earth's
Fields and woods ever renew Their green and golden Immortality.
Nature is no longer the not self but our other-self, and our beloved brethren the

Waves, flowers, clouds, woods. rocks, and all that we Read in their smiles and call reality. But what of human souls? Ah ! They are strangled in the coils of a beautiful necessity, while misery—shadow- vested misery—keeps funeral watch, and sorrow with her family cf sighs bears ghostly company.

We decay Like corpses in a charnel ; fear and grief Convulse us and consume us day by day. And cold hopes swarm like worms within our living clay. We rest—a dream has power to poison sleep We rise—our wandering thought pollutes the day. We are as clouds that veil the midnight moon ; How restlessly the spread and gleam and quiver, Streaking the darkness radiantly I Yet soon Night closes round and they are lost for ever.

What could be more desolate, more hopeless, more heartbreaking than the above? Sad notes in a still sadder requiem—the requiem of a priest of an evil faith. Says Goeth, " Man's hour on earth is weakness, error, strife," and man's destiny, writes Shelley, consists in
Seeking alike from happiness and woe A refuge in the cavern of grey death.

Shelley's " Alastor " is perhaps the most gorgeous poem in the language, the beauty and subtlety of its expression and imagery is unsurpassed ; but the taint of death is in it. No hope, no faith, an epic Indeed of loss. eternal loss. Does the dark gate of death Conduct to tky mysterious Paradise 0 sleep? Let Shelley answer his own Query. The blackness of never-ending night lurks in the reply. Does the bright arch of rainbow clouds. And pendant mountains seen in the cairn lake Lead only to a black and watery depth— While death's blue vault with loathilest vapours hung Where every shade which the foul grave exudes, Hides its dead eye from the detested day ? Conduct 0 Sleep to thy delightful realms I

0 heart and mind and thought I What thing dolt thou Hope to inherit in the grave below ? Barely does Shelley's faith rise higher than the follow- ing, and even in this instance it is mingled with a bitter cynicism : It is a modest creed. and yet Pleasant if one considers it, To own that death itself must be Like all thereat a mockery. Yours truly, W. H. BUTLER. Wilderspool.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

COMBINED SUNDAY SCHOOL TRIP. —The annual trip in connection with the Wesleyan Primitive Methodist and Zion Chapels was held on Monday. The excursion this year was to Southport, and 700 persons, for whom the services of two trains had to be requistioned, partook of the opportunity thus provided for a cheap trip. The party returned at eleven o'clock the same night, after having spent an enjoyable day. FRIENDLY SOCIETIES' l'uocesszori.—On Bunday after- noon the friendly societies in connection with Lymm and Oughtrington, assembled at the Cross, Lvmm, and, accompanied by three bands, proceeded by way of High-lane, to St. Peter's Church, Oughtrington. There a special service was held, and the sermon was preached by the Rev. S. Wainwright, vicar of St. John's, Altrinc- ham. Special anthems were sung by the Lymm and Oughtrington choirs. Mr. 0. G. Smith, Mus, Bac. pre- sided at the organ. The members again assembled after the service, and marched back to the Cross.

ALLEGED THAFF OF A PIIRSE.-At the Lymm Police Court before Mr. W. P. Norris, and Mr. W. P. Brabazon, George Sheridan, fireman, Liverpool, was charged with having stolen a purse containing £1 2.5. the property of "Nurse Gray." From the evidence given it appears that the complainant was in a swing-boat when she dropped her purse. The prisoner, who was in charge of the swings, picked it up, and was seen to do so by a man named Shellorn. The prisoner, who was appre- hended by Sergeant Wynne, was committed to Knuts- ford Gaol for a fortnight.
- - CROFT. THE ItHerons.

Yesterday Archdeacon Clarke, as commissary for Bishop Ryle, instituted the Rev. 8.. I. Wadeson for the rectory of Croft-with-Southworth, near War- rington, vacant by the resignation of the Rev. T. P. Kirkman.

BOWLING AT CROFT, The village of Croft was a favourite resort of bowlers on Saturday, as no fewer than three clubs visited the village, whilst one local ' club played, their last match away. The members of the Horse Shoe Inn Bowling Club, at Croft, to the number of about 25, were conveyed to Halton Castle. The prizes, which consisted of a copper kettle, small clock, garden spade, &c., were won as follows :-1 W. F. Pennington ; 2, T. Houghton; 3, J. Houghton 4, C. Allen; and 5, W. Green. The members of the bowling club hela at the Colliers' Arms, Tyldesley, had a picnic to the Horse Shoe Inn, Croft, when they played their closing game for the season. The members, to the number of 20. competed for prizes, when the tollowing won :-1, W. Derbyshire; 2, Isaac Elliott ;3, John Leech. The members of-the bowling club held at the Church Inn, Farnworth, near Bolton, played their closing game on Saturday afternoon, on the bowling green at the Horse Shoe Inn, Croft, the number of members competing being 33. The prizes consisted of copper kettles, teapots, blankets, &c.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

A Turn TO JAPAN. The Rev. E. S. Jackson, vicar of Great Sankey, on Saturday morning set out on a four months' tour to Japan. The duties of the parish will be under- taken by the Rev. Mr. Jones, the curateoluring Mr. Jackson's absence. Bnese BAND TRIP.

On Saturday the members of the Penketh Wes- leyan Brass Band held their first annual trip, the place selected being Lymm. The party started at 1.15 from the Crown and Cushion in a four horse bus, the band enlivening the journey by playing lively music. Tea was partaken of at the Spread Eagle Hotel, and the party. wandered about the beautiful village till it was time to return. Home was reached at 10 p.m., the party having enjoyed themselves to the utmost.

div.head: NOVEL CRICKET MATCH AT PENKETH.
div.p: NOVEL CRICKET MATCH AT PENKETH.

On "Sa-t.usr-d-ai-Tn--a-musing cricket match was played on the Recreation ground between the "Penketh Bullies" and a team from Sankey Bridges. The " Bullies" are a team of boys of ages ranging from seven to nine years. They are under the management of Mr. James Woodward, who takes a great interest in the small boys of Penketh. The match resulted in a win for the home team by 26 runs. The boys behaved themselves fairly well,the victorious " Bullies " contenting themselves by chasing their opponents cif the field.

On Monday morning two girls named Robina Frascir and Florrie Bedell were drowned at Penmaenztawr while bathing. One of the victims was the daughter of Mr. Bedell, J.P., Wilmslow, Cheshire, and the other ;I Mr. Alexander Fraser, Bowdon, Cheshire. It is surmised that they were carried off their feet );.y the force of the waves.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, AUGUST tO, 1892,
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, AUGUST tO, 1892,
BRI,USTOOAN. AN' TRA.YCLE.
(MIXED.)
BI TIM 0' DICK OP Boa's.

Like as there's nobbut bad news i'th' 'Rippers this week so far, an' aw dorn'd meean th' eases o' dreawnin' an' suicide, atogether, nor th' boostin' accidents an' railway collisions, though there's, plenty on 'em. But there olez is at halladay times, ' wod wi' extry traffic an' th' extry keerlessness, tie last especially. Id were nobbut t'other week as th' hatters coom eawt on strike, an' th' tailors hes followed suit ; they've getten "as mad as hatters" some bock wod say, but there's method i' their madness. Aw dudn'd use to be i' favour o' strikes, but aw begun to see as th' employers olez wanted things their own way, an' as a satisfactory settlement couldn'd be med bi arbitration i' nine cases eawt o' ten, sooa aw howd up mi hand i' favour o' strikin', when no other way 'II do. Id means a gret loss, an' a lot o' pinchin' nay, clammin' for us mony a time; but we lievn'd to think o' thad when we're feightin' for thad as is reight ;we mon think o'th' good werk we're doin' for eawr childer, an' their childer after 'am, an' wheere we should ha' bin iv eawr faythers hedn'd fowt an' suffered for eawr sakes. This tailors' strike doesn'd mek mich difference to me, becose aw nobbut ged one suit a yeer an' aw geet this year's abeawt two month sin' ; sooa aw'm reight up to next summer, for aw could wear mi Sunda' clooathes for wertday at a pinch, an' aw've known Id to be done, mind yo'. But its th' two lads aw hey as bothers me ; they're olez wantin' new suits an' new shoon, an' petchin', an' shoon soilin' ; iv aw'd moore clooathes mysel' id wodn'd matter so mich. becose they could be cut deawn for th' childer. But aw heyn'd, an' there'll be theawsands moore sittiwated like me, sooa we'll join i' hooapin' as th' strike 'll be short and sweet, iv nobbut for th' sake o' members o' perlyment en' others, but espe- cially th' fost ; a lot on 'em want new clooathes, on Keir Hardie i' pertickler, accordin' to wod some o' th' London pappers say—an' they owt to know. Do aw agree wi' Ged eawt wi' yo' Let every mon pleease hissel say aw, iv he geds laughed at he hes but hissel' to thank for id, an' bein' laughed at breyks no booans. Iv a chap's bin a collier let him gooa to his weik theere in his collier's clooathes, Davy lamp an' o' yigh, an' coyl- dust, too, iv id'il do a bit o' good; same wi' Arch iv he wants to gooa in a smock, an' hale a steoan o' hay an' straw scattered abeawt him. Happen th' Hooam Rulers 'll spoort shilaleys, an' long-tailed cooats, sooa as they con invite th' Unionists to treyd on 'em; then id'll nobbut want th' we his chopper, an' Randy we his lion flayer to mek th' whol thing a tremendous success. Venice i' Lon- don wodn'd be in id, nor th' Lyceum, nor the Opera; even tie World's Fair wod seem little compared wi' Id. An' wod gate money they wod tek : There'd be enough for payment o' members, on quite as liberal a scale as footbo' players are paid; an' wi' th' odd tooathri million left o'er they could do away wi' th' income tax, an' duties on impoorts, an' buy eawt o' th' sweaters, an' aw dorn'd know wod else beside. This is another good idea o' mine, an' aw mek Har- court a present on't. Aw med his predecessor Goschen th' present o' mi idea o' chergin' tow' to hear nasty divoorce cases, an' mertherers sentenced; but id worn'd acted on th' consequence bein'— wheere is he ?

Aw olez believe i' doin' at Rome as they do at Rome, an when aw ged toed into a M.P. aw shall ride to th' Heawse in a cab, an' hey a new suit o' black, an' a top hat wi' sleeves in; yo' know aw think aw could tawk as sensible i' good togs as aw do i' poor uns. Hardie hissel wod say "well, aw'll be—summat" iv he were to see a collier goon deawn th' pit wi' his Sunda jump on, or a collieress wi' a white frock werkin' at th' pit meawth.

Tother bit o' bad news is as meawld is spreykin' i' th' hop plantations i' Kent, an' as poor crops 'll be th' result. This isn'd as had as it looks when yo' come to consider as they dorn'd use hops i' mekkin' drink, ony moore nor they use grape-juice i' mek- kin' wine; it's logwood, an' o' soorts o' "chemical combinations." Still id may meean as a lot o' !fops 'll nod be wo'th pickin', an' thad meeans no werk or halladay for a lot o' poor fooak abeawt London, an' that's bad._ _ _

A London papper were commentire on a case t'other day, an' id med some varra sensible remerks. Id were a assault an' battery case, between a young wife o' seventeen an' her husband o' eighteen ; they'd getten wed on eleven shillin' a week between 'em, an' findin' they couldn'd mek ends meet th' lass went hooam, After a bit th' husband axt her to come back, but hoo wodn'd, soon he peyled her. Th' Globe says: "Now, had this unfortunate girl only been taught while at school how impossible it Is for two townapeople to live on 115. a week in anything like decent comfort, she would probably have told her suitor to repeat his proposal as soon as he had doubled his income. In many cases it is ignorance about domestic economy and its require- merits that leads to these ill-starred unions. The young couple do not go into the arithmetical part of the problem ; their general assumption is that what has been enough for one can be made suffi- , cleat for two by a little re-adoption of ways to means."

Iv ony young three-loom weyver as is addlin' abeawt fourteen bob a week, an pays a tenter eighteenpenpence a week eawt on 't, sees this aw hooap he'll read, mark, learn, an' inwerdly digest id; forther, aw how he'll go on payin' his dad an' mam nine bob a week for booard an' lodgin' an' weshin' for some time to come. It's a lot too mich, aw' dorn'd deny, but wi' heawses at four an' six a week, an' flesh meyt th' price id is aw see nowt else for id. Ile mon wait till he geds to managin' four looms beawt tenter afoore he geds spliced ; an even then he mon be prepared to spend varra little i' gooin' to see play-actin' 44' 1.9909' Datchn good owd proverb as says marryin' is easy, but ' heawsekeenin' is herd; yo corn'd live on love alto- ' • gether, an yo' happen know thad other sayin' abeawt wod. flies eawt o' th' window when poverty knocks at th' door. Aw've bin single at one time whether yo' believe me or nod, an' aw geet wed beawt a extry-special license, an' id costs varra little for the performance; an' iv aw may rely on mi memory aw should say as a couple" i' my humble spear o' life corn'd live com- fortably on less nor five an' twenty shillin' a week. I' thad sum aw should alleaw four an' six a week for rent, another three an' six for clooathes ; food aw think twelve an' six, an' coyles, gas, an, extrys th' remainder. An' there isn'd a greeat deal left to'rt hevire a month on th' continent every summer. noather—except yo' save a bit bi a moonleet flit, an" jew th' grocer eawt o' tooathri peawnd. No deawt somebody 'll write to me au' say they con ged a nice little heawse th' country at one ' an' tuppence a week, wi' a gerden as 'le mek three times as mich. That's o' varra wed, but aw'm tawkin' o' th' same two fooak as th' London papper does. A chap as hes to be at th' pit, or th' factory, or th' feawndry, at six o'clock th' mernin' doesn'd feel inclined to walk two or three mile theere so soon on ; an' he's less inclined at neet after a herd day's werk. An' tram fares are nooan so chep as yo'd think.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY TRAGEDY IN AMERICA. DEATH PREFERRED TO DISHONOUR.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY TRAGEDY IN AMERICA. DEATH PREFERRED TO DISHONOUR.

A sadal-cl-c-xt;a-o—rdi-na-r-y—t-raie-dyTa-sTus-t—o-cc-u-rred at Smithville, Missouri. One of the best-known farmers in that region, Peter Macaulay, who, in addition to being well-to-do, holds a prominent position in local church and town circles, drove into Smithville on Wednesday, and during his stay imbibed too freely and got into a political dispipte, which became so warm that he was placed under arrest. There is little likelihood that the charge would have been pressed, or even entered, owing to the respectability of the parties; but reverthelesa his sou, a proud and sensitive young man of nineteen, who is engaged to be married to one of the belles of the town, seems to have made up his mind that the stain on the family name was irreparable. upon hearing the news he went to a gunshop and pur- chased a revolver and had it loaded by the shopkeeper. fie put it in his pocket and hastened after the constable who was procgedin,g to the police station with his father in charge. He stopped them, faced his father and said, " I have always been a good son to you. I have done all in my power to protect our family name and guard our family honour. No member of our family has ever been taken te gaol, and death is preferred." With these words he drew the pistol, placed it to his father's breast and fired, Macaulay falling dead before the horrified constable could recover his senses. The young man placed the pistol to his own head and killed himself. He fell upon his father's body. The event has caused great sorrow in Smittiville, where the parties are well known,and the deepest syinpathy is felt for Mrs. Macauley and daughters. The son was a young man of the highest character, and remarkably popular in the district.

The Paris " Figaro " states that owing to an impor- tant discovery by the French Inspector of Telegraphs the great difficulty in the way of long-distance tele- phonic communication under water has now dis- appeared.

div.head: CHESHI RE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.
div.p: CHESHI RE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.
SRO W AT WARRINGTON.

The annual show of this Society was yesterday opened under very favourable circumstances in a field off Wilderspool Causeway. The weather • was exceedingly fine, and the attendance, especially in the afternoon, was very large, amongst those pre- sent being Sir .Gilbert Greenall. For some time past workmen have been engaged in erecting tents and wooden structures of various kinds, and the whole of the arrangements in this respect seemed to be of an adequate character. The programme of yesterday included the judging, a display of turn- outs, jumping, and a parade of prize animals in the ring, the yard closing at 7.30. The show will be again open to-day from 9 o'clock till half-past four when exhibits are allowed to leave the yard. With regard to the entries the fol- lowing particulars will be of interest. The entries in 1891 reached the total of .504, and were made up as follows :—Farms 6,•cheese and butter 51, cattle 85, pigs 27, horses 118, sheep 38, seeds and veget- ables 99, farm produce 2, cottage tenants 20, im- plements 58. The previous year no returns were kept owing to the society amalgamating with the Royal Manchester and Liverpool Society,but in 1889 when the show was held at Congleton, the total number of entries was .603, comprising farms, 2; cheese and butter, 48; cattle, 91; pigs,,2l ; horses, 194; sheep, 53; seeds and vegetables, 139 ; farm produce, 2; cottage tenants, 12; implements, 38! The returns for 1892 are as follows :—Farms, 4: cheese and hinter, 45; cattle, 66; pigs, 30 ; horses, 191; sheep, 53 ; seed and vegetables, 85; farm pro- duce, 1; cottage tenant, I; implements, 48; mak- ing a total of 546.
