THE LOCAL EXHIBITS. Not the least interesting features of the show to War- ringtonians are the displays of local exhibitors. These are not confined to any one part of the ground, but are to be found in different parts of the field. One of the largest and most interesting of these stands is that of Mr. J. S. Garland, ironmonger, of Bridge-st., which is numbered 44. There is a great variety of exhibits upon it. Having regard to the character of the show Mr. Garland has on view, among other agricultural imple- ments, a patent improved garden turnip cutter, a new pattern hollow dix gorge turnip cutter, a new pattern turnip slicer, an oil cake breaker, and chaff cutters of different designs. But, in addition to these there is a fine assortment of fire grates, some of them purely useful and others highly ornamental ; and a variety of stoves for burning coal, coke, and petroleum. A kitchen range which is particularly worthy of atten- tion is the Yorkshire and Leamington collapsible range. It embraces many ingenious contrivances for economis- ing fuel and facilitating cooking and boiling operations. Another of Mr. Garland's specialities in this line is the "Nautilus" grate for which many advantages are claimed. A special show is also made of Bissell's carper sweepers,which are evidently a very great improvement on the old broom and dust-pan method of sweeping carpets. By running these sweepers over a carpet all the dust is automatically gathered into boxes, film which it can be emptied by merely pressing a spring, and without in the least soiling the fingers. Among the other exhibits on this stand are sewing machines, wringing machines, knife cleaners, garden chairs and swings, and tents.and a wide selection of domestic articles. The stand of Messrs. Henry Mil- ling and Cempany, Limited, is a particularly attractive One. Its attractiveness is largely due to the veri taste= ful grouping of a great quantity of preserved fruits, Sze., in tins and bottles,with artistically designed lebels. In ad- dl.:, on to these, however, there is at this stand some fine specimens of home-cured bacon and hams, home-ren- dered lard, and home-made sausages. A display is made too, of chests of dietetic tea, a speciality of Messrs. Milling and Company. At the further end of the field is the stand of Messrs. Williams and Clay, of Crossfield- street, Warrington. Prominent on the stand is the " Swinton" improved patent lifting fire range with closed or open fire. It is an ingenious piece of mechanism, and it is claimed for it that it combines all the latest improvements, saves one half in fuel, and cannot get out of order. It certainly seems to offer every convenience for all kinds of cookery, and for the saving of laboer. Around the stand are also grouped a collection of hand- some grates for dining, drawing, and bedrooms, and many beautiful examples of painted tiles. Near to this stall is that of Mr. W. Ashton, of Sankey-st., contain- ing bassinettes, bath chairs, and invalid carriages. The invalid carriage has been admirably contrived for the uses to which it is intended to be put, and the arrange- ments era such that it might be used in any weather with comfort and safety to the inmate. A noticeable exhibit is a perambulator and a swing cradle combined, the invention of Mr. Ashton. When fixed in a certain way the apparatus is as rigid as need be for a perambu- lator, hut by an easy readjustment the body of the perambulator is so hung that it at once becomes a swinging cradle. Altogether, the stand is a very ' interesting one. Of an altogether different description are the exhibits of the Stockton Heath Forge Company. The patent shovels and spades of this Company which have won such reputation amongst users of that class of article, are here to be seen in much variety. These spades are made by a process,only used by the Company, out of one solid piece of steel without a weld, and there- by several advantages are secured over similar imple- ments made in a different way. During the day a medal was awarded this Company for their spades. A highly interesting stall was that of the Castle :tub- ber Company, Limited. It contained a very varied collection of India rubber goods manufactured by the Company, including waterproof clothing, carriage mats, rugs, hose pipe, waterproof cart sheets, and every description of vulcanised india rubber for general mechanical purposes. This Company was also successful in winning a medal for specialities. Mr. C. Jackson Holmes, of Market Gate, has on view a wide selection of horse clothing, macintoshes, travelling rugs and bags of various descriptions, and all evidently of high quality. Other local stands that we noticed were those of Mr. Peter Newton, of Wilderspool Causeway, containing a collection of churns and dairy utensils; Messrs. George Venn and Son, sadlers ; Messrs. Sut- ton and Company, ironmongers, who obtained a medal for their grinding mills ; Mr. Joseph Muskett, Higher Walton lurry works; M. Spann, hurry and van works, Friar's-green. Both Messrs. Pierpoint aud Co., and Mr. G. Starkey, of Golden Square. made a capital display of seeds and garden and field produce. Messrs. Pierpoint's show is hugely composed of flowering bulbs, a magnificent lot orgladioli adding effect to the display. This firm had the decorating of the luncheon tables and cheese and butter tents, a work which they carried out with much effect.

div.head: LUNCHEON.
div.p: LUNCHEON.

Luncheon was provided in a marquee on the ground. The Mayor (Mr. E. Greenall) presided, and there were among those present Alderman Francomb, Councillors Heaton and Jenkins, Mr. R. Davies, Mr. John White, the Rev. J. H. Armitstead, Mr. Mclver, and the Misses Greenall. The Mayor having proposed the usual loyal toasts, Mr. JOHN WHITE proposed that of the Cheshire Agri- cultural Society, and the Warrington SAire Horse

Society. In the absence of the chairman, he remarked that he had never before been at a show of the Cheshire Agricultural Society, therefore he was unable to say , whether their present show compared favourably OT ' unfavourably with any that Lad gone before it. But he. could say this, that if they never held a better show than they held that day they would have a very full clainiupon the support aud sympathy of the public. ' The exhibits might not have been very numerous in some cases, but he thought they were all of great merit, and, after all, it was better to see a few good things than a great lot of things of only average merit. lie hoped the success that had attended the exhibition in that part of the county might Induce the society to pay it another visit at no distant date. (Applause.) As regarded the Warrington Shire HcirseSociety, which was absorbed for the time being into the Cheshire Agricultural Society, he might say that-during the short time it had been in existence it had done a great deal of good in that neighbourhood, and if the trade in horses was not what it used to be, he hoped that horse breeders would not be discouraged in their effoits in breeding horses in the county of Cheshire and the adjoining county of Lancashire. (Applause.) Mr. Thomas SMITH of Chester responded. Be said he was quite sure the Cheshire Agricultural Society were quite proud of the ?Tarty welcome they had met with in Warrington, and would be only too delighted to receive an invitation to repeat their visit. (Applause.) Mr. knit{ DAVIES also responded, on behalf of the War- rington Shire Horse Society. He said he was very sorry to say that their Chairman was not present, and he was only the vice-chairman, and a very retiring member of the society. Their part of the show was rather a small one as far as numbers went, but, as Mr. White said, it was better to show a few good animals than a ruck of poor things. (Applause.) Mr. ALFRED ASHWORITI proposed the toast of "The Mayor and Corporation of Warrington," coupled with the name of the Mayor. He remarked that when the question was raised as to where the show should be held Warrington stepped forward with great spirit, and won in a canter, and not only won, but induced the Society to extend their show overtwo days. (Applause.) The MAYOR in responding, said he was especially pleased to see Li show held again in that district, after the lapse of many years, and they hoped that in years to come they might again be called upon to welcome the Cheshire Agricultural Society there, and that that meet- ing might be marked in their list as a most successful one ; and if the interest with which it had been looked forward to were any criterion, it could not fail to be a success. Those who were concerned in the municipal life of Warrington were always glad to promote, in any way, the presperity of the town. Warrington was a most enterprising place ; and when they considered that it was within a stone's throw of two great undertakings, which they hoped would be completed in the course of a year or two. the Ship Canal, and the Lan- cashire, Derbyshire. and East Coast railway, they might venture to look forward to years of in- creased trade and prosperity to the town from the ex- ceptional position in whieh it would be placed in regard to both canal and railway routes. (Applause.) Mr. R. Dams proposed in a felicitous speech "The Judges" coupled with the name of the Rev. J. H. Armitstead, vicar of Sandbach.

The Hev. Mr. AnmiTsTses responded. He said he had attended many shows of the Cheshire Agricultural Society and he never saw there such general excellence as there was that day in light horses, both in point of quality and quantity. (Applause.) He thought judg- ing from them, all those interested in horses especially in young horses and brood mares might look forward to . . .
that county ultimately taking a higher place year by year so far as the breeding of horses was concerned. (Applause.)
The company then dispersed.

div.head: NEW. MINISTRY.
div.p: THE NEW. MINISTRY.
MR. GLADSTONE'S FIRST CABINET COUNCIL.

The first official meeting of Mr. Gladstone's Cabinet was held at eleven o'clock yesterday morning, at 1, Carlton-gardens. The first Ministet to join Mr. Glad- stone was Mr. Arnold Morley, who was followed by Lord Herschel!, Mr. John Morley, Earl Spencer, the Marquis of Ripon, Lord Kimberley, Sir William Har- court. and Mr. Campbell-Bannerman. Sir Charles Lennox Peel visited Carlton gardens, this morn- ing, and handed Mr. Gladstone his seal of office. The meeting was also attended by Lord Rosebery, Mr. H. H. Fowler, Mr. Shaw-Lefevre, Mr. Asquith, Sir George Frevelyan, H. Acland, and Mr. Mundella, who arrived later, the latter not reaching Carlton-gardens until afternoon. The Cabinet, which had been princi- pally summoned to discuss the future course of action of the Government, broke up about one o'clock, when the members drove off to their respective offices. It is understood that unless anything untoward happens no further meeting of the Cabinet will be held until the end of October.

div.head: PRESCOT AND ELECTRIC MIMING.
div.p: PRESCOT AND ELECTRIC MIMING.
ADOPTION BY THE LOCAL BOARD.

For several weeks the authorities at Prescot hive had under donitideration'a proposal to abolish the old method of lighting the town by gas, and to substitute for it the,new system of eletric lighting. At the last meeting of the Prescot Local Board some correspondence with the British Insulated Wire Company, whose works are at Prescot, was read. The firm wrote that the town of Prescot was favourably situated for lighting by electricity, and offered to light the town and district with twelve arc lamps and 70 incandescent lamps at a cost of £350 per annum for five years. They proposed to light the junctions of the most important streets with the arc lamps, ten of which would be of 2000 candle power, and two of 800 candle power; and the 70 incan- descent lamps would be placed in the smaller or back streets, or in such places in the principal thoroughfares as might be found desirable. The estimate of the firm included everything connected with the lighting of the town. The board ultimately decided to hold a special meeting for the consideration of the subject, and this meeting was held on Tuesday night. In the absence of the Chairman (Mr. C. Spencely) the chair was occupied by Mr. James Hewitt. —The Clerk (Mr. Cross) read a further letter from the British Insulated Wire Company in respect to the hours of lighting and other details, and a communication was also read from the chairman of the board expressing the opinion that the present proposals were indefinite, and suggesting that the matter might again be adjourned.—Mr. James Berry and Mr. Joseph Preston asked questions in regard to the cost of gas, and Mr. E. Dyson replied that the total cost for the year ending 31st March last was £204 Bs. 3d. ; while repairs, wages, &c., made the total ex- penditure into £312 10s. 81. The Gas Company, how- ever, had offered to make a reduction of 2d. per 1,000 feet, which would amount to about a 3s. Bd. on the consumption of last year.—Mr. Berry said he did not think there was any need to waste more time discussing the question. Science had made vast progress of late, and it was now admitted by all that electric lighting had a considerable advantage over gas. Be proposed that the offer of the British In- sulated Wire Company for the lighting of the district with electricity be accepted, and that a contract be en- tered into between the Board and the company for carrying it out.—Mr. J. Blundell seconded.—Mr. Dyson said they ought not to lose sight of the effect it would have on the rates. There had been many complaints about the high rates, and if the rates were increased by the adoption of electric lighting there would be more grumbling.—Mr. Berry urged that the Board ought to look at the question from a commercial point of view. They would obtain full value for their money, and the difference in the cost would be very slight—Mr.he room,ye° man, representing the Arm, was called and in reply to a question, explainer' airch)athttohlaetoiff the ' Board decided to adopt electric tlnie new arrangements could be comp' d and the district supplied with the light in the o oourse ofab of the one montb.—Mr. Dyson, with the view f testing feeling of the Board, moved an amendment that the. tender of the Gas Committee for the lighting of the town by gas be accepted.—This received no .seconder, and the resolution of Mr. Berry was carried unanimously.

THE LABOUR WAR IN AMERICA. SCENES OF BLOODSHED. KNOXVILLE, THURSDAY 9 p.m.—News has been re- ceived that the miners at 'Coal Creek to-day made tvni attacks upon the soldiers under the command of Colone Anderson, but were repulsed on both occasions. 'old fighting is reported to have been attended by consider- ' able bloodshed. A local journal punlishes a despatO 1 announcing that a third attack was made on Colonel Anderson's camp, and was repulsed, each side losing heavily. Five hundred of the Militia and twiner; ous citizens of this place are hurrying forward to relieve Colonel Anderson. Meanwhile great ex- citement prevails, and business is at a standstill. An outsider, indeed, could scarcely distinguish between the existing state of things and civil war. Although the wires to Coal Creek have been cut, advice,s which have, been received up to a late hour state that Gatlin" have been fired upon the miners on strike with deawY, effect, and many have been killed or wounded. It simultaneously reported reported that Colonel Anderson is being held under special guard to prevent an angry faction lynching him. There are no details to hand regarding his reported capture. It is stated, however, that the in- cident has tended in no small degree to dkhearten tbe Militia, who are fighting desperately, knowing that car Cure means death at the hands of the mob. Military reinforcements are being hurried forward, but the "Tj ber is few, and it is feared that the forces which le Knoxville in the afternoon will be butchered before hells is available.
